en: The Six-Limbed Yoga (*Ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), titled *Guṇabharaṇī*, together with its supplement (*ṭippaṇī*): Homage to the glorious Kālacakra!
To you whose cloud-mass of all obscurations has been dispelled, and who are the wind that brings to an end the entirety of conceptual constructions—homage to the glorious Kālacakra!

Having prostrated to the Lord Śrī Kālacakra and to the gurus who are venerable due to their qualities, I, [Abhayākaragupta], compose here this *Tippaṇī*, which bears the weight of excellence, concerning the glorious six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*).

Indeed, the teacher Anupamarakṣita, whose mental continuum was purified by the practice of both external and internal sciences, spent twelve years at the glorious Khasarpaṇa through the cultivation of the instruction on the reality of the "wish-fulfilling tree" (*kalpataru*) that is without support (*nirālamba*).
And there, as he failed to attain any special realization and fell into a state of mental distress and sleeplessness, a command from Vajrayoginī came to him.

"Go, my son, to Vikramapura; there you will attain a special realization. Taking that command upon his head, he went to Vikramapura accompanied by a great scholar, the venerable Śrīdhara, who was then his disciple and a virtuous son. There, on a certain festival day at the hour of midnight, having assumed the state of an *avadhūta*, he was directly instructed by the Blessed One: "My son, this is the Reality. Upon merely receiving that instruction, he entered into meditative absorption (*samādhi*). At that very moment, the Blessed One vanished. In the meantime, the night passed and he arose from his absorption. Then that Great Soul, the venerable Guru, said: "The noble light, the full moon of the Lord of the World, has risen in the sky of one's own nature and shines brilliantly in the world."

The illustrious Śrīdhara himself attained it and taught it; that most compassionate Illustrious Guru, having in every way obtained a worthy recipient, graciously bestowed it upon the great scholar Bhāskaradeva. From him, the great scholar, the Illustrious Guru, who was omniscient even in this age of degeneration (kaṣāyakāla), taught Dharmākaraśānti. And from him, I, Raviśrī—who am skilled in the service of the feet of the Illustrious Guru and who am a mine of jewels such as ineffable and faultless compassion—have likewise attained the reality. Such is the lineage of the Gurus.

Thus, by virtue of the request of a true disciple, the master named Ācārya Anupamarakṣita, desiring to compose the *Ṣaḍaṅgayoga*—the cause for attaining the state of a Vajradhara—illumined the *Ṣaḍaṅgayoga* by means of a hymn to his own chosen deity.

"Dispelled," and so forth: "dispelled" means rejected. "All-obscuring" refers to all obscurations (*sarvāvaraṇa*), which are like masses of clouds (*abhrajāla*). In that [state] where such [clouds] have been entirely (*niḥśeṣasaṃkhyayā*) and completely (*sāmastyena*) destroyed—since conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), being of a wandering nature, is like a bird or the wind (*vāyu*, *nabhasvān*)—therefore, in the element of one's own space (*svākāśadhātu*), upon the surface of the autumnal, stainless sky, the Lord of the World (*lokeśvara*), whether he be the Buddha or Padmapāṇi, has arisen and appeared as his own light; that very light, being the light of auspicious bliss, is the full moon because it gladdens all people.
And everything [described] regarding the moon should be applied here as well.

But for one whose purpose is respectful, [the goal] is that which is free from the net of clouds of all obscurations and devoid of the notions of grasped object and grasping subject; having thus stated these two limbs of yoga, withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they say: "Withdrawal is the non-engagement of the ten pairs of sense objects and sense faculties within the body; wisdom (*prajñā*), reasoning (*tarka*), investigation (*vicāra*), delight (*rati*), and immovable bliss (*acalasukha*) constitute meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), as well as one-pointedness of mind."

Thus, by means of the complete enumeration, he is the end, the ceased, the bound, the absence of outward departure, devoid of support for the cessation of saṃsāra; the pervasive Lord who is non-different from those two, the Void, yet consisting of compassion, and having transcended all states. Furthermore, "speech" (*vāk*) refers to conceptualization characterized by eighty-four thousand moments of mind along with their latent impressions; "wind" (*vāyu*) refers to the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths.
By this, the limbs of *prāṇāyāma* (breath control) and *dhāraṇā* (concentration) have been explained.

Likewise, breath control (prāṇāyāma) is the stumbling of the two paths; the entry of the breath into the middle [channel] is the entry of the vital force (prāṇa) into the drop (bindu), for it is the cessation of both movements; and concentration (dhāraṇā) is one-pointedness of mind.

Thus, one’s own self is the mind; that itself is the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), the universal image (*viśvabimba*) perceived in all its aspects. By this, the limb of recollection (*anusmṛtyaṅga*) is explained. And so it is said: "The vision of Caṇḍālī which indeed occurs within the body is recollection in the sky.
And having arisen from the touch of Caṇḍālī, it has come from the crown wheel (*uṣṇīṣacakra*).

Because it is a luminosity free from appearances, it is the self-light of all worlds; because it is the support for all of them, it is held by all Buddhas upon their heads and at the tip of the vajra, and thus it is Lokeśvara; because it is the semen of the sixteen joys, it is the full moon. This is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). By this, too, a limb of meditative concentration (*samādhy-aṅga*) is stated: through the power of immutable bliss consisting of wisdom and method, there is meditative concentration upon the image of gnosis (*jñānabimba*).
Thus they say; by this [statement] that "it shines" and "it conquers," the act of salutation is implied, and from that it is understood that one is bowing down toward it.

Now, demonstrating the subject matter of this six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga) by way of the absence of contradiction, he says "He who," and so forth. That which is the Lord (nātha)—the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), the continuous succession of birth and death, which is conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya);

and its cessation, which is ultimate truth (paramārthasatya)—is the object of support (ālambana) for each of those [two] respectively. Because he is devoid of that, he is likewise [devoid of objects].

For this very reason, by means of those two—the conventional and ultimate truths—the mind (*citta*): [in *T₁* we read *svātmacittam* (one’s own mind)]. Therein: [in *G* it is *tatra*; in *T₁* it is *candra* (moon)]. From the touch of *Caṇḍālī*: [in *G* it is *caṇḍālyasparśād*; in *T₁* it is *gtum mos reg pa las*]. *°candraḥ*: [in *T₁* it is *zla ba*; in *G* it is *°candaḥ*]. Afterwards, a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*): [this is a conjecture, cf. below, fol. 8b4 and p. 238, note 3]; afterwards, a compound (*samāsa*): [in *G* and *T₁* it is *phyin tshig sdud*]. By this too: [in *T₁* it is *'dis kyang*; in *G* it is *anenānapi*]. Before *jayati*, there is a daṇḍa in *G*. "By that, it is understood that one bows down toward him": [this is a conjecture based on *T₁* (p. 187)]; "by that, it is understood that in this [state] one bows down toward him": *G*; "by that, it is understood that in this [state] one is bowed down" is also possible; another possible emendation, which is much closer to what *G* reads, would be *tena tam praty asmi praṇata iti labhyate* (*asmi praṇataḥ* = *praṇato 'smi*, although the latter is the more common word order in Sanskrit) (H. Isaacson, personal communication). May the Lord—who bestows all happiness upon embodied beings, who is free from conceptual construction, who is without departure, and who is the arising of the mind beyond the mind—adorn the mind of the world.

[Kha] Having taken up a slight conceptualization (*kalpa*), he is like a predator with a firm grip for the sake of devouring; undifferentiated and non-dual in form, he is "yoked in union" (*yuganaddha*). Because the three worlds have a single nature, he is all-pervading (*vibhu*).

He is "empty" (*śūnya*) because he is luminous (*prabhāsvara*) through the emptiness of the empty, the very empty, the great empty, and the universal emptiness; the meaning is that he transcends the nature of even the most subtle atom (*paramāṇu*).

Because he is endowed with the excellence of all aspects, being like a reflection in a mirror, he consists of compassion; the meaning is that he is both "possessing all aspects" and "devoid of aspects."

The meaning is that he is "well-established" by way of non-abiding, his mind unattached to objects having transcended [ordinary] stability. The *bhūmis* are specific stages of the excellence of non-conceptual knowledge; their Lord is the "Lord of the Twelve Bhūmis. Expanding—that is, spreading—the bliss of all beings, which is the bliss of enjoying the five supreme imperishable sensual desires, he is free from conceptual construction (*kalpa*) and devoid of dualities.
He is "without exit" because he is immutable; he is "of immovable form";
he is the "Lord" because he is to be served by the world;
and he is "some [one]" because he is beyond the range of speech.

May he adorn and preside over the mind of the world; the "arising of the mind devoid of mind" (*vicittodaya*) refers to that which arises as the mind of the world—the mind that is without mind—thereby [transforming] the distracted mind.
The contradiction, however, is easy to understand.
The Guru is the Buddha, the Guru is the Dharma, and likewise the Guru is the Sangha;
the glorious Vajradhara is the Guru, for the Guru alone is the cause here.
Thus, preceded by the manifestation of his truly existing qualities, he offers salutation to the venerable Guru, the teacher of the unerring reality, with the words "kiñcit" (something).
*kiñcitkal-* [is the beginning of the verse].
*Parigraha* is the acceptance of even the slightest thing as "mine";

the meaning is that it is the eternal view (*śāśvatī dṛṣṭi*) that "it exists. It is a firm grasping because it is necessarily a cause of suffering for the experience of the miseries of *saṃsāra* within the good realms (*sadgati*). And it has been said: "Even a splinter the size of a sesame seed or a mustard seed causes inevitable pain."
The readings *saukhyam* (which is very common in Kālacakra literature) and *āgatimatām* are conjectures based on the requirements of the meter.

In G we find *akhilasukham* and *gatimatām*. In G II, *'dvaidha*; *'dvedha*: G I. Before *yuganaddha*, a daṇḍa is present in G II. *°sarvaśūnya*; *sarvaśunya*: G. *sthitim*: conjecture; *sthitam*: G. After *nirvikalpakajñāna*, a daṇḍa (perhaps erased) is in G. *dvandva*; *dvanda*: G. *akṣaratvena*: conjecture; *anakṣaratvena*: G, T₁ (*mi 'gyur ba med pa nyid kyis*). *nāthaḥ*: conjecture based on T and T₁ (*mgon po*) (cf. also Grönbold 1969: 16); *nārthaḥ*: G. After *alamkarotu*, a daṇḍa is in G. After *acittacittam*, a daṇḍa is in G. *virodhas*; *virodhās*: G; in T₁ we read: *'gal ba'i don ni go sla'o* ("the meaning of contradiction is easy to understand"). This stanza is also quoted in the *Abhisamayamañjarī* (Dhīḥ XIII, p. 154).

The first half of the verse is very similar to *JS* I, 24ab (*gurur buddho bhaved dharmo saṃghaś cāpi sa eva hi*). *°puraḥsaram*: conjecture based on *T₁* (*sngon du 'gro bar*); *parasparam*: *G*. After *grāsāya*, there is a daṇḍa in *G*. *uktam ca... avassa* is missing in *T₁*; the verse has been restored on the basis of Bagchi 1938: 32, 129–30 (cf. also below, p. 239, note 7).

In section G we read: "Even a single sesame seed's worth of the thorn of worldly existence causes great suffering; its sudden abandonment, however, gives rise to the attainment of the further shore after a long time. Thus, when the true path has been lost, he who points out the image of the sky—the sky-like self that transcends the mind—I joyfully and forever revere that supreme Guru. Therefore, the "glorification" (*kīrtana*) of such a great-souled Guru consists precisely in the proclamation of one's own awakened realization.

For indeed, apart from Arjuna, whose form was shimmering, no blazing crest of smoke is perceived. [g] The abandonment of even that slightest trace of conceptual construction is the abandonment of that; the meaning is that it is the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). That [view] is suddenly discarded without investigation—meaning it is the view of annihilation.

Because it is the cause of suffering for infinite eons and because it is the cause of intense great suffering, its consequences extend for a very long time. Furthermore, it is a precipice, and it is a fall into the Avīci hell and other hells; one falls into it, or it produces and impels one there. And thus it has been said:
"But those for whom emptiness is a [mere] view, they declared to be incurable.

Thus, in this manner, when there is a collapse of the true path and a destruction of the way to liberation, that glorious Guru—who points out and bestows upon his excellent disciples the orb of the sky, which is the universal image in all its aspects beginning with smoke, which transcends the mind, whose nature is non-mind-yet-mind, which is the essence of space and compassion inseparable from emptiness—I praise that most excellent Guru, the glorious teacher; I bow down to him with body, speech, and mind.

"Always with joy," that is, with delight, at the three times of day. [Objection: If the discovery of the true path occurs solely through the grace of the venerable Guru, then one should only perform the glorification of the qualities of the true Guru; why then have you set out to compose this treatise on the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*)?
To this he says "tataḥ" and so forth:

Since this is so, therefore, from that—namely, the glorification of such a Guru, the great-souled one who teaches the path as it truly is and whose nature is supreme compassion—the manifestation of his qualities and the proclamation of one's own awakening is nothing other than the making manifest of the self-knowledge obtained through the Guru’s grace.

He states this very point by means of an illustrative analogy (*arthāntaranyāsa*): For, since no one other than Dhananjaya, who possesses a radiant form, is known to me as the cause of faults, how could a person proceed toward the accomplishment of their desired goal if they act upon the words of a speaker whose intent is not certain? Ministers whose minds are arrogant from grasping at the literal meaning, having abandoned the true path due to their dull intellect, do not perceive even the prohibitions that serve as the doorways to the prescribed rules.

Without the blazing fire, a column of smoke, though bright and firmly rooted, is not perceived; by this it is said that my skill in composing this work arises solely from the grace of the venerable Guru. Now, one might ask: "For you who have attained the path of reality (tattva) free from all conceit, how can there be the acquisition of knowledge of reality? To answer this with the rebuttal that it is merely the inflation of the mind, he says "No" (na).
The ellipsis is: "My pride of understanding does not become a cause of fault."

Since this matter serves as a means for accomplishing the welfare of others by motivating those who seek liberation, my revelation of knowledge is not out of a desire for gain and the like; rather, it is for the sake of engaging those who are terrified by the fear of worldly existence by demonstrating the state of being a refuge. To this end, he states an illustrative analogy (*arthāntaranyāsa*).

When some object that serves as a cause for engagement has been cited—that is, stated—yet remains undetermined and doubtful, how could a person who themselves lacks certainty proceed toward the speaker, the utterer, for the sake of achieving their desired goal? The meaning is: they would not proceed at all. Alternatively, when a statement belonging to the speaker, the utterer, has been cited, those of dull intellect—who, through various commentaries composed by ordinary persons, are arrogant in their understanding of the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) in the many tantras—are like bad ministers who go to hell.

In the *Śrī-laghukālacakra-tantra-rāja*, through the commentary composed by Ārya Avalokiteśvara, there is the realization of the distinction between the interpretable (*neyārtha*) and the definitive (*nītārtha*) meanings. Thus, illuminating the majesty of this sovereign tantra, he says: "The interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) is the meaning according to the literal expression; those who have abandoned the path are unskilled in the distinction between the conventional and the ultimate."

Precisely for this reason, because those of dull intelligence do not understand prohibitions by way of injunctions—that is, through the medium of positive prescriptions—the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, by the command of the glorious Vajradhara and the command of the Blessed Lord Kālacakra, spoke the *Śrī-laghukālacakra-bhagavat-tantra* and recited it in the land of Sambhala.

By this, the greatness of Śrīvajrapāṇi—the requester—is illuminated by implication, as well as that of the teacher and the compiler of the recension. At the command of the glorious Vajradhara, for the benefit of the three worlds, the Lord Mañjuśrī spoke the *Laghukālacakrabhagavattantra* in clear words. And therein, the glorious and greatly compassionate Lord Lokeśvara was emanated; he composed this most pure commentary (*ṭīkā*) in words, which are stainless in their light and purpose.

Having attained that heart of the Buddha-jewel revealed by him, those of meritorious nature, through the service of the nectar of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), shatter the poison of cyclic existence and rejoice. In that [work], which is the locus for the entire mass of all that is to be known and which possesses the designation "Omniscient One" for the Blessed One, even the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)—the source of the reality of beings where even the grass [of worldly views] was [rendered insignificant] as taught by Īśvara and others—is present; it is the mother of the Buddha born from space, whose pure self has utterly destroyed the tree of all proliferating conceptual constructions. And in that Great Tantra (*mahātantra*) known as the *Śrīmān*, there is the glorious Puṇḍarīka, who is the emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Lokeśvara.

Because it indicates all meanings, it is called the *Sarvārthasūcanī* (Indicator of All Meanings); thus he composed the commentary named *Vimalaprabhā*. By means of that commentary, he has clarified and made manifest the Heart of the Buddha-jewel, which is the essence of the instruction on the true path. Having received this from the presence of his venerable Guru, who is the very embodiment of merit, they—by partaking of the nectar of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and by attaining the ambrosia of the supreme fourth bliss (*paramārthacaturthānanda*)—shatter the poison of existence, the great venom of the cycle of birth and death (*ajavamjava*), and lead it to the state of the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*).

For this very reason, they always rejoice because of the uninterrupted bliss of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-sukha*); by this, he also illuminates the greatness of the author of the commentary (*ṭīkākāra*). Furthermore, he demonstrates the majesty of the Sovereign Tantra (*tantrādhirāja*) with the words "all," etc.;

it is said that [this tantra] is the abode—that is, the support—of the entire collection of external and internal branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), which constitute the *ya*-group. And it is stated:

Therefore, there is nothing that was not proclaimed in this sovereign tantra of the *Ādibuddha* which is endowed with the designation "the Omniscient One"—the name "Sarvajña" given by the Blessed Buddha being consistent with its actual meaning—and wherein the jewel-mine of the true reality (*sattattva*) is like straw, due to its lack of essence as it floats away like that taught by Īśvara and others;

and wherein even the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the realization of the emptiness of all phenomena, and the total destruction of those burgeoning and proliferating trees of conceptual construction—which consists in the state of the supreme immutable (*paramākṣara*) flavor—are likewise [proclaimed]. Thus it is.

She is the mother who gave birth to the Buddha— who arises from space, who arises as the universal reflection, and whose pure self has a form unmarked by any conceptual construction— from that very emptiness (*śūnyatā*) which, within the stainless sky of her created [form], suddenly arises as an inseparable unity of existence, non-existence, and both, through a basis that is a blazing fire of intention moistened by vast compassion shimmering in her half-eye, and which follows the sequence of all smoke and other signs.

Thus, for the purpose of clarifying the stage of generation (*utpannakrama*), in accordance with the cultivation of the path of Mahāmudrā, the jewel-like words from the *Śrīmad-Ādibuddha-tantra* and other sources—which bestow the fruit of perfect Buddhahood—are here summarized, as they were spoken in the *Ādibuddha*, the king of tantras within the *Buddharatnakaraṇḍaka*.

Now, teaching the glorious lineage of the Guru which relies upon the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) as the cause for the arising of the signs beginning with smoke, he says: "Vimala... [The verse begins: In that pure sky, free from the veils of clouds and the like, when the half-eye is directed—meaning when the eyes are half-closed and fixed upon the intermediate space—the conceptual mind, which has its support in the heart, devours—that is, renders it devoid of intrinsic nature—from the heart-mind that is moistened by the outpouring of vast compassion.
Therefore, by this, the lineage is described.
And it has been said:
The instruction is that one should not think of anything at all in the darkness;
otherwise, having leaped up and made the mind its root, there is the rubbing [of the eyes] in emptiness.
What could be a better collyrium for those blinded by the cataracts of ignorance than this?
Thus it was said by Saraha-pāda:
"One should regard all phenomena as equal to space;
within the nature of space, one should maintain the state of equanimity."
Thus, by making both with and without parts, one attains unsurpassed awakening.

Indeed, the state of oneness of the vowels and consonants, and of the moon and sun, is the seat of the Vajra-holder; the symbol is not transformed merely by the syllable *hūṃ*, nor is another form of color desired.
By the phrase "of this arisen divine faculty, which has reached the destruction of flux through the syllable," it is stated that the cause is both with-form and formless;
it is the differentiator of existence, non-existence, both, and neither, and is entirely free from the four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) such as existence and non-existence.
The remainder [of the meaning] is that self-experience occurs spontaneously, without depending on the cause of conceptual construction.

That which arises—meaning that which is being produced—is accompanied by all the signs such as smoke and so forth; these signs belonging to emptiness (*śūnyatā*) illuminate the sequence of their arising and reveal the unity of conventional and ultimate truth.

In the *Kālacakra*, within the *Jñānapaṭala*, by means of the verse immediately following the one hundred and twenty-sixth, [it is stated]: "Oneness," and so forth. Because there is a negation of phenomena (*dharma*)—namely, the conceptual construction of the form, color, arms, and posture of the *sahajakāya* arising from syllables, which consists of the transformation of the *āli* and *kāli*, the lotus, moon, and sun seats, and the *hūṃ* syllable into a symbolic sign (*cihna*)—therefore, the "attainment of the supreme immutable gnosis" (*paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*) of the Blessed One is spoken of. The "A-beginning" (*ādi*) is the collection of vowels beginning with *a*, which is the Moon; the "Ka-beginning" (*kādi*) is the collection of consonants beginning with *ka*, which is the Sun. Their "oneness" (*ekatva*) is their unification, which serves as the seat or support. The lotus has the nature of the consonant *pa*; the lunar disk has the nature of the vowel *a*; and the solar disk has the nature of the letter *ra*.

For the Vajrī, who possesses the knowledge of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*), [the notion of] "no" is rejected; likewise, the vajra symbol produced from the transformation of the *hūṃ* syllable, and the dharma consisting of the conceptualization of the deity’s body—its color, arms, faces, and shape—which arises from that [symbol], are not accepted as having the characteristic of being supported (*ādheya*).

This is because they possess the nature of the changing (*kṣara*) due to their characteristic of clinging (*abhiniveśa*), whereas [the reality] has arisen through the unchanging, which is the bliss of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*).

And therefore, for the supreme Lord of Jinas, Vajrasattva, the holder of universal illusion (*viśvamāyādhara*), who has entered the imperishable death (*kṣaranidhana*), who is devoid of the perishable forms and so forth imagined by ordinary people, who is free from arising and cessation, who possesses divine faculties, who has arisen through mastery over the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), who is omniform, whose nature is the bliss of the forms of the three worlds,

and who is the drop (*bindu*)— for him, the Universal Illusion (*viśvamāyā*) is the Mother of All (*viśvamātā*), the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*); [this is] for the supreme Lord of Jinas, the holder of universal illusion, who is the omniform drop.

Since this is so, therefore, by a yogin who delights in the means for achieving supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*), who has received the instructions of a true guru, who has avoided association with the wicked, who has cultivated the signs such as smoke and so forth, who is a beginner, who has purified the central channel, whose mind is bound by supreme affection toward all sentient beings as if they were his only son, who relies upon the mundane and supramundane truths, who is indifferent toward wife, children, and his own body, who has turned away from the enjoyment of the property of the monastery, the vihāra, or the guru, who relies upon the path of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who dwells in the four sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*) of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, who is free from the desire to achieve mundane accomplishments such as rites of pacification, who has received the instructions of a true guru, who has obtained the lineage of the glorious gurus, and who has avoided association with the wicked—that is, who has shunned evil friends.

Because it is cultivated through signs such as smoke, by one who is skilled solely in stabilizing the *bodhicitta* through the cultivation of signs such as smoke; because it is the first engagement, by a beginner (*ādikarmika*); and because the central channel has been purified, by one for whom the central channel is purified—it is said:
Having meditated upon smoke and the other [signs], and having made the mind immovable, one should purify the central channel and then meditate upon the supreme unchanging.

Thus, a *matha* is a residence such as a temple (*chattra*) and so forth; a *vihāra* is the dwelling of the community of monks. Within the element of space, in the universal image (*viśvabimba*), it is like emptiness in all its aspects; therein, it is like a reflection in a mirror, like the visualization of the practitioner.
By means of the vision of non-arisen phenomena, through the vision of phenomena that are non-conceptualized—

because external objects imagined by foolish people do not exist, and because [this vision] is like a dream, a manifestation of the radiance of one’s own mind, appearing as objects while being no different from the mind itself— and because it does not fall within the views of the Vaibhāṣika, Sautrāntika, or Yogācāra schools, it is empty of any investigation into phenomena consisting of an aggregation of atoms.
Because he has distanced himself from the doctrine of nihilism by having moved far away from entering the Cārvāka school, he is one who has kept himself remote from the emptiness of annihilation.

Desiring to ascend to the state of omniscience through that very divine internal bliss, having abandoned the conceptual cultivation of the maṇḍala-circle and so forth, one should proceed by means of the Bodhisattva path consisting of wisdom and skillful means—[a path] characterized by viewing all phenomena as unarisen, like a reflection in a mirror or a prognostic image within the expanse of space; [a path] where the mind perceives objects as resembling a dream, being the radiance of the diffusion of one's own mind; [a path] empty of any investigation into phenomena as being composed of an aggregation of atoms; [a path] where emptiness in the sense of annihilation has been cast far away; [a path] devoted to the phenomena of self-cognizable internal bliss; and [a path] which has abandoned the phenomena of bliss cognizable by the external senses.

One who has obtained the instruction on the path of the wisdom-knowledge of supreme unchanging great bliss does not accept the dharma of conceptualizing the deities of the maṇḍala—along with their bases, supported forms, symbols, colors, arms, and postures.

Thus, one who is solely skilled in stabilizing the mind of suchness, yet is devoid of the [true] path, does not attain reality; rather, one should be devoted to that very dharma which the Tathāgata proclaimed as self-cognizable bliss.
Because of non-attachment to the pleasure arising from the *karmāṅganā* and *jñānāṅganā*, and being devoid of the dharmas of pleasure perceivable by the external senses and self-reflexive awareness,

one who consists of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*), having tasted the passion for a well-disciplined *karmāṅganā*, [should practice] immediately after the arising of the signs such as smoke in order to manifest the limb of meditative absorption (*samādhyanga*).
And it has been said:
Having placed the vajra upon the lotus, one should cause the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to enter the drop (*bindu*);

one should cause the drops to enter the wheels (*cakra*), and one should restrain the vibration (*spanda*) of the drops within the vajra—thus continuously, with a mind absorbed in Mahāmudrā; or else [by means of the following].

With the verse beginning with "tathā" and so forth, [the author] explains the path (*mārga*) by means of the group of Āryā verses stated in the *Vimalaprabhā* commentary; now, with the verse beginning with "tathā mārge" and so forth, he describes the failure to attain reality for one who has strayed from the path.

That which was taught by the Tathāgata—the sixteenfold fourfold division—is the fourth reality, the *Śrīguruvaktra*. A non-yogin does not attain it through various paths of conceptual construction and the like; for "various conceptual constructions" refers to the transformation of the lotus, sun, moon, Rāhu, Kālāgni, seed-syllables, and emblems, as well as the faces, arms, colors, and postures of the *Vīrakrama*, the *Svādhiṣṭhānakrama*, and so forth. By the word "and so forth," [is meant] the doctrines of the annihilation of all phenomena and emptiness. Just as a reflection appears in the element of space, so too the sixteenfold fourfold division [is perceived] through the path of various conceptual constructions and the like.

[1] The yoga of the completion stage (*utpannakrama*), which is free from the conceptualization of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) such as the utterances of *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*, is the reality; there is no other means for realizing that reality.

[2] The reality of this is made manifest in the Chapter on Consecration: first is the union of the fourfold yoga consisting of desire-bliss (*kāmānanda*), trembling, and the syllable; second is the arising of power (*śakti*) which is indeed full bliss (*pūrṇānanda*); third is the flame, the drop (*bindu*), and the whirling, which is the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*); and fourth is the emission (*oddā*), the resonance (*nāda*), and sleep, which is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).
Thus [it is said].
Therefore, by way of conceptual construction, that reality (tattva) is not established, nor is there a so-called "non-reality" of reality that serves as a means (sādhana).
If this is not the means, what else could it be? To this he says:

"arising," and so forth. The means for the reality of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is that by which it is accomplished; the means is reality itself and nothing else, such as the mental construction of a lotus and so on.

What is that reality? It is the yoga of the perfected stage (*utpannakramayoga*), which is devoid of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) as previously described, free from the sequence of entering the womb, and devoid of the mantra "hūṃ phaṭ" and so forth—the word "and so forth" including the conceptualization of mudrās and other such things. He asks: what is that reality? [The answer is: it is the yoga of the perfected stage.

The "arisen" is the "perfected" which is to be attained through the meditation on space; its sequence is the path beginning with smoke and so forth; its yoga is the attachment to the arising of imperishable gnosis together with the image of wisdom.

Now, the Noble One, through non-duality, speaks of the means for perceiving the bodhicitta that is with demonstration, while rejecting the lack of means, beginning with the words "situated in wood" and so forth: Just as fire, though always present within wood, is not seen by means of cutting or splitting, yet is seen therein by rubbing together stalks of grass and palms; even so [is bodhicitta].
[3] Likewise, the appearance of mind is not seen through the means of conceptual cultivation;
it is seen right there through the single union of the female and male organs.

It is not seen by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma) characterized by smoke and other signs through the central channel (madhyavāha); let it be that it is not seen because it is without support for the time being. The meaning of the word "api" (even/also) is [to include] "by means of methods such as cutting and piercing"; here the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*).

Cutting is by means of axes and the like; splitting is by means of tree-splitters and the like. The "means" (upāya) is the door; the arrow is the shaft, the staff, the hand, or the palm—by churning with those two, that fire arises. "Abiding therein" (*tatrastha*) means it abides in that wood used for churning; thus, "abiding therein. Like that, so too is the appearance of the mind (*cittābhāsa*), which is the manifestation of the three realms. It is not seen through the means of conceptual cultivation (*kalpabhāvanopāya*), that is, through the doors of repeatedly directing the mind toward conceptualization. This appearance of the mind is seen through the single yoga of *lalanā* and *rasanā*.
The instrumental case is used here for the sense of "instrument": "the single yoga" is the non-dual yoga; it is stated that this occurs "right there," namely within one's own mind.

Even in the practice of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), let those who are fit take [the essence] by means of the appropriate methods: clarified butter from wood, water from a moonstone, curd from yogurt, ghee from a mass of iron, and unimpaired bliss from the union with a woman's womb.
In the mind, there is nothing to be established, nothing to be rejected, and no decrease or increase within the mind;
the triple world is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, like the sun reflected in water.
Thus, the meaning is that the single mind itself becomes manifold when it has entered into the reflection of wisdom.

Demonstrating this very point, he says: "Therefore, thus... and so forth. That which was stated in the *muktaka* (isolated verses) regarding those who have attained the five limbs beginning with withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*)—namely, that [the practice] is for the sake of clarifying the limb of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) by means of that which is uniquely skilled in stabilizing the *bodhicitta*—is accomplished through the *vidyāvrata* (vow of knowledge) by means of the *vajrāpāta* (thunderbolt-fall), which is the upward-moving semen.
By this path, the yogin easily attains the supreme unchanging accomplishment of all Buddhas, or the innate [bliss] of all female messengers.

"Thus, indeed, smoke... and so forth. That by which the intended causal sign (*nimitta*) is indicated—such as smoke and the like—is the *prāṇāyāma*. The *kumbhaka* consists of the cessation of the three channels above and below; it is the entry of the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) into the channel of consciousness (*cittanadī*) via the central flow. Regarding the "vow of knowledge" (*vidyāvrata*): the vow is primarily characterized by knowledge, namely celibacy (*brahmacarya*). Knowledge is to be accepted from a Guru who has been consecrated by the *svajina* [initiation] and possesses virtuous qualities. This is also stated in the *Abhidhānottara*.
And having obtained another Pukkasi woman, adorned with beauty and youth,
who has practiced the single yoga, knows the samaya, and is firm in her vows;
The knower of mantras himself should practice the vow of knowledge together with her, who is shameless, free from desire, steadfast, devoid of thirst, and without egoism.
Thus, by that "vajrāpāta"— that is, by the falling (āpatana) or striking (stābdhya) of the vajra—
[it means] by the semen (śukra) moving upwards from the maṇi-lotus to the forehead by way of retrograde motion.
And it is said:
"The yogi should always have steady sexual organs and always remain one whose vital essence flows upward; through the practice of Mahāmudrā, he is empowered by the penetrations of the Vajra."
And with twenty-one thousand six hundred supreme syllables.

By means of this path characterized by the six-limbed yoga beginning with smoke (*dhūma*), the practitioner who possesses the yoga of the completion stage attains the innate (*sahaja*). This is the bliss of all Buddhas, devoid of the senses, the supreme accomplishment of the ultimate immutable (*paramākṣara*); for by it, the ultimate immutable is accomplished and produced in its entirety. It is the emptiness of the innate, so-called because it is the *ḍākinīs*—the seventy-two thousand channels whose nature has been stilled—and it is described as being free from the three realms and unstruck (*anāhata*).

But it is not according to worldly convention; rather, the word "or" (vā) signifies that the innate (*sahaja*) state, consisting of the fourth enclosure, is indeed called "unity in emptiness" because of the departure of all enclosures.

Through the conceptualizations of form and so forth, and through the practice of meditating on the mandala circle and other such forms, worldly accomplishments are achieved; how much more so, then, the desired great accomplishment?

The path for pure disciples arises through the grace of the true guru. Now, since it has been stated that the yoga of the *utpannakrama* (the stage of arising) is the reality (*tattva*) and the means of accomplishing reality, and nothing else, one might ask: "Let that alone suffice; what is the use of other [practices] that are of no benefit? To this he says "form" (*rūpa*), and so forth. "The world" (*loka*) refers to the triple realm (*traidhātuka*). That which pertains to it is "mundane" (*laukikī*), and this is "accomplishment" (*siddhi*). Thus, accomplishment is the sovereignty extending as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven. It is accomplished "by means of the mental constructions of form and so forth. Form (*rūpa*) is so called because it is "shaped" (*rūpyate*) or bound; that which has form as its primary object is "form and so forth" (*rūpādi*). The "construction" (*kalpana*) of that is mental action (*mānasaṃ karma*).

In this context, the cultivation of form (*rūpa*) is the action-seal (*karmamudrā*); by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [is meant] gnosis (*jñāna*), and its cultivation is the gnosis-seal (*jñānamudrā*). Through the practice of cultivating the mandala-circle and so forth—wherein the "mandala" is the supporting characteristic (*ādhāra-lakṣaṇa*) and the "circle" is the supported assembly of deities (*adheya*)—the word "and so forth" includes the mantra-seal, posture, and so on. Their cultivation is the act of bringing them into manifestation; their practice is the repeated and persistent application thereof. If this is so, then by this very path all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*) are achieved.
"It is enough with the instruction on the path of smoke and so forth," he says;

"what is it?"—it is the great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*), namely the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā. Is it desired? It is supramundane. What then? What indeed is accomplishment? The meaning is that it is certainly not [attained] without the instruction on the path of smoke and so forth.

Now, one might ask: does this instruction on the path arise for everyone whose minds are intent upon attaining perfect enlightenment from every [source], or rather for only some who are pure and diligent in performing the welfare of the world from a specific [source]? To this he says, "The path," and so forth. A "true guru" (sadguru) is a venerable master (śrīguru); his characteristics have been explained in detail in the *Paramārthasevā*.
For example: he is a meditator (*dhyāyin*) yet free from attachment to becoming; he is a lover (*kāmī*) whose mind is bound to great desire;
he is a practitioner of the great vow (*mahāvratī*) who, even in the union of the bliss of the two organs and in the context of the *mudrā*, has not lost his passion.
The union that has entered the path of the moon and sun, having entered the fire of wisdom through the power of yoga—
that very sprinkling of the nectar of infinite bliss is the glorious Guru, the Vajradhara, the destroyer of the world;
such is the detailed explanation.
From his grace— which is the favor of instruction in reality—

there arises [compassion] for those beings who possess compassion and who always exert themselves for the welfare of others; this jewel of the excellent path has been given by him to a being who was heedless.
The jewel of the excellent path is carried away by the thieves of evil sense-objects for one who has entered the forest of his own home;
and it is carried away by the thieves of doubt, regret, sleep, sloth,
and restlessness for one who has entered the thicket of family life.

Thus it arises for certain pure disciples; those disciples are "pure" because they have abandoned the impurities of ordinary egoism through empowerments (*sekādi*) and the like, and they are "to be instructed" because they are to be guided in performing the welfare of others and so forth. As it is stated in the *Mahāmudrātilaka*: "Just as poison, when being purified by means of mantras and the like, becomes an elixir (*rasāyana*), so too a disciple who is impure becomes pure through empowerments and the like."
Thus, their noble exertion for the welfare of others is "wholesome enthusiasm.
Now, regarding those who have attained the path but are negligent, [the author] speaks of the cause for the loss of that path, beginning with the words "anyathā" and so forth.
This aforementioned Buddhahood is the "path" (mārga), because by means of it, Buddhahood is easily sought or pursued.

It is called a *ratna* because it extends delight (*rati*), like the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇiratna*); it is a jewel because it is difficult to find and because it bestows the fruits of desired objects. It is a "jewel of the excellent path" (*sumārgaratna*); this is a subsequent descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). A "sentient being" (*sattva*) is one who is heedless, acting with negligence, and indifferent to welfare and happiness; such a being sinks into the miserable states of existence (*sadgati*). Any other person who is devoid of qualities such as compassion and whose mind is not inclined toward the welfare and happiness of others is such a being. For him, his own home—which has entered [into the cycle of existence]—and his wife are themselves a forest, a refuge for cruel creatures.

"By the thieves of evil objects": objects (*viṣaya*) are those things such as forms (*rūpa*) and so forth that intoxicate the sense faculties; they are "evil" because they provide little relish, because they are contrary [to the path], and because one serves unrighteousness through a mind of infatuation. They are indeed "thieves" because even the jewel of the excellent path, once given, is stolen—that is, carried away by them.

Not only is the jewel of the excellent path stolen from one who has entered the wilderness of his own home by these [thieves], but it is also stolen from one who has entered the thicket of the household by the thieves of doubt and the like.

The family—consisting of wife, sons, grandsons, and so forth—is a dense forest. It is "dense" because it is frequented by the three: intoxication, delusion, and dharma; because it is harsh in its maturation (*vipāka*); and because one frequents it with a mind of infatuation (*mūrcchā-citta*). Furthermore, there are thieves who are killing, falsehood, taking what is not given, another's wife, harshness, slander, frivolous speech, covetousness, malice, and wrong view. [11] There are also those who commit great evils and minor evils, such as murder, violence, and addiction to the sense faculties.
And by these five groups of five thieves, the jewel is constantly carried away.

Even when the jewel of the excellent path has been ascertained through conditions, there is doubt and hesitation (*vicikitsā*)—the thought, "Is this the excellent path or not?"—and remorse (*kaukṛtya*), which takes the form: "A despicable deed has been committed by me; therefore, I shall not realize the path. Sleep (*nidrā-svāpa*) is that which causes the body and mind to become unworkable (*akarmaṇyatā*); it is what is meant by *styāna-middha*.

Laziness, lack of enthusiasm, restlessness, mental distraction— meaning the wandering of the mind toward cities and such— these are declared by this noble verse to be the impurities of concentration for those cultivating the path;
not only are they carried away by these [impurities], but also by [the misdeeds] such as taking life.
"Jewel" refers to the jewel of the excellent path;
"always," throughout the three times;
"killing" is the slaughter of sentient beings; "false" refers to untruthful speech.

"Taking what is not given" is the seizing of another's property; "another's wife" refers to sexual misconduct; "harsh speech" is the exposing of another's vital flaws; and "slanderous speech" is the utterance intended to divide others by one with an afflicted mind.

Frivolous speech (*sambhinnavacaḥ*) is speech associated with sensual desire and so forth, such as "Alas! Oh! Come here! and the like, which generates passion. Covetousness (*abhidhyā*) is an improper longing for the property of others. Malice (*vyāpāda*) is the intent to kill. Wrong view (*kudṛṣṭi*) is the view that things do not exist.

Likewise, there is the fivefold major evil consisting of violence and so forth; the fivefold minor evil consisting of gambling and so forth; the fivefold [evil] consisting of cow-slaughter and so forth; and the fivefold [evil] consisting of betraying friends and so forth.

"The pentad of attachment to the sense-faculties such as the eye" means that which has five as its measure; thus, "of the pentads" refers to those very five [faculties], and "by those very thieves" is likewise.

Abandon violence, untruth, another’s wife, and the wealth of others; likewise, the drinking of intoxicants is a vajra-noose in saṃsāra that destroys one’s own merit. O Lord of Daityas, these five are evils: gambling, the eating of forbidden food, the recitation of wicked words, and one should not commit the five killings of cows, children, women, men, and the Teacher of the gods and men.
One should not [be led astray] by those many thieves through excessive eating and drinking and various enjoyments.
Even for one who possesses vigor, if they fall into the stupor of negligence, they are carried away; for indeed,
an expert examiner would not show a jewel to another person of little discernment, lest that person, failing to recognize its great value, release the gem from their grasp.

[14] Betrayal of friends, lords, the Teacher of gods and men, and those trusted by the Saṅgha, as well as attachment to the sense faculties—these, O Lord of the World, are the twenty-five vows. Thus, evil action is known here as that which causes obstacles; it is understood to apply even to those who commit the five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*), for not only by these is the jewel of the Excellent Path stolen, but also by excessive eating and drinking and various enjoyments. Here, "excessive eating" (*atyantakhāna*) refers to the consumption of meat and so forth; "drinking" (*pāna*) refers to the drinking of liquor and so forth; and "excessive" (*atyanta*) means characterized by a state of intoxication.
"Objects of enjoyment" (*bhoga*) are things such as garlands and sandalwood paste because they are enjoyed;

"various" means manifold. The word "even" (*api*) has the sense that [objects of enjoyment] carry away even one who possesses vigor—that is, one who is enthusiastic in cultivating the path—not only one who lacks the aforementioned firm vigor.

"Negligence" (*pramāda*) refers to excessive indulgence in food and drink and association with unwholesome friends. Because of that, for one who has reached a state of mental distraction or stupor, [the objects of enjoyment] are indeed carried away.

It has been stated that attachment to existence, enjoyments, and so forth, acts as an obstacle even for those who perform virtuous deeds; indeed, these faults that create obstacles were spoken with reference to one who examines the jewel of the path. But what is the case for one who does not examine that path himself? To this he says "himself," and so forth.

Since he himself is not an examiner, he shows it to another person, a commoner who has committed great sins, so that [the latter] may know: "This is a highly precious great jewel. That man says: "It is not so. Therefore, because of those words—that is, the speech of the commoner—he releases [the jewel] immediately. It is just like this: [the Buddha], having intended [this], spoke [the verse]. *svayam ityādi* (and so forth). (Note: The text contains various orthographic variants such as *aparīkṣakaḥ*, *viṭasya*, *mahārgham*, *mahāratnam*, *jñātum*, *sa āha*, *na bhavati*, *atas tadvākyād*, *viṭavacanān muñcata eveti*, *evam eva*, *bhāvanā*, *atyantakhāna*, *mitrā*, *mātra*, *vikalatām*, *vikalatātām*, and *sandhāyoktā*.)
In the case of those from whom he has the examination of great jewels performed by experts in fine gems,
his own jewel is indeed to be recognized through their pure words.
Māra creates obstacles by assuming the forms of fully enlightened Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
as well as those of fathers, mothers, daughters, sisters, sons, brothers, uncles, and wives.
Therefore, having abandoned the company of thieves, disciples must diligently keep the jewel of the excellent path bestowed by the true guru strictly concealed.

One who is by nature of poor wisdom, even having obtained the priceless jewel of the excellent path, loses it due to the words of a bad friend; thus, the fault of associating with a bad friend has been described even for those seeking to examine the path.

If it is asked, "In that case, how can the jewel of the path be known by one who does not examine it himself?"—it is true that if he causes a great examination of the jewel to be conducted through those who are experts in fine jewels, then by their pure words and non-deceptive speech, it is clearly to be understood and determined as "this is priceless. In exactly the same way, a son of noble family who has attained the path should, having examined it through the words of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), realize "this is priceless," and should follow it rather than abandon it. Thus, reliance upon a spiritual friend is the best for those who cultivate the path.

Thus, even for one who has set out upon the cultivation of the path, the mind does not become stable without abandoning the activities of Māra; therefore, demonstrating that very point, he says "Māra," and so forth.

For Māra, the Evil One, having conjured forms such as those of a Buddha and others, creates obstacles for the practitioner, saying things such as, "This is not the path to awakening; no one has ever emerged by means of this. This should be understood from the *Mārakarmaparivarta*.

Having thus introduced the fault of the deeds of Māra and summarizing everything, he says "Therefore," and so forth. Since this exists as the cause for the theft of the path, therefore, having abandoned even the "thief's family"—which is a figurative expression for doubt and the like—one must carefully keep secret the jewel of the path bestowed by the true guru. *V; parīkṣām: V₁; *V₁; bhaginī: V, V₁; bhagini: VP ed.; parityajya: V; parityajyaḥ: V₁.
Before *sumārgaratna*, there is a *daṇḍa* in G.

To those who know the excellent jewel: conjecture; suratnavettṛsya: G ||
The path has been attained: G; the jewel of the path has been attained: T₁ (the precious path has been attained).
"This is priceless," [saying] thus, having examined it thoroughly—*parīkṣā*: G; *suparīkṣā*: T₁ (*having well and thoroughly examined*)—one should follow it.
After *anubaddhavyo*, there is a daṇḍa in G. *Yathā*; *yāṭhā*: G.
