Having abandoned: G; having completely relinquished: T1 (yongs su btang ste) ||
The jewel of the path is well-guarded: G; the jewel of the excellent path is exceedingly well-guarded: T₁ (the precious path is especially exalted [well-concealed]).
The sequence of heroes and the sequence of self-consecration are not the path to liberation;
the perfectly pure sequence alone has been shown by the Buddhas as the means to liberation.
By whom those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution are gathered through happiness;
[they] are gathered; [it is] all; [it is] all.
The immediate transgressions; the five immediate transgressions.
By those who have desisted from karma: through self-consecration; by means of self-consecration, [it is] not otherwise; the sequence of self-consecration.
Now, if it is thought: "Is it not so that what is called 'simultaneous' is actually non-sequential? And what is called 'non-sequential' is sequential?"—[this is] considered [so] out of contempt.
In the body; in that body. Externally; in the body. The locus of presiding; the presiding locus.
If it is argued that this is not so: [it is] not. [For] Buddhahood is the fruit within this essence-less saṃsāra;
therefore, through its exhaustion, it arises for persons like a ripe plantain fruit, which comes into being through the destruction of the plantain tree.
Just as those beings who are scorpions or crabs bring about the destruction of their own mother,
so too does that mind of yoga become the destroyer of illusion.

Non-dual, immovable, and without succession, it is held to be the supreme syllable, the Great Passion; it is well-known as "Me," and thus the establishment of the sequence of perfect purity has been declared even for those who act for the benefit of the world.

Now, one might object: "Has it not been stated that self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) is the vision of the triple world? Since that vision does not cease, how can Buddhahood, characterized by the cessation of saṃsāra, possibly occur?
To this he says: "Saṃsāra," and so forth.

In the threefold saṃsāra, which is devoid of essence and characterized by falsehood and deception, Buddhahood—characterized by the power of qualities such as omniscience—is the essential fruit. Because of its exhaustion, that is, immediately upon the exhaustion of saṃsāra, how is this so? He says: "like the fruit of the plantain tree. Just as when the plantain tree is devoid of essence, a ripe fruit becomes the essence through the destruction of the plantain tree, so too is Buddhahood.
Now, it might be objected: "The thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is held to be the means of achieving Buddhahood;

and according to the statement that 'the reality (*tattva*) is the means of achieving reality,' since that [thought] arises from illusion (*māyā*) and exists as ignorance (*avidyā*), being itself unreal (*atattva*), how can it be the means of achieving Buddhahood? To this, he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "scorpions" (*vṛścika*) and so forth: scorpions are *śūka*-insects; crabs are *karkaṭas*. Just as those [insects] would be the destroyers of whichever mother they belong to, so too is the mind of yoga destroyed. Yoga is the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of wisdom and means; the mind within that is the fourth consecration (*abhiṣeka*), which is coemergent (*sahaja*). That [mind] becomes the destroyer of whichever illusion (*māyā*) it comes from—that illusion characterized by ignorance and the nature of death. Thus, by the cessation of illusion, the non-returning of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is stated for the sake of encouraging the practitioners of reality (*tattvayogin*).
Now, it might be objected: "Is it not the case that *bodhicitta* here is said to be the seminal essence (*sukradhātu*)?
How then can it be described as the means for achieving Buddhahood, which is insentient (*ajaḍa*) and the knowledge of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣarajñāna*)?
This is true, so it was said.

"One should accomplish the supreme syllable by means of the nature of the immutable seminal essence (*śukrākṣara*). Because of this statement, [the author], manifesting the sixteenfold fourfold division of this very reality—the mind of yoga—in the form of the supreme syllable, says "non-dual" (*advaya*) and so forth.
"Non-dual" means that which does not possess a duality, namely, the mind of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Then, from that: therefore.
Plantain fruit; plantain fruit.
The supreme syllable; the supreme imperishable.
suviśuddha°: (extremely pure); svaviśuddha°: ||
In saṃsāra; in the wandering through saṃsāra.
In that which has the nature of falsehood and deception;
Because it has arisen from illusion; and because it has arisen from illusion, that [is so].
śūkakīṭāḥ: conjecture; sūkakīṭaḥ:
[variant]; karkaṭā; karkkaṭaḥ: [variant] ||
Of the female possessor of attributes; of the female substratum.
*māyopaśamena*: conjecture; in [the manuscript] we read *sgyu ma dang bral bas*; *māyopamena*: [conjecture]. *°yoginām*: conjecture (see also); *°yoginyām*: [manuscript reading].
For the sake of consolation; for the sake of encouraging: II [of one who is] not dull-witted (*ajaḍasya*); [of one who is] not agitated (*majalasya*).

That which does not exist [in something] is "non-dual" (*advaya*); in our text we read: *gang la yod pa ma yin pa de gnyis med do*. That which exists only slightly is "subtle" (*tanu*). Knowledge that is the absence of the existence and non-existence of entities is "Being" (*sattva*) and "Samantabhadra."
The one without conflict, the great conflict, the innate, the bearer of the drops of glorious bodhicitta,
the glorious Kālacakra-vajra, the yoga whose nature is wisdom and means.
Thus, this Vajrayoga, which has been practiced, taught, and chanted by immeasurable Sugatas, as well as by all the Bodhisattvas who hold the supreme vajra and are knowers of mantra—

at the outset, one must serve a Guru who is likewise a holder of the commitments (samayin), mounted upon the Vajrayāna, a meditator on reality, free from greed, devoid of defilement, patient, virtuous, abiding in the [right] path,
the giver of the way to disciples, the remover of the fear of hell, and in truth a practitioner of celibacy (brahmacārī).
He is the Vajra-staff of the Māras, and he is renowned as Vajrasattva upon the surface of the earth.
Because he does not waver from the lotus, he is "Immovable" (Acala).
Because he has no lineage—that is, no partiality toward either wisdom or means—he is "Without Lineage" (Ananvaya).

Because it bestows unsurpassed bliss, it is "desired"; this is the fourth yoga. Because of the cessation of twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths, it is the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*). Because there is no staying or going between passion and dispassion—the white and the black—it is the great passion (*mahārāga*). Because it is free from both cause and form, it is the absence of both existence and non-existence. Because it perceives all objects of knowledge, it is "gnosis" (*jñāna*); this is the third yoga. Because it is unattached to the welfare of beings preceded by bringing joy to the world, it is "sentient being" (*sattva*). Because it brings about excellence in the beginning, middle, and end, it is "Samantabhadra."

Because he is free from the conceptual constructions of Māra and the afflictions (*kleśa*), there is no *raṇa*—that is, no internal or external verbal discourse, nor any clamor, nor any battle consisting of the lion’s roar of liberation; thus he is *araṇa*.
Because his nature is that of the unstruck sound (*anāhatadhvani*), he possesses a great *raṇa*—a great sound—and is therefore called *mahāraṇa*; this is the second yoga.

Due to his avoidance of worldly conduct, he is *sahaja*; due to the exhaustion of the obscurations of the four bodies (*kāya*), he is the holder of the glorious drops of bodhicitta (*bodhicittabindu*).

Because emptiness and compassion are inseparable, the glorious Kālacakra-vajra is the yoga consisting of wisdom and means, since he is fully endowed with the accumulations of gnosis and ethical discipline; this is the first yoga.
Now, for the sake of propitiating the Guru, he states the examination of the Vajrācārya.
Regarding the word "at the beginning": here, in this Mantra system, disciples who desire mundane and supramundane accomplishments must serve a Guru and examine him thoroughly; thus it is said.
Because of his protection of the *bodhicitta*, he is to be served according to the commitments (*samaya*) and propitiated with one's sons, wife, and so forth.

Mounted upon the Vajrayāna, mounted upon the Mantrayāna, and because he cultivates the wisdom of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara-jñāna*), he is a meditator on reality (*tattvadhyāyin*); because he is indifferent toward his own body, including all sons, wives, and so forth, he is free from greed; [he is] the non-existence of existence and non-existence (*bhāvābhāvābhāva*).
One whose nature is patience; one who is cool through patience.

"It does not move" means it is "unmoving"; this is the state of great passion (*mahārāga*) with its formal aspect (*sākāra*). This is the third yoga. "Sprinkled" (*prakṣedita*) and "scattered" (*prakṣetrita*)—this is the second yoga. Worldly conduct, worldly meditation, the morality of knowledge, and knowledge itself are absent. One should propitiate that which is mundane, supramundane, and conventional. Regarding the vehicle of mantras (*mantrayāna*), one who is prior to [the vehicle] of mantras is non-greedy; "without punishment" (*adaṇḍa*) is found in the manuscript G. Here, perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) are of two kinds. That which is the support of the deity through the yoga of reality is perception; like the moon in the sky, it is the manifold body of enjoyment (*saṃbhogakāya*).

When an object is not directly perceived, inference is like a corpse in that it is not the reality; for it is a conceptual construction to be shown in paintings and the like for the sake of meditation by yogis whose intellects have not yet matured.

O Lion, according to the disposition of sentient beings, there are two kinds of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) for yogins regarding the focal point of the deity. Of these two, direct perception and inference, that which is direct perception arises from the yoga of reality like the moon in the sky, appearing as a multitude of enjoyment bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*) like a constellation of stars. It is perceivable by the eyes of flesh and so forth, resembling an illusion or a dream, and consists of the three worlds throughout the three times.

In this regard, first the beginner yogin perceives the universal image with the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*), being devoid of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*). Thereafter, he perceives it with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) by virtue of the range of the superknowledges. Then, he perceives it with the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) by virtue of the range of those free from passion (*vītarāga*). Finally, he perceives it with the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*) by virtue of the range of the bodhisattvas.

Then, by means of the eye of wisdom (*jñānacakṣus*), he perceives—through the power of the higher mental state (*avadhicitta*) of a perfectly awakened Buddha—that [the disciple] is liberated from all substrata (*upadhi*).

Thus, the five eyes of the Tathāgata, beginning with the fleshly eye, have been described. Having attained the vision of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), he is stainless due to the removal of defects such as passion and the like. One whose conduct is natural (*svābhāvikī pravṛttiḥ*) and independent of results is one whose morality is patience (*kṣāntiśīlaḥ*). He who abides on the path of the Buddhas is "abiding on the path" (*adhvavartin*); being a teacher who has been propitiated, he becomes the giver of the path to disciples and the remover of the fear of hell.
And he is, in reality, a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) who has attained the bliss of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣarasukha*).
He is the "Vajra-staff" (*vajradaṇḍa*), like a staff of adamant, because of his power to destroy the four Māras.

And that venerable Guru, possessing the aforementioned characteristics, is renowned on the surface of the earth as Vajrasattva by means of his emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), because he is the embodiment of the empowerment of Vajrasattva.
Now, the focal point of the deity for the sake of attaining both mundane and supramundane accomplishments is described.

"Direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) means that through the yoga of reality (*tattvayoga*), by means of the yoga of the meditation on the universal image (*viśvabimba*), like the circle of stars, within a drop (*bindu*) having the form of a blue jewel and a lunar disc, preceded by the manifestation of the infinite, infinite *saṃbhogakāya*s of the Buddhas, there occurs the vision of the three realms—pots, cloths, and so forth—by the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*), even when obstructed by a hundred *yojanas*. Here, that which is "the moon" (*uḍu*) would become [the vision]; it would arise from the yoga of reality as the universal image (*viśvabimba*). By mastery, by mastery, the mind (*citta*) [is purified]; thus all residual substrates (*sarvopadhi*) [are removed], and the five eyes of the Tathāgata have been explained. Before the venerable Guru, for the sake of accomplishment (*siddhaye*), all sentient beings are like those blind from birth regarding the object of the vision of emptiness; such is the rule for the meditation on reality (*tattvabhāvanāniyama*).

Furthermore, when the reality is not directly perceived, inference is a conceptualization that is unreal, like a dead body; thus, it must be shown [to the mind] through paintings and so forth. Having painted a mandala circle of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—either as a painting, a sculpture, or a cast image—with a fixed form, it is to be shown for the sake of meditation by those beginner yogins who are dull-witted; such is the rule for the meditation on conceptual constructs. Service (*sevā*) occurs through the five nectars and so forth, through the oceans and vajras, and through mantra recitation and so forth, as well as through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other [limbs of yoga]. Accomplishment (*upasiddhi*) occurs through the nectar born from the vajra-lotus.

The meditation on the union in a single flavor with the three vajras and the lotus by means of Ānanda and the others constitutes the *sādhana*; indeed, when there is union with wisdom (*prajñā*), the *mahāsādhana* arises through the non-emission of the seminal essence (*acyuta*) via the subtle yoga.
In this context, the beginner must first perform the *sevā* (service) according to the ritual procedure for accomplishment.

Regarding the statement "the *sevā* is performed with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth," externally, the five nectars are excrement and the rest; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), cow’s urine and the rest are included. By consuming these, the *sevā* is performed for the purpose of pleasing the deity. Internally, the five nectars are the five aggregates (*skandha*); by the word "and so forth," the five sense-faculties are the five lamps. The *sevā* is the state of non-dependence upon them, which is the renunciation of craving for the body and material things. Through that *sevā*, the deities become granters of boons, not by the consumption of excrement and such.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the thunderbolt-like ocean":
it refers to one who perceives the lack of dependence on the enjoyment of the body, the lack of dependence on the enjoyment of speech, and the lack of dependence on the enjoyment of the mind.

By means of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), specifically the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), he perceives forms that are extremely subtle and concealed within infinite world-systems; this is his mastery (*vaśa*), which is his power (*sāmarthya*).
With the Buddha-eye, which knows the minds of others;
with the wisdom-eye, characterized by non-conceptualization regarding all phenomena;
and with the knowledge-eye, which perceives all things in all their aspects.
Other beings are of limited vision;
[the corpse] is like a dead body because it lacks movement and pulsation— [a corpse] fashioned from clay or similar materials, or cast from bronze or similar metals.

The five [substances] beginning with feces are the five roots of the *viraśuṃā*; the five beginning with cow dung are the five products of the cow's digestion. In the inner self (*adhyātman*), these are the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*), and the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*).

And it is said: after *iti* in V, we find *rajñānasiddhau vaktavya iti*; furthermore, that [passage] is missing. *Citraṃ sambhavati sevā pañcāmṛtādyair iti* is shown by one who perceives through supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and so forth, by one who perceives the most subtle, by one who has the vision of the *osamdarśanā*: the power of mastery (*vaśa-sāmarthya*) is missing in *°sarvavastudarśinā*; *osarvavastudarśanā*: before *calana°* there is a *daṇḍa* in *viraśumāmū°*; *viraśumāmu°*: *adhyātmani*; *adhyātmanaḥ*: *pañcāmṛtāni*; *pañcāmṛtādi*:
the five sense faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*); *pañcendriyāni*: *°pradīpāni*.

"Pradīpām": Service characterized by detachment from the pleasure of falling [from the state] and involving body, speech, and mind—meaning restraint—is the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). By this, the deities become granters of boons, not through longing for worldly existence or enjoyments, nor merely through the recitation of mantras and so forth. Here, "recitation of mantras" (*mantrajāpa*) refers to the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇasaṃyama*); by the word "and so forth," the yoga of exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*) is included. Constant service by means of that [yoga] makes the deities granters of boons, not by unrestrained breath or idle chatter. This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Furthermore, according to the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), the recitation and other practices should be performed with a rosary and so forth for the sake of ordinary accomplishments (*sāmānyasiddhi*).

Now the *upasādhana* is described, beginning with "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth. Here, for transmigrating beings, "food" (*āhāra*) is the grasping of objects such as forms by means of the sense faculties such as the eyes; the abandonment of that is called "withdrawal. In the empty image (*śūnyatābimba*), the grasping of other objects such as forms by means of other [faculties] such as the eyes—[the eyes] consisting of flesh and so forth—is the *upasādhana*. Likewise, meditation (*dhyāna*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and concentration (*dhāraṇā*) constitute the *upasādhana* through the non-falling nectar produced from the vajra-lotus. According to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), this is the accomplishment of *upasādhana*; according to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), it is through the external offering to the deity. Thus is the accomplishment of *upasādhana*.
That white stream which falls from the drop day and night is my *māmakī* wine; it is not liquor, nor is the constant flashing of the eyes and other senses ever "meat.
This is the service of the five nectars performed by the deities who have entered their own family-ground within the pure body.
It is the bliss of union in the innate state (*sahaja-bhūmi*) through the entry of the mind into emptiness, and not [union] in a womb.

Thus, the yogas of exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*)—characterized by the observation of the exit of the syllable *ĀḤ*, the entry of the syllable *OṂ*, and the abiding of the syllable *HŪṂ*—are for the sake of attaining common accomplishments (*sāmānyasiddhi*) through unrestrained and non-stabilized [breath], and for the sake of worldly accomplishments such as pacification (*śānti*) and so forth;
"taking food" (*āhāra*) refers to its manifestation before one.

Service (*sevā*) consists of the body, speech, and mind being indifferent to the pleasure of falling away (*cyavana*), which is the antidote to manifesting ordinary forms and so forth. [This is] a conjecture based on *kāyavākcitta*. Regarding *kāyavākcitta*: by means of this deity... [before *na prāṇena* there is a daṇḍa]. In the phrase *vāgjalpiteneti*, [it means] "again" (*punar*). [The sequence] beginning with "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*) refers to the abandonment of that. Thus, [by means of] meat and so forth, [one abandons] other forms and so forth (*anyarūpādi*). The term *anyarūpādi* is commented upon in the section on *dhāraṇā*. By means of the "unfallen" (*acyutena*), [there is] accomplishment (*siddhiḥ*). Puṇḍarīka does not comment on this verse regarding the drop (*bindoḥ*). Day and night (*dinaniśam*). No. Cow-dung (*gokv*). Of the eyes and so forth (*cakṣurādeḥ*). By the deities who have gone into the pure body (*śuddhakāye*), there is bliss in the ground of the innate (*sahajabhuvi sukham*). (The innate mind-bliss). The "yogas" are the yogas. In this context, we find the yoga of retention (*kumbhakayogaḥ*). Departure (*nirgama*). Now, the practice (*sādhana*) is stated.
"Ānanda," and so forth.

Here, the three vajras—consisting of the drops (*bindu*) of body, speech, and mind—having attained the single flavor (*samarasa*) within the lotus, constitute the meditation; this is the "means of accomplishment" (*sādhana*). The meaning is that the abiding of these drops occurs in the heart, the navel, and the secret place.
Thus is the means of accomplishment.
Then, when the unchanging bliss arises in the embrace of wisdom (*prajñāsaṅga*), that indeed is the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*). Because of its connection with the subtle yoga— that is,
through the union of the semen (*śukra*) upward within the *suṣumnā* channel— it is called "great accomplishment" according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Furthermore, according to the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), there is a fixed rule that [the object] is a mustard seed or the like at the tip of the nose within the dharmodaya of wisdom;
in this way, it becomes the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*).

First, indeed, is the awakening to emptiness; then, moreover, is the gathering of the lunar drop (*candrabindu*), and from that, the arising of the image. Therefore, the placement of syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*) by means of the families of the excellent essences is the common service (*sāmānyasevā*).
With the oceans and the vajras, this is the middle practice with its ritual components; likewise, the means (*upāya*) here becomes fourfold, being soft or firm according to the parts of the ritual.

In the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), first comes the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatābodhi*); the meaning of "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*) is that which constitutes the interval between sentient beings' relinquishing the aggregates at the end of death and their grasping the aggregates pertaining to rebirth.

"Other form and so forth" refers to supramundane form and so forth that transcends the nature of atoms; "meditation" (dhyāna) is characterized by the bliss of being unmoved by the delight of wisdom, reasoning, and deliberation; "breath control" (prāṇāyāma) is characterized by the cessation of the movement of the moon and sun; "retention" (dhāraṇā) is characterized by the restraint of the breath within the drop (bindu) by way of the coming and going [of the winds] through the secret place, navel, heart, throat, and forehead; "the vajra-lotus" is the crown-lotus (uṣṇīṣapadma), because [the drop] has arisen there; therefore, "by the nectar born from the vajra-lotus" means by the non-emitted bodhicitta.
"Attained to the equal flavor of the lotus" means having become of one flavor within the pericarp of the lotuses of the heart, navel, and secret place; by this, the *binduyoga* is taught.
"The *suṣumnā* channel, [known as] *śaṅkhinī*, above that, through the union with semen from the movement of the *bodhicitta*"—by this, the *sūkṣmayoga* is taught.
Now, the practice of service (*sevā*) and so forth is described according to the distinctions of "mild" (*mṛdu*) and so on,
beginning with the words "In the beginning," etc.

"By the abandonment of the aggregates" means by the abandonment of the present body. "Upapatti-ihānandādyaiḥ": this is the reading suggested by the verse. "Ihānande khalu" (in the joy of this world), "ity" (thus), "punaḥ" (again), "nāsikāgre" (at the tip of the nose), "tathaiva" (just so), "yad antarālam" (that which is in between) is *pratyāhāra*. After *dhyānam*, there is a *daṇḍa* in the manuscript *°niścalasukha°*. "*Lakṣaṇah*" (the characteristic). In the *bindu*, the breath (*śvāsa*) is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇā*); the characteristic (*lakṣaṇam*). [G] "Because it has arisen there" (*tatroditatvāt*; because of its having arisen from that). [G I] "Because it has arisen from that" (*tadroditatvāt*). [G II] "*Kulisa°*" (thunderbolt); "*śuliśa°*". [G II] "The *suṣumnā* channel is the *sankhinī*"; "*susumanā samkhini*". [G II] "And so forth. [T₁] A *daṇḍa* is placed before "*vārtamānika°*". "A single moment of emptiness is the vision of the three worlds; that is called 'emptiness'."

*Khalu* means "certainly. Then, after that moment, "the gathering of the moon-drop" (*candrabindu*) refers here to the gathering (*saṃgraha*) of the drops of semen within the mother's womb by the *ālayavijñāna*. From that gathering of the semen and so forth, "the arising of the image" (*bimbotpatti*) means the completion of the embryo over seven months; the meaning is the completion of the body.

Then, with the six aggregates (*ṣaṭskandha*) consisting of the most excellent essences, the beginner should meditate upon the arrangement of syllables for the eyes and so forth, as well as their engagement with objects such as form; likewise, even in the practice of the deity (*devatāsādhana*), one should cultivate that which is conceptual in nature. This is the "general service" (*sāmānyasevā*). With "the oceans and the vajras"—that is, by means of the perfected vajras of body, speech, mind, and gnosis—there is the "intermediate accomplishment" (*madhyamasādhana*) and the production of the vital breath (*prāṇaniṣpatti*). Here, the method (*upāya*) becomes fourfold: in the limb of service (*sevāṅga*) it is soft; in the limb of near-accomplishment (*upasādhanāṅga*) it is firm; and likewise in the limb of accomplishment (*sādhanāṅga*) it is so until the limit of sixteen years; this is the rule.

"Because of the grasping of the shoulder [of the mother] by the shoulder [of the father]" means because of the grasping of the future state of existence. That which is the interval between these two, characterized as the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), is the vision of the three realms of existence, the direct perception of the three existences.

It is the gathering of the *ālayavijñāna*, which is the substratum of all latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). It is the entry of the mind into the midst of the drops of semen and blood; it is called "gathering" because of the seizing of the drops of semen within the mother's womb. Regarding the phrase "by seven months," this is stated generally; in terms of its actual nature, it is said to be "by nine months" through the illustration of the womb in the practice of deity yoga (*devatāsādhana*).
By the words "then" (*tena*) and so forth, there is an indication of the three limbs beginning with the *upasādhana*:

by means of the six aggregates characterized as form, sensation, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and gnosis (*jñāna*), this is the general service (*sāmānyasevā*), which is the service for worldly accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*);
likewise [are] the *upasādhana*, the *sādhana*, and the *mahāsādhana*.
Therefore, by the passage beginning with "the ocean," etc.,
it is stated that there is the accomplishment of the vajras of body, speech, mind, and gnosis;
this is the middle sādhana, which is the *upasādhana*.

Because the means (*sādhana*) is qualified by the term "middling" (*madhyama*), it is for this very reason explained that "the accomplishment of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) occurs here. Regarding the phrase "the method is fourfold," this refers to the previously mentioned service (*sevā*) and near-accomplishment (*upasādhana*), meaning the fourfold [stages] beginning with "mild" (*mṛdu*). Among those four, it is applied in two ways here within service and near-accomplishment; it is to be applied in both ways within the accomplishment (*sādhana*) and the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*). For this very reason, he says: "the limb of service" and "the limb of near-accomplishment," and "mild and firm" refers to the service and near-accomplishment just mentioned, as well as the accomplishment and great accomplishment to be described hereafter.
*tribhavadarśanam*: V3, VP, G; *tribhuvanadarśanam*: SUȚ, equally possible.
*devatāsādhane*: V3, SUȚ; in T we read *lha'i rnal 'byor la* (= *devatāyoga*).
*kalpanātmakam*: V3, T; *kalpanām ekām*: SUȚ.
°Because of the grasping of the aggregates; because of the non-grasping of the aggregates: GI Because of the grasping of future existence; because of the non-grasping of future existence: G ||
grahaṇam; grahaṇam: G ||
The universal; from its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*): G; in T1 we read *spyi'i ngo bo las* (= *sāmānyasvarūpataḥ*).
Before *garbhanidarśanena*, there is a *daṇḍa* in G. Regarding *jalanidhītyādi*:
in G II, *°vajra°* is missing from both G and T.
In the manuscript G, there is a daṇḍa after *atre* and another daṇḍa before *upāyaḥ*.
This is to be applied in two ways: first, as a conjecture; second, it is to be applied later—both as the practitioner (*yogin*) and as the method (*upāya*). In T₁ [D1], we read:
"Regarding the phrase 'fourfold,' the two types, beginning with the small, are to be applied subsequently to both the practice (*sādhana*) and the great practice (*mahāsādhana*)."
Before *sādhanamahāsādhanayoḥ*, there is a daṇḍa in G; *aha*: conjecture based on T₁ (*gsungs pa*); *hi*: G I; *sevāṅga*: G II; *sevāṅge*: G II; *vakṣyamāṇena*: conjecture; *vakṣāmāṇena*: G.

In this context, the "infant" stage is soft; from the eruption of teeth until their falling out is the "middle child" stage; from the falling out of teeth until their re-eruption is the "boy" stage; and from the re-eruption of teeth until the age of sixteen and beyond is the "mature" stage, due to the capacity for procreating sons and daughters. Thus, the yogi should meditate upon these fourfold limbs of all deities; such is the rule regarding conventional truth (*laukikasatya*).
Now, the accomplishment of the Buddha-image by means of ultimate truth is described.
Here, first, regarding "the awakening to emptiness," one should not think of anything at all in the darkness.

Then, "the collection of the moon-drop" refers to the grasping of the signs beginning with smoke up to the drop (*bindu*), as well as the arising of the image (*bimba*) from that drop; "the vision of the universe" is the arising of the image from that drop. "By the families of the excellent flavors" means by the six aggregates (*skandha*) which are free from obscurations; "the placement of syllables" is the cessation of the limited aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth. Thereafter, the distinction of the stages such as "mild" and so on occurs through the attainment of the *bhūmis*, until one becomes a master of the twelve *bhūmis*.
Then comes the meaning of the truth in its twelve aspects and the knowledge of reality in its sixteen aspects; this is the connection with the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
And that inclusion of the beginning and the end is by means of a *pratyāhāra* for the sake of metrical convenience.

Therefore, it should be understood that here there is also the inclusion of the "child" (*bāla*) and the "youth" (*kumāra*). [The phrase] "firm, mature, and likewise at the root" means that they are limbs of the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*). The "youth" is soft, being the third limb.
By this, the fourfold set beginning with service (*sevā*) is joined with the fourfold set beginning with "soft" (*mṛdu*).
"Regarding 'here' and so forth: 'mild' means having newly acquired strength.
Because of the gathering of the lunar drops (*indubindu*), it is 'mild' up to the limit of birth.
Having spoken starting from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), he now speaks of "one who is mild by birth" and so on, meaning that once born, at sixteen [years of age], and so forth.
By means of the illustration of the body, he demonstrates the subject at hand:
"The attainment of the stages (*bhūmi*) through the distinctions of 'soft' (*mṛdu*) and so forth" means that each of the fourfold set beginning with 'soft' is joined to each of the three stages.

Because of the attainment of the twelve stages beginning with *pramuditā* and ending with *jñānavatī*, he is the "Lord of the Twelve Stages"; therefore, the meaning of the verse beginning with "the twelve aspects" and so forth has been explained by us in the *Amṛtakaṇikā*, the commentary on the *Nāmasamgīti*, and thus is not elaborated upon here.
jātabālo: SUȚ; jātabālaḥ: V3 (followed by a daṇḍa).
putra°: SUȚ; putrā°: V3 ||
The manifestation of the universe as the arising of the reflection: V3, SUȚ; in T we read *sna tshogs gzugs* (= *viśvabimbotpattiḥ*).

Then: SUȚ; from that: V3 | The distinction of "weak" and so forth occurs through the attainment of the stages: V3, SUȚ; [the reading] *mṛdvādibhedena bhūmilābhāḥ* is found in GI within V3; a daṇḍa is placed after *bhavati*.
The prince is gentle, having the nature of the third limb; in T₁ we read: "The prince is not inferior, having the nature of the three limbs."
The fourfold [classification] beginning with the weak is found in D1.
In manuscript G, the sentence beginning with *atretyādi* and ending with *mṛdur iti* is placed after *darśayati*.
Regarding *jātabālaḥ*, this is a conjecture based on T₁ (*skyes pa'i byis pa'o*); G reads *jātabānaḥ*.
Regarding *indubindu*, G reads *indrabindu*; however, *candrabindu* is equally possible.

Having begun by speaking from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)—[the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is missing in T₁]—and having spoken [using the words "of the mild type" (*mṛdujāta*) and so forth]: [this is a conjecture; G reads *āramboktvā*;
the conjecture is *mṛdujātādiśabdena*; G reads *mṛdujātādikṣānto*].
By means of the demonstration of the body: conjecture; śārīranirdaśena: G; in T₁ we read: "Because of the firm establishment of the body, he was born."
The attainment of the stages (*bhūmilābha*); [the forms] *bhūmilābhāt*, *bhūmilābhī*, and so forth; thus, "and so forth" (*ityādi*):
this is not elaborated here. [The reading] *pratyanyate* is corrected to *pratyanyate*.
He is the supreme omniscient one, awakened through the twenty aspects of enlightenment.

Thus, in the void, one should meditate on the path of smoke and so forth according to the guru’s injunctions, up to the limit of the visualized form (*bimba*) within the wheels of channels (*nāḍīcakra*); from that, one makes the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the downward-voiding wind (*apāna*) firm.
Afterwards, the yogi effects the arrest of the moon—the *bodhicitta*—like a planet; therefore, whatever is desired is attained here in this very life within a few days.
Thus it is said:
"This is the royal road.

The instruction on the stages of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanākrama*) was spoken in the *Paramādibuddha* as follows: "Having cultivated smoke and the other signs, one should make the mind immovable."

Now the supramundane path of accomplishment is described: "In the void, [one should meditate] on the path of smoke and so forth" by means of the sequence to be explained through the power of the guru’s instructions. One should meditate on the "image" (*bimba*) at the "limit of the image"—that is, the image possessing all aspects—as being the mind itself.

From that point, the yogi makes both the *prāṇa* and *apāna* winds stable within the channel-wheels at the navel-cakra; subsequently, there is "cessation," like Rāhu seizing the moon, meaning the yogi possesses the mutual union of *prāṇa* and *apāna*. Thus, he is called a "yogi."

The cessation and pacification of the moment of emission of the *bodhicitta* produces the immutable (*akṣara*) [state], such as the outflow (*niṣyanda*) and so forth. From that outflow, there arises the maturation (*vipāka*), the human effort (*puruṣakāra*), and the purity (*vaimalya*); whatever is inexpressible [therein] occurs within a few days, or within the three years and three fortnights of the Kālacakra. This is the rule. Likewise: from the limit of the reflection (*bimba-sīman*), from the limit of the reflection, from the limit of the universe (*viśva-sīman*); from that, afterwards, the drinking (*āpāna*). Regarding the cause, cf. "of the moon" (*indoh*), "of the drop" (*bindoḥ*): this... namely, stanzas b, c, and d (pādas ab) are also quoted in G (fols.).

The path beginning with smoke (*dhūmādimārgam*); on the path beginning with smoke (*dhūmādimārge*); [referring to] that which will be explained (*vakṣyamāṇa*); [referring to] that which is being explained (*vakṣamāna*); [the word] "should meditate" (*bhāvayet*) is followed by a daṇḍa in manuscript G;

[the phrase] "up to that" (*tatparyantam*); [the variant reading] *tatpraryantam*; "mind" (*cittam*); "by the mind" (*cittena*); "in the navel-cakra" (*nābhicakre*); "in the channel-cakra" (*nāḍīcakre*)—this is missing in manuscript T₁; [the word] "grasping" (*graha*) is preceded by a daṇḍa in manuscript G.
In the G script, a daṇḍa appears before the letter *i*.
From the outflow [comes] the maturation: after a few days; "after a few days" (*katipayadivais*): it is also possible that the correct reading is *katipayadinais*, as suggested by G.
mah (VP, ed., vol. I, p. ...). Having purified the middle [channel], one should meditate upon the supreme syllable.
Having established the vajra within the lotus, one should cause the vital breath (prāṇa) to enter the drop (bindu).
One should arrest the vibration of the drops within the wheels (cakras) by means of the drops into the vajra.
The yogi should always remain steadfast and always have his vital energy drawn upward;
through union with Mahāmudrā, he is empowered by the penetrations of the Vajra.

O Great King, in twenty-one thousand, six hundred, and sixty moments, one becomes Vajrasattva himself. Elsewhere, one should not form an attachment to wisdom as long as the ten [signs] have not arisen;
for these are the signs of the yogin’s discernment of external mental activity.
Withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is the Lord of Jinas and is tenfold; meditative concentration (dhyāna) is Akṣobhya; breath control (prāṇāyāma) is Khaḍgin; furthermore, retention (dhāraṇā) is Ratnapāṇi;

mindfulness (anusmṛti) occurs in the Dombyā [channel] and is Padmadhara; and the glorious samādhi (samādhi) is Cakrin. Each one is further divided into five types by means of the vowels and consonants beginning with *a* and *ka*.

Withdrawal is the non-engagement of the ten objects and sense-faculties within the body; meditative concentration consists of wisdom (*prajñā*), reasoning (*tarka*), investigation (*vicāra*), delight (*rati*), and immovable bliss (*acalasukha*), as well as one-pointedness of mind (*ekacitta*).

Prāṇāyāma is the stumbling of the two paths; it is the entry into the central channel (*madhyama*), the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the *bindu*, which indeed destroys both movements. Dhāraṇā is one-pointedness of mind, and *anusmṛti* is that which truly occurs as the vision of Caṇḍālī within the body and in space. Samādhi is the reflection of gnosis (*jñāna-bimba*) arising from the abode of the imperishable bliss consisting of wisdom and means. This practice of the Lord of the Universe may be threefold according to the divisions of "soft" (*mṛdu*) and so forth. There are three mudrās—Karma, Saṃkalpa, and Divya—having three measures (*mātrā*) by virtue of the three types of movement.

By means of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), the yogi, freed from sense objects, is empowered by all mantras and becomes a possessor of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñāna*), O Lord of Men. Purified through the yoga of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and purified by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), being devoid of the moon and sun, he is worshipped by the Bodhisattvas; he enters the Ten-Powered One (*daśabala*) for the destruction of Māras, afflictions, and so forth.

Completely purified by the power of retention (*dhāraṇā*), there arises the stainless *bhāmaṇḍala* (orb of light) from the image of gnosis (*jñānabimba*); the meaning is that the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrāsiddhi*) is thereby attained.
Vajra in the lotus; lotus in the vajra.

The verse GII.st.e, which is not commented upon in G, has been retranslated based on T (cf. below, p. bāhya°; *bāhye* is also possible). II *°pāniḥ*: *°pāṇi*: II *ḍombhyām*: *ḍombyā*: || *°ādyaiḥ*: *°ādyai*: || *°vṛttiḥ*: *°vṛtti*: | *°cittam*: *°cihnam*: || *divyāḥ*: *°devyāḥ*: II *yogi*: *yogi*: *adhiṣṭhyate*: *adhiṣṭyate*: | *sarva°*: *sama°*: *balena*: *balenaḥ*: || *anusmṛteḥ*: *anusmṛtaḥ*: | *vimalam api ca*: *vimalamanasi*: *maṇḍalam*: *maṇḍale*: II From that, being purified in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one succeeds as the body of gnosis (*jñānadeha*) within a few days.

If, through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other [limbs], that desired accomplishment does not arise for practitioners of mantra, then by the forceful practice of *nāda* and the restraint of the *bindu* within the jewel of the lotus-thunderbolt, one should achieve it.

In the stage of service (*sevā*), there is the primordial yoga (*ādiyoga*) which is tenfold in the sky for the Wielder of the Wheel (*cakrin*) by means of the wrathful gaze; and in the stage of near-attainment (*upasādhya*), there is the six-limbed yoga by means of the gaze of the Destroyer of Obstacles (*vighnāntaka*) and the movement along the path of nectar.

Furthermore, in the stage of attainment (*sādhana*), the three-syllabled [mantra] of the moon-drop produced by wisdom should reside in the jewel of the thunderbolt; and here, in the great attainment (*mahāsādhana*), the innate (*sahaja*) yoga of gnosis is the singular peace beyond the eight worldly pleasures.
Now, the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) is explained beginning with the words "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*).
Here, withdrawal is the aggregate of gnosis (*jñānaskandha*) for the beginner, O Lord of Jinas;

and that aggregate of gnosis is tenfold according to the distinction of signs (*nimitta*), being unconstructed through the distinctions of seeing smoke, mirage, fireflies, lamp, flame, moon, sun, Rāhu, the digit (*kalā*), and the point (*bindu*).

Dhyāna is Akṣobhya himself; it is the tenfold aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), the unification of the ten objects and subjects within the Universal Image (*viśvabimba*). Prāṇāyāma is also tenfold, as described in the *Khadgi*; it is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) because of the state of being a single fusion of the ten mandalas of the left and right [channels].
Furthermore, Dhāraṇā is tenfold, as described in the *Ratnapāṇi*; it is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*).

The retention (*dhāraṇā*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is tenfold, according to the distinction of its movement through the lotuses of the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown; this is *anusmṛti* in the *ḍombī*, and it is also designated as "the Holder of the Lotus" (*kamaladhara*). Thus, the aggregate of recollection (*saṃjñāskandha*) is tenfold, and that *anusmṛti* occurs in the *ḍombī* within the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) through the distinctions of the ten states of passion (*kāma*). Furthermore, the "Glorious Samādhi" (*śrīsamādhi*) is the "Wheel-Bearer" (*cakrī*), which is Vairocana; this tenfold samādhi arises from the cessation of the ten winds.
Thus, the meaning is that the Blessed One is "non-abiding nirvāṇa" (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*) because he is the downward flow (*avāha*) of the winds.
Now, the characteristics of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other [limbs] are stated, beginning with the words "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*).

Here, what is called "withdrawal" consists of the [cessation of] the connection between the ten objects and their corresponding subjects within the body. Now, he explains the yoga of six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) by means of six verses.
Regarding "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth:

in the initial stage of practice, during the cultivation of the signs beginning with smoke, "Jinendra" refers to Vajrasattva; as the state of being an object and subject free from obscuration, he takes the form of the ten signs.
"Khaḍgin" refers to Amoghasiddhi, according to the distinctions among the ten states of desire.

Therefore, he is pure (*śuddha*): L₁, L₃; therefore, he is awakened (*buddha*): L₂, L₄. He is accomplished (*sidhyati*): SUṬ (ed., p. ||). By means of the *dhaṭha* [mantra], he who is in the lotus (*abjaga*): L₁, L₂, L₄; by means of the *dhaṭha*, he who is in the lotus: L₃. The moon of emission (*sṛṣṭendu*): L₁, L₃; the moon of touch (*sparśendu*): L₂, L₄. Here (*iha*): L₁, L₂, L₄; thus (*iti*): L₃. V₃; absent in T. Tenfold: V₃; absent in T. The ten states of desire (*daśakāmāvasthā*); the ten states of desire: V₃. The flow (*avāha*); the wind (*avāta*): V₃. After "pratyāhāra" and so forth, this is absent in T₁. In G, before "ādikarmaṇi," we find "sādhanāke vṛ," which is absent in T₁. The object free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇaviṣaya*) ... having the form of a sign (*nimittarūpaḥ*); this is absent in T₁ before "nirāvaraṇa°. There is a daṇḍa in G. The activity of consciousness (*pravṛttir vijñānasya*) toward the image of emptiness (*śūnyatābimba*), the activity of the fivefold [consciousness] through other [faculties] such as the eye and so forth.

Likewise, in that very same reflection (*bimba*), "wisdom" (*prajñā*) is the illumination; "reasoning" (*tarka*) is the grasping of the object of meditation; and "investigation" (*vicāra*) is the purpose of its ascertainment. [The signs are: fever of thought and longing; drying up of the limbs, the face, and the lotus-like mouth; the onset of food [cravings]; trembling, madness, and dizziness; mental delusion, intense fainting, and so forth—these ten types manifest for the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (*vajrin*). These states in the bodies of living beings are well-known in the world; they are clearly established as belonging to the God of Love (*manmatha*). Who is the Victor (*jina*), and who is the one possessed by desire?

Thus, regarding the visualization of the image within the recollection (*anusmṛti*), ten stages arise subsequently for the yogin due to his state of great passion (*mahārāga*). These stages, which correspond to the states of desire (*kāma*) and are preceded by the vision of the results of meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*)—such as smoke and so forth—are personally experienced (*svasaṃvedya*).
They consist of the cessation, pacification, and transformation into the imperishable state of the ten winds: prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna, nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
Because of the absence of the sides of passion and dispassion, he possesses non-abiding nirvāṇa;

each one is further divided into five types by means of the vowels beginning with *a* and so forth— thus, [the letters] consisting of the thirty consonants shine forth, having the nature of the elements of space, wind, fire, water, and earth, and being differentiated by the five short vowels beginning with *a*.
In the same way, [the letters] are associated with the intrinsic natures of earth and the other elements, differentiated by the five long vowels beginning with Ī,
according to the sequence of emanation and withdrawal,
and through the divisions of the twelve solar transits beginning with Aries and Taurus.

For every staff (daṇḍa), there are three hundred and sixty breaths. During the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), the moon consists of a single consonant and a short vowel; during the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), the sun consists of a conjunct consonant and a long vowel. At the moment of transition (saṃkrānti), Rāhu consists of three conjunct consonants and a protracted (pluta) vowel.
The meaning is that [the breath] is differentiated as it moves according to the distinctions of the constituents (mātrā) of sattva, rajas, and tamas.

Perception by means of other [senses] such as the eyes and so forth, or by means of the flesh and so forth, is the perception of the universal image (*viśvabimba*). *Śūnyatā*: SUṬ (ed., p. ...), T (*stong pa nyid*); *śūnya°*: V₃ || *cintā°*: L₁, L₃, G; *citta*: L₂, L₄ | *°ājvaro*: L₂, L₃, L₄, G; *°ājjvaro*: L₁ | *varamukha°*: L₁, L₃, G (SUT, ed., p. ...); *varasukha°*: L₂, L₄ | *suṣkir annāpravṛttiḥ*; *śuṣkir anyāpravṛttiḥ*: G; *śuṣkir annāpravṛttiḥ*: L₃; *śuṣko 'nnāpravṛttiḥ*: L₁; *śuktir annāpravṛttiḥ*: L₂; *śuktir antā pravṛttih*: L₄; *Suṣkadravyāpravṛttiḥ*: VP ed. "Delight" (rati) is attachment to the *bimba*;
"unwavering bliss" (*acalasukha*) is the unification of the mind with the *bimba*.
Thus, meditation (*dhyāna*) is tenfold, distinguished by the categories of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).

Here, what is called *prāṇāyāma* is the stumbling of the left and right channels, their cessation, and entry into the middle channel; it is of ten kinds due to the cessation of the ten maṇḍalas. Here, "in the *bindu*" means the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the forehead.
"Struck by both movements" means devoid of coming and going. *Dhāraṇā* is the one-pointedness of mind upon the vital breath at the forehead.
"The vision of Caṇḍālī" is that which occurs within the three worlds; this is the previously mentioned tenfold *anusmṛti*.

"By means of that which consists of wisdom and method" refers to the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) upon the gnosis-image (*jñānabimba*) by virtue of the non-emission of bliss, through the state of being a single fusion of the object of knowledge and the knowing subject;
and that [absorption] is also tenfold due to the absence of the vital breaths and so forth.

Thus, this six-limbed yoga is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), and though it is threefold according to the divisions of "mild" and so on, it is the means of accomplishment for Kālacakra, the Sustainer of the Universe.

The three seals (*mudrā*) have three measures: the apprehension of the object of meditation, the determination of that object, and the ascertainment of the nature of that object as being emptiness. "Attachment to the image" refers to the joy (*saumanasya*) that arises when one, through the turning away from sense objects, by means of mind-only directed inwardly, takes as an object the self whose nature is the deity; and when one contemplates this as the single flavor of unsurpassed wisdom and method, facing toward the entry into reality—that is "delight" (*rati*), meaning joy. It is the bliss consisting of physical pliancy (*kāyaprasrabdhi*) and so forth, which is immovable bliss.

"Entry into the middle path" means that through the dissolution of the ten maṇḍalas, beginning with space and ending with earth, there is the cessation of *lalanā* and *rasanā*. It is the subtle activity of the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) characterized by entry, abiding, and exit solely through the path of the *avadhūtī*; this is what is meant by "breath control" (*prāṇāyāma*). "Struck down in both directions" means being devoid of coming and going because of the absence of movement and non-movement at the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown; thus, due to the gradual diminution of the winds, the settling of the vital wind—which is the vehicle of the mind—into the drop (*bindu*), which is the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*), as having the single flavor of emptiness, is called "concentration" (*dhāraṇā*).

The tenfold [meditation] previously mentioned is as follows: when the mind is established in *dhāraṇā*, there arises—preceded by the manifestation of the ten signs such as smoke and so forth—the vision of the deities of the maṇḍala, which is non-conceptual and has the form of a reflection. From that, there is the radiation of many rays of light. Through the cessation of the ten maṇḍalas; through the obstruction of the ten maṇḍalas: it is devoid of coming and going (*gamanāgamanarahita*); [this term *rahita* is missing in the Tibetan version]. By virtue of being in a state of fusion (*lolībhūtatvena*), it is imperishable (*akṣara*). That too is tenfold. Thus, the three measures (*trimātrā*): "the three measures" refers to focusing on the nature of the deity. [The terms] *rasanayor*; *rasanāyor*: in the subtle channel (*sūkṣmanāḍyām*); in the middle of the subtle (*sūkṣmamadhye*); *gatihata*; *gatihata*: from diminution (*apacayād*); from increase (*upacayād*): in the *bodhicitta*. [The word *la*]; awakening is the settling of the mind (*niveśana*); in the settling: [this term is missing between *dhāraṇā* and *pratiṣṭhe*]. A punctuation mark (*daṇḍa*) is present after *'nekaraśmi*; *'naikaraśmi*: "by virtue of the threefold movement"—here, the movement of the *bodhicitta* toward emission is the soft measure (*mṛdumātrā*).
The movement of vibration (*spandagati*) is of medium measure, while the movement of non-vibration (*niḥspandagati*) is of superior measure;
thus, the action seal (*karmamudrā*) bestows the bliss of emission (*kṣarasukha*),
whereas the wisdom seal (*jñānamudrā*) bestows the bliss of vibration (*spandasukha*).
Mahāmudrā bestows the bliss of the motionless; thus, the cultivation of the three mudrās has been taught by the Blessed One through the yoga of the six limbs.

Therefore, the yoga of the six limbs should be cultivated by the yogin for the sake of Buddhahood. Now, the fruit of withdrawal (pratyāhāra) and the other branches is stated, beginning with the word "withdrawal."

In this context, when the yogi becomes purified through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and [the deity] is stabilized by means of the *bimba*, then he is empowered by all mantras; through his speech, he bestows boons and so forth, and he becomes a possessor of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñāna*), O Lord of Men, being purified by the yoga of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Here, when his eyes become unblinking, then he possesses the divine eye; likewise, one who is purified by meditation becomes possessed of the divine ear.

"Purified by breath-control" (prāṇāyāma) means that when the yogin here becomes devoid of the paths of the sun and moon and always flows through the central channel (madhyamā), then, being purified by breath-control, he is honored and praised by the Bodhisattvas—this is the meaning. "He enters the ten-powered one who destroys Māras and afflictions" means that by the power of retention (dhāraṇā), he enters the image of emptiness (śūnyatā-bimba); [he enters] the mind of subject and object, and through the cessation of the coming and going of the vital breath (prāṇa), it becomes unified as a single mass.

Then, preceded by the radiation of the deity-mandala throughout the three realms, there is the recollection of the characteristics [of reality] (*lakṣaṇānusmṛti*), consisting of the ten stages of desire beginning with thought (*cintā*). Due to the absence of the vital winds (*prāṇa*) and so forth, the bodhicitta—abiding at the very tip of the crest of the vajra-jewel—is ignited by the blaze of the *caṇḍālī*. Thereafter, the twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths are sequentially arrested within the six wheels. Thus, the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) has as its intrinsic nature the Great Vajradhara, whose body consists of gnosis (*jñāna*) and is of the nature of the union (*yuganaddha*) characterized by non-conceptual yoga and immutable great bliss.

If it is asked: "How is it designated thus that 'the bodhisattva becomes [one who possesses] the fruit of withdrawal and so forth, characterized by the benefits of the six limbs,' since he has not yet attained the qualities of a Buddha within his own continuum?"—the intention is that although he does not yet turn the wheel of the Dharma of birth, awakening, and so forth, by turning those [wheels], he indeed becomes one who shares the designation of a "Perfectly Awakened One" (sambuddha) in a buddha-field. Regarding "the ten masteries and so forth," these are the masteries over lifespan, karma, liberation, requisites, aspiration, miraculous power, dharma, mind, birth, and gnosis.
The mind that grasps the object and the subject is said to be the agent; and elsewhere, the benefits [of this practice] have been described.

°dāyikā: °dāyinā: °dāyikā: °dāyinā: °dāyikā: °dāyinā: by means of the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga): when the yogin: the yogin when: possessing the divine ear (divyaśrotas): [the qualities] beginning with the divine ear: the carrier of the central channel (madhyamāvāha): the one who causes the flow through the central channel (madhyamāvāhaka); is praised; is extolled: the image of emptiness (śūnyatābimba); the image of emptiness by way of non-existence; having caused to flow: established; established; the breaths (śvāsa); the breaths: consisting of bliss (sukhamaya); consisting of bliss: the Bodhisattva... [the powers] such as mastery (vaśitā) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in one's own continuum" (*svasantāne*)—if this is the objection, it is absent from the *cet* [particle]. Thus he says: "birth... because of the turning of that [wheel]: because of the turning of the wheel of Dharma of the birth-enlightenment (*jātibodhidharmacakra*). Because of the turning of that: before *āyuṣ* [there is the phrase] "purified by recollection" (*saṃśuddho ’nusmṛteḥ*). Here, "recollection" (*anusmṛti*) is the visualization of the image (*bimbāliṅgana*), which is the state of the mind being free from all conceptual construction (*sarvavikalparahitatva*). When, due to that, one is purified, then the stainless circle of light (*vimalaprabhāmaṇḍala*) arises.

Furthermore, by the word "also" (*apica*), it is said that five rays flash and issue forth from the pores of the skin, from the image of gnosis (*jñānabimba*), which is the image of emptiness (*śūnyabimba*).

Therefore, [it is said] "pure in meditative absorption" (*samādhi*); here, the imperishable bliss (*akṣarasukha*) that arises through the unity of the mind of the apprehended and the apprehender is called "blissful meditative absorption.

From that pure meditative absorption, being "pure," meaning having attained stainlessness (*vaimalya*), one succeeds in becoming the "body of gnosis" (*jñānadeha*) within a few days, three fortnights, or three years; thus, one becomes a Bodhisattva who has attained the ten masteries (*daśavaśitā*) and so forth. This is the rule for withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other [limbs of yoga].
Now, haṭhayoga is described.

Here, when the image (bimba) has been seen through withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) and so forth, yet the imperishable moment (akṣarakṣaṇa) does not arise because the vital breath (prāṇa) is unrestrained, then—by means of the practice of the sound (nāda)—one should, through haṭha, cause the breath to flow into the central channel (madhyamā). By arresting the drop of the thought of awakening (bodhicittabindu) within the vajra-jewel situated at the lotus of wisdom, one attains the imperishable moment. Having achieved this through withdrawal, and having entered the meditative knowledge (dhyānajñāna) empowered by all mantras, one shall attain the state of the five superknowledges (pañcābhijñā). This is certainly observed by the Bodhisattvas through the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).

One who possesses the power of retention should always enter into Vajrasattva. Through the union of recollection (*anusmṛti*), a mandala of light arises; by the mere mastery of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one becomes free from obscurations. Thus, through gentleness, by means of the uninterrupted flow in the left and right [channels] and the state of the breath being unrestrained—

Through the practice of *nāda* and the practice of the innate bliss of gnosis (*jñānasahajānanda*), by means of the *hūṃ*-sound of the *nāda*, and through the arrest of the drops of *bodhicitta* at the *kuliśa* (penis) situated upon the lotus of wisdom— having inserted the *bola* (phallus) into the *kakkola* (vagina) of the aforementioned passionate woman according to the ritual, resting there with unwavering steadiness, and pressing the *vajramaṇi* against the opening of her stamen— one should not move for even a moment due to the intense flavor of joy.

Then, when the arising of the flowing fluid occurs for those two, preceded by the utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*, one should bring to mind that which has been granted by the grace of the feet of the true guru. Through the experience of the fourth, the innate joy (*sahajānanda*), there is the recollection of the *bodhicitta*;

thus, here, "recollection" (*anusmṛti*) is [the state] devoid of [conceptualization]. It becomes pure; the moment of the imperishable (*akṣarakṣaṇa*) does not arise through the force of the practice of *nāda*. [The state] is consecrated (*adhiṣṭhita*); one should attain it. [It is] merely [the power of] the *bolam* according to the rule. When the arising of the flowing fluid occurs, one should accomplish it through the motionless [state]; this is *haṭhayoga*.
The practice of *nāda* (sound) has been taught here in this very *Sādhanapatala* by the Blessed One:

"That power (*śakti*), starting from the center of the navel, goes to the supreme state at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths] and the end of the *kalās*. When she is restrained at the navel, resembling lightning and fire, and having risen in the form of a staff, she moves with a soft and graceful gait from wheel to wheel along the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*). Once set in motion, she forcefully touches the aperture of the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) like a needle piercing through external leather."

At that time, one should impel the *āpāna* wind upward with supreme force; having pierced the *uṣṇīṣa* on the upper path, it proceeds to the city of the other (*parapura*). When the pair of winds is restrained, through this awakening of the *vajra* in the mind, one attains the state of moving through space (*khecaratva*) along with the sense objects. Furthermore, she becomes for yogins the Mother of the Universe (*viśvamātā*), whose nature consists of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*).
Then, from the cessation of the *bindu*, there is the attainment of the moment of the immutable (*akṣara-kṣaṇa*); such is the meaning.

In this very context, related to the *Śrī Kālacakra*, it is said that "the power (*śakti*) goes to the supreme state. This means the vital power (*prāṇaśakti*) proceeds to the supreme state, the supportless place, the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*). Thus, in the left nostril, from the mandala of space up to the mandala of earth—extending from sixteen finger-breadths down to twelve finger-breadths, ending at the *kalā*s; and in the right nostril, from the mandala of earth up to the mandala of space—extending from twelve finger-breadths up to sixteen finger-breadths—by means of the resonance of the utterance of the syllable *HŪṂ*, there is the conjunction of the winds of *prāṇa* and *apāna*. That same vital power, restrained at the navel, resembles lightning and fire, being like a flash of lightning and a flame.
The quality of motion, like a needle, enters— that is, it goes into— the drinking vessel, just as a needle [pierces] its way.
Even if one desires to enter another's city—that is, another's body—entry into that other city does not occur; therefore, he says that it must be done in this way:

"In this manner," by this sequence, "from the awakening of the vajra," which is the awakening of the gnosis of supreme bliss, "in the mind," meaning in the consciousness that has become a single fusion of the grasped and the grasper.

Regarding "with the vibration of the poisonless": the practice of *nāda* was taught by the Blessed One: "completely restrained," "fire," "up to the *uṣṇīṣa*," "the lower [aperture]," "supreme," "objects," "the moment of non-emission," "Kālacakra"; "space" (from the sixth [day] onwards, up to the end of the twelve fingers); "sound," "thunderbolt-fire"; "moving"; "there is no grasping of signs such as smoke by the mind."

And that [perception] becomes a tenfold cognition together with smoke and the other signs; thus it is tenfold. And that belongs to the "Wheel-bearer" (Cakrin). By means of the "wrathful gaze" of the Uṣṇīṣa—that is, by an upward gaze that does not blink—it becomes the sign. There are four kinds through the yoga of night and six kinds through the yoga of day.
Then the image (*bimba*) arises.
Thus, up to the limit of the image, it constitutes the limb of service (*sevāṅga*) by means of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
"By the gaze of Vighnāntaka" means that Vighnāntaka is Amṛtakuṇḍalī;

his gaze is directed toward the place of nectar, located at the forehead. By that gaze, and by [the gaze] of Vighnāntaka which has entered the path of nectar, the six-limbed [practice] is applied to the one being accomplished.

From the word "and" (*cakārāt*), it follows that breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and retention (*dhāraṇā*) must be performed once the reflection (*bimba*) has been seen; this constitutes the *upasādhana*. Regarding the phrase "of the moon-drop created by wisdom" (*prajñāsṛṣṭendubindoḥ*): here, that which is both "created by wisdom" (*prajñāsṛṣṭa*) and a "created moon-drop" (*sṛṣṭendubindu*) is the "moon-drop created by wisdom. Of that very drop of bodhicitta created by wisdom, when it has entered the vajra-jewel, there occurs the "union of the three syllables" (*tryakṣarayoga*) in the secret place, the navel, and the heart; this constitutes the *sādhana*, meaning it occurs as the third limb of the *sādhana*.

Thus, the limb of the means (sādhanāṅga) should be performed as "the sole peace of unperishing bliss. Here, that single moment of the *bodhicitta* which is unperishing through bliss is called "peace"; in this Great Means (mahāsādhana), it is the "yoga of gnosis" (*jñānayoga*), which is the oneness of the mind with imperishable bliss.

The fourth limb of the Great Accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*) is as follows: that which has become unified with the objects of the senses is *śakti*; she attains the state of moving through space (*khecaratva*) and sovereignty extending as far as the world-sphere of Akaniṣṭha. To show that it is not merely thus, he says "the five," and so forth. She is the Mother of the Universe (*viśvamātā*), whose nature consists of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*)—namely, the miraculous powers, the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of the minds of others, and the recollection of former abodes—and she is Mahāmudrā. Through the passion of wisdom (*prajñārāga*), by means of the flame of the non-conceptual Caṇḍālī.
The "three-syllable yoga" is as follows:

the mind-drop (*cittabindu*), having entered the secret place, is restrained; the speech-drop (*vāgbindu*), having reached the navel, is restrained; the body-drop (*kāyabindu*), having reached the heart, is restrained. Through bliss that does not perish—the non-emission of the mass of drops at the opening of the *vajra*—the gnosis-drop (*jñānabindu*) is restrained; this is the yoga of gnosis (*jñānayoga*).
By the phrase ending with "the two winds are restrained," the accomplishment of *bhūcarī* (the earth-walker) is indicated;

[and] "service to the sky-goer" (*khecarī*) and so forth. Furthermore, in the practice of that [accomplishment], there is the *amṛtakuṇḍalī* located at the forehead, which is the emitted lunar drop (*bindu*).

Thus, the nature of the recollection (*anusmṛti*) of the *bodhicitta* is the yoga of the three syllables; the drop of gnosis (*jñānabindu*) is restrained within the vajra-mouth and the pair of winds. The Seal (*mudrā*), corresponding to illusion (*māyā*), shines forth in the mind, in space, in form, and in the mirror—like lightning or fire—with many rays quivering. Undifferentiated from the external bodies, devoid of objects, and situated in the mere sky of appearance, that single [Seal] embraces the mind of the world in its manifold forms.

The mere appearance of the mind, produced within one's own consciousness like a reflection in a mirror, is indeed to be cultivated by the lords of yogins and practiced by all the sons of the Conquerors and the Buddhas. When this flame of gnosis has increased, it burns away the entire host of Māras together with their objects, and through the yoga of the rains, it bestows equal bliss upon the bodies of the yogins.

By the end of the passage ending with "attains the state of reality" (*ratvaṃ prayāti*), the accomplishment of Khecarī is described; by the end of the passage ending with "Mother of the Universe" (*viśvamātā*), the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā is indicated.

The seal (mudrā) is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā), which conforms to illusion and is like a reflection in a clear mirror. And because it exists in the mind and in space—that which is both non-mind and mind—it is said: "like a form in a mirror."
Like form itself, they pervade and expand as possessors of form;

externally, within illusory bodies, they have become unified with the objects and sense faculties, being non-different from them. For this very reason, they are devoid of objects that appear as phenomena (dharmas) through any distinction. Although she is one, she embraces the mind of the world of manifold forms; for this very reason, she consists of mind (*cetomayā*), having the nature of a mind that is no-mind (*acittacitta*).

The mere appearance—which consists of the form of the manifestation of one’s own mind, arising as the divine mudrā within one’s own mind in the form of all-aspectedness yet devoid of aspects—is that which has been produced from the mind when the grasped and the grasper have become a single fused mass.

This "mere appearance" is the flame of gnosis; it is the blazing gnosis, the intensified blaze of Caṇḍālī, which [consumes] the host of Māras along with their objects—the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—as well as the web of the conceptualizing mind.

And it has been said: "There is no other than one's own mind; it is Māra. It is produced as mere radiance, like a reflection. When fully developed, it proceeds toward equal bliss and is thus undivided. In the formless state, the flame of gnosis blazes; the fire of Caṇḍālī is increased, and wisdom becomes gnosis and mind. Its manifestation is tenfold, and immersion in this is the consecration. Indeed, it is like the reflection of a stainless moon in a mirror. Therefore, that glorious Guru is he in whose heart and mouth resides the fourth state—the innate, imperishable, and non-falling bliss of Nirvāṇa, which is the very mouth of the Buddha."

In this context, *prajñā* (wisdom) and *jñāna* (gnosis) are, respectively, the apprehending mind (*grāhakacitta*) and that which is the tenfold appearance of the apprehended—beginning with smoke and so forth—which, like a counter-force, is the reflection of that very apprehending mind; the meaning is that it is the apprehended mind. Thus, just as one's own eye is reflected in a mirror and is itself apprehended by one's own eye, *prajñā* and *jñāna* constitute the "consecration" (*seka*) which is immersion (*majjana*) therein. This immersion refers to the entry of the apprehending mind into the apprehended mind; it is the non-engagement with external objects, known as withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and retention (*dhāraṇā*). Because of this immersion within the six-limbed yoga, there arises the bliss of nirvāṇa, which is unchanging, innate, and imperishable—the fourth bliss. It is beyond the states of the child, the mature, and the vibrating, transcends worldly analogies, and is free from the conduct of the three worlds; such is the meaning.

Free from laughing, gazing, touching, embracing, grasping with the hands, and union; free from the causes of the *karmamudrā* and *jñānamudrā*; characterized by the manifestation of all aspects within emptiness—this is the mouth of the Buddha, the mouth of gnosis (*jñānavaktra*). That master in whose heart this has been cultivated as a personal experience and who exists at all times for the purpose of communicating it through his own mouth to his disciples is the illustrious Māra. He bestows, he grants the equal bliss, the bliss of innate joy (*sahajānanda*), by means of the "rain of the wheel" (*cakravarṣa*) over the period of three years and three fortnights; such is the meaning.

"Insight (*prajñā*) and gnosis (*jñāna*)" correspond respectively [to the following]: insight is the realization of the emptiness of all phenomena; it is the apprehending mind (*grāhakacitta*). The appearance of smoke and so forth within that [mind] is the apprehended mind (*grāhyacitta*), and that very thing is gnosis.

By this it is meant that just as one's own eye reflected in a mirror is perceived by one's own eye, so too the mind whose nature is emptiness perceives the mind in all its aspects, which has emptiness as its nature.
Within this apprehended mind characterized by smoke and so forth, the immersion of the apprehending mind—the mind of emptiness—is its becoming a single, unified mass.
He speaks of recollection (*anusmṛti*).
Regarding the phrase "pure," [it refers to] the movements of the "child" and the "adult": the bliss of emission (*kṣarasukha*) of the means (*upāya*) is twofold—the child and the adult;
the bliss of vibration (*spandasukha*) of wisdom (*prajñā*) is pierced. Of these two, when there is no vibration (*niḥspanda*) of either wisdom or means, in that [state]: L1, L2, L4.

*grāhya* is missing in T.

in G, the stroke after *darpane* has been erased.
After [the stage of] the characteristics such as smoke, there is a staff in G.
[The reading] *grāhaka* is found in G; *grāhyaka* is found in G II. [The reading] *śūnyatācittasya* is found in G; it is absent in T₁.

The "Guru" means Vajradhara; it does not refer to others who merely understand the pleasure of the two sexual organs.
With minds unattached to space, with unblinking eyes, having entered the path of the vajra, from emptiness there appear smoke, a mirage, a clearly manifest pure firefly, and a lamp;
then flame, moon, sun, and vajra, as well as the supreme digit and the drop (*bindu*). In the center of that, the image of the Buddha—the manifold *saṃbhogakāya* free from sense objects—is seen.
Now, the entry into the appearance of this very mind is explained by the words beginning with "space" (*ākāśa*).

Here, in both the Mantrayāna and the Pāramitāyāna, there is a twofold practice of yoga: the practice of yoga in space and the practice in an open area. He who would attain yoga in space, having his mind fixed on space within a windowless house in darkness during the night, beholds the signs (*nimitta*) such as smoke and so forth.

"With eyes not blinking, one enters the vajra-path"—here, this means that having entered the central life-wind (*madhyamā-prāṇa*), those whose minds are unattached to space and whose eyes do not blink see from emptiness alone, by night-yoga: smoke, a mirage, a clearly manifest stainless firefly, and a lamp.
Then one sees a cloudless sky; then, from that sky, by day-yoga, one sees the flame of the great self-arisen fire of wisdom-knowledge arising from the sky in a cloudless sky.
Thus, Vairocana is the great radiance, the light of gnosis, the illuminator, and the moon-like appearance;
he is the lamp of the world, the sun, the torch of gnosis, and the vajra-Rāhu;
he is the one of great splendor, the luminous one, the lightning, and the supreme syllable.
He becomes the King of Vidyās; that which arises from the divine mudrā is the fourth, meaning the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) of the Vajra-holder.

Now, the entry of this very mind into the appearance of the mind—which is like a reflection in a mirror—is described by the words beginning with "ākāśa" (space) and so forth. The phrase "at night" is an indicator for darkness.

"With a mind attached to space" means a mind dissolved in space. By those whose minds are attached to space—that is, whose minds have become of one flavor (*samarasa*) with it—and who have entered the vajra-path, the vital winds (*prāṇavāta*) having gone into the *avadhūtī*, there arises from the sky—the cloudless sky, which is the form of the causal sign (*nimitta*)—the manifestation of forms. This is because of the appearance of forms that are unobstructed and stainless, comparable to reflections in a mirror.

"It appears as sound" means that because one experiences the mere unstruck resonance (*anāhatadhvani*) arising from the radiance of great bliss produced by the efforts of the throat, palate, and so forth; by this much, through this verse, the two bodies of the Blessed Lord Śrī Vajradhara are illuminated.
