After *tair*, there is *a-daṇḍa* in G.
The two bodies; "the body and the transcendent body" (*kāyam udvayam*) [is the later correction]:

the ten signs (*daśanimitta*), such as the "entry of the letters" (*gramantreṣa*) and the "dot" (*binduka*), were taught by the Blessed One in the *Samāja* and other tantras through the yoga of night, and in the *Nāmasamgīti* through the yoga of day.
Therefore, it is said: "The King of Mantras, the accomplisher of great purpose," which refers to the vision of the image (*bimba*) in all its aspects, such as the jar, the cloth, and so forth.

In the center of that, within the *bindu*, is the form of the Buddha, devoid of objects due to the absence of substance and the absence of conceptual construction; thus, there are many *saṃbhogakāyas*. Then, by means of the yoga of the form, that very sound of the unstruck (*anāhata*) is heard. In this way, the *nirmāṇakāya* is the manifestation of form, while the *saṃbhogakāya* is the manifestation of sound—this is the meaning. The sky, free from clouds, should be gazed upon by the yogi with a fixed gaze, until the black line (*kṛṣṇarekhā*), shimmering and pure-rayed, is seen in the channel of time (*kālanāḍī*).

Within that [state], one's own mind—devoid of objects, possessing all colors and all forms, and stainless like the sun in water—is the image of the Omniscient One; it is nothing other than mind itself.

In this regard, the daytime yoga (*divāyoga*) is to be observed by the yogin with a fixed gaze upon the cloudless sky during the forenoon and afternoon, keeping his back to the sun; otherwise, due to the sun's rays, there is darkness, which causes obstruction. Therefore, it should be observed daily until a black line the thickness of a hair, brilliant and stainless, is seen within the *bindu*. The image of the Omniscient One, the entire threefold world, is contained within the *avadhūtī*, the channel of Time (*kālanāḍī*), as stainless as the sun in water. It is of all colors and all forms, one’s own mind devoid of objects. There is no other mind; indeed, the "mind of another" does not exist, because of the absence of knowledge of another's mind.

In this context, first the appearance of one's own mind is seen by the Tathāgata with the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*); through the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and so forth, the knowledge of others' minds is seen. Thus, the five eyes spoken of by the Blessed One in the *Dharmasaṃgraha* belong to the Blessed One.

In this way, through the power of cultivation, there will sequentially arise the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the Buddha-eye, the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*), and the gnosis-eye (*jñānacakṣus*); thereafter, for the Omniscient One, there is nothing whatsoever that is not seen.

"Space" refers to a fixed gaze, a motionless gaze; [it is so called] because of the absence of knowledge of another's mind, since there is no object of knowledge consisting of another's mind apart from one's own mind.
And it has been said:
"The vision of an object of knowledge here that is neither born nor ceased..."
That [is] one's own mind and not something else, due to the absence of any division from external objects of knowledge.

The stages: V; the stages of knowledge: SUȚII. Its form is earth, yet it is not solid; it is not liquid water, for it is not fluid because it lacks fluidity; it is not fire, for it is motionless while fire has the nature of moving wind; it is not wind, for it is immobile. It has the form of emptiness, yet it is visible; it possesses white, green, great, and universal colors, yet it is not a color. Though possessing all forms, it is invisible due to the power of the Māras and the afflictions that cloud one’s own heart.
Earth dissolves into water, and water likewise into fire; fire goes into wind, and wind into space; indeed, the tenfold sign dissolves into the signless.

The unstruck (*anāhata*) body of gnosis (*jñānakāya*), which is the supreme immutable bliss, attains every form through gnosis; and from that gnosis, O King, supernatural power and perfection arise for men even in this very life.
Therefore, it is never possible for the self to seal itself;
how can a great sword cut itself with its own blade?
Just as pleasure might arise from union with the daughter of a barren woman in a dream,
so it is for the self through the enjoyment of the image arisen from space.
Thus [it is said].

By this verse, the accomplishment of the *dharmakāya* is explained. Regarding the phrase "having the form of earth" and so forth: here, the appearance of emptiness is a non-substantial manifestation of the characteristics of the [five] images; earth and the others are seen, yet they are not solid. Their form is fluid like the water of a mirage, yet it is not water because it lacks fluidity. Likewise, its form is fire, yet it is not fire because it does not burn. Its body is like a moving wind, yet it is not wind because it lacks substantiality; that which is motionless is not wind because it lacks substantiality. It has the appearance of space, yet even that is seen like a city of illusion (*māyānagara*). Although it possesses colors such as white and so forth, it is not color because it lacks substantiality.

Although it possesses all aspects, it is not seen by the ignorant at any time; for what reason? It is a fixed rule that this is due to the power of the afflictions and Māra, and to the movement of the vital breath through the left and right channels.

Now, the destruction of the five mandalas is described by the passage beginning with "earth," and so forth. Here, when the yogin becomes one whose eyes are unblinking, having fixed his mind upon the void through the wrathful gaze, then—taking "earth" as an illustration for either the left or the right—when the yogin performs meditation at the time the earth flows in the right [nostril], this is the procedure. It is not, however, during the flow of the left channel; rather, it follows the sequence of the mandalas beginning with space.
Therefore, whichever mandala the vital breath (*prāṇa*) flows through, whether on the left or the right, that very mandala is so designated because it possesses that nature.

By that [process], the vital breath of the earth-maṇḍala moves into the petal of the water-maṇḍala in the southern channel; in this manner, it proceeds up to the maṇḍala of consciousness (*vijñāna*) in the left channel, [proceeding] through space and the other elements as follows:

In the center is the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the binding of the movement of the sun and moon in the right and left [channels], the mind fixed upon the consort (*mudrā*), and the awakening of the *vajra* through supreme bliss.

The sound of the *vajra* in the lotus, or the splashing of water from one's own hands for the sake of pleasure, and the emission of the seed-syllable (*bīja*)—that pleasure removes the fear of death; this is the mouth of the glorious Guru.
This instruction on Mahāmudrā is also proclaimed in the *Paramādibuddha*:
"One should perform the sādhana of this very [deity] by means of inconceivable appearances—
those signs beginning with smoke, which are the reflections of wisdom equal to space."

Thus it proceeds; it goes toward the tenfold signs beginning with smoke (*dhūmādi-nimitta*), and it proceeds toward the image (*bimba*) of all aspects. That very image proceeds toward immutable bliss (*akṣara-sukha*), which is the gnosis (*jñāna*) of the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). From that gnosis, there arises supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) such as traveling through space, and accomplishment (*siddhi*) consisting of lordship over the three realms. O Lord of Men, for men in this very life, such is the rule for entering the path.
Now, the conclusion of yoga is stated with the words "In the center, the vital breath," and so forth.
Here, first of all, the yogin must effect the entry of the vital breath into the center—that is, into the *avadhūtī*—by means of which he perceives the sign (*nimitta*).
This is the first [point]: the body-vajra of the venerable Guru-Buddha.
The mouth is so called.

Therefore, the rule is that the binding of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) occurs through the conjunction of the lunar movement—the flow in the left channel—with the solar movement, which proceeds to the right.
Breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is the second *vāgvajra*.
The mind, attached to the reflected image during the engagement with the mudrā, becomes the melted bodhicitta.
The third is the Mind-Vajra, which has attained supreme bliss and is the vajra-awakening.
Now, if through the door of the reflected image blissful joy does not arise, then the sound of the vajra should be made gently within the lotus.

Now, if a woman is not obtained, then one should perform the waving [of the seed] with one's own lotus-hand for the sake of increasing bliss, but never for the sake of emission; thus there is no loss of the seed, which becomes blissful and removes the fear of death. This is the fourth mouth of the venerable Guru, the Knowledge-Vajra; such is the rule for the practice of yoga.
For the *Sekoddeśa* has been extracted from the twelve-thousand-verse *Paramādibuddha*.
"Of this very [fire]," and so forth.

The yogi should make manifest the fuel for this very fire of omniscient gnosis—which burns away the fuel of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations without remainder—by means of smoke and other signs. By what means? By those objects of cognition of one's own mind which have transcended all extremes of existence and non-existence, and which are entirely devoid of the accumulation of atoms.

By means of the "appearances"—namely smoke, firebrands, fireflies, lamps, flames, the moon, and the sun—which are well-known in the *tantras* and in definitive-meaning (*nītārtha*) sūtras such as the *Āryaprajñāpāramitā*; which are "inconceivable" because they are appearances that suddenly manifest as emptiness and because all conceptual constructions have ceased; and which are "signs" because they are the preliminary forms of the fruit of reality.

Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the cognition of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, free from the grasped and the grasper. Through its images—which appear as the direct perception of the yogin; which are like the sky because they are untainted by external or internal impurities; which transcend existence and non-existence because they are unmarked by the stains of conceptual constructions such as the faults of being and non-being; which are the objects of experience for the yogin’s own self-reflexive awareness;
and which are in every way uncontrived, marvelous, and devoid of intrinsic nature—[the yogin perceives] that [reality] which is entirely free from the mass of even the most subtle atoms.

"Smoke," and so forth, refers to the appearance of emptiness (*śūnyābhāsa*) in the form of smoke that pervades all external and internal [realms]. This arises immediately after the appearance of clouds, as it has been said: "First it appears like a cloud; secondly, it resembles smoke."
Thus:
a mirage has the appearance of moving water;
fireflies and lamps have well-known appearances.

These four signs arise when the mind has entered the *nirodhavajra*, as described in the *Śrīsamāja* and other texts; they occur through the night yoga and the space yoga in reverse order of the first and second [stages], because of the occurrence of darkness in a windowless room.
That sign is indeed explained as fivefold by Bodhivajra:
first, the appearance of a mirage; second, resembling smoke.
The third has the form of a firefly; the fourth is a blazing lamp;
the digit of darkness is the great bindu; and the luminous is the universal image.
When that which is not conceptually constructed is seen in emptiness with eyes that are both closed and half-closed,
like an image in a dream— one should always meditate upon that image.
Meditation on the form in its absence is not true meditation for yogins; rather, the fifth is the constant light, resembling a cloudless sky.

Thus, preceded by the appearance of a cloudless sky, there is the appearance of fire, which is the appearance of emptiness (*śūnyābhāsa*); this is *jvālā*. The appearances of the moon and the sun are well known. "Darkness" (*tama*) is the light of Rāhu, an appearance like a black jewel; "streak" (*kalā*) is the appearance of lightning; "the great bindu" (*mahābindu*) is the appearance in the form of a lunar mandala with the color of wind, illuminating the moving and the unmoving. These are the signs (*nimitta*). Because they arise from the vision of a cloudless sky, they constitute the yoga of the day and the yoga of open space.

Then, preceded by the vision of the Buddha-image consisting of the *saṃbhogakāya* situated in the center of that [light], there arises in a single instant the universal image (*viśvabimba*), which is luminous and possesses all aspects, as clear as water in the palm of one's hand, wherein jars, cloths, and so forth are perceived.

"Closed," and so forth: with eyes that are both closed and open—meaning with eyes half-opened, suspended in the intermediate space—one should meditate upon, that is, bring to personal experience, the "image" (*bimba*) such as smoke and so forth, which is non-conceptual, devoid of subject and object, and empty; this refers to the yogic direct perception (*yogipratyakṣa*). Both types of yoga have been taught in the *Śrīmad-Ādibuddha* with the passage beginning "unattached to space" (*ākāśāsakta*), and it is also stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: "The samādhi called Jewel-Light (*ratnāloka*);
the samādhi called Jewel-Lamp (*ratnapradīpa*)."
The concentration named *Candrāloka*,
the concentration named *Sūryapradīpa*,
up to the concentration named *Sarvākāradarśin*, and so forth— from these, one who seeks Buddhahood should cultivate the path beginning with smoke (*dhūmādimārga*) without any doubt.

[Objection: But surely the Mahāmudrā is marked by the stain of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), and meditation (*bhāvanā*) is a superimposition (*samāropa*); so how can it be said that one should "meditate"? To this he says, "non-existence," and so forth.

According to the instruction, when there is the non-existence of both the external and the internal, whatever meditation of yogins occurs upon that very [mental] image (*bimba*), that is not "meditation" precisely because of its non-existence.
[Objection: But are not existents always like the appearance of a cloudless sky, an appearance of uniform radiance?
Darkness, together with all that moves and is stationary.
The [cognition] leading to [liberation], preceded by [the preceding moments], is equally possible in a single moment in all its aspects.
Before [the state of] "hanging in the intermediate space," after "in the void," and after "not imagined"—yogic perception [is not like] smoke and so forth.
Before *svānubhavam*, there is a *daṇḍa* in manuscript G; [the text] should read *svānubhavam kuryāt ākāśā°*; [it is] called the "Lamp" (*pradīpa*) by one who desires Buddhahood;
"there is neither existence nor non-existence of the mind, because of the perception of the image (*bimba*) as non-conceptual."
Just as a young girl might see a reflection in a mirror that is not a real object,
so too does one who is disciplined in reality perceive past and future phenomena in the sky.
Its existence would not be an [ultimate] existence, because it is seen as an object devoid of substantial reality;
since there is no substance, the object exists like a magical illusion, a dream, or a conjuring trick.
For even when a substratum does not exist, this arising of qualities is observed,
like a wish-fulfilling gem that fulfills the hopes of infinite sentient beings.
A young maiden sees thieves and so forth in a mirror-divination (*pratisenā*) even though they are unseen.

Since there is no difference between the conceptualization of existence and the conceptualization [itself] in terms of being conceptualizations, one might ask: "How can there be no cultivation of non-existence? To this he says "existence," and so forth. This is because for the yogin, within the image of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bimba*), the conceptualizations of existence and non-existence do not exist.
Why? Because in the image of emptiness, there is the direct perception of unconstructed smoke and so forth.
This is the intended meaning:
if it were imagined (*kalpita*), then it would be a [mere] existence like a jar or a cloth; if it were unperceived, then it would be a non-existence like the son of a barren woman.
But here, because there is the perception of the unimagined (*akalpita*) through direct experience (*pratyakṣa*), everything is well-established.

In order to establish the vision free from conceptual construction (*avikalpita-darśana*), he provides a corresponding illustration, beginning with "prati-senā" and so forth: *pratisenā* refers to the visualization produced by the practitioner, which—though devoid of substantial reality—is perceived within a mirror, a sword-blade, a thumb, a lamp, the moon, the sun, water, or the eye, and is generated by [the presence of] thieves and the like.

For this non-conceptual vision, existence and non-existence do not exist, because it is perceived solely as the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) despite lacking a substantial entity (*nirvastuka*).

Even in the world, an object is seen to be without a substantial basis, as in the case of illusions, dreams, and magical displays (*indrajāla*). For this very reason, he says "non-existent" (*asatī*): when the subject (*dharmin*), such as the self and so forth, is non-existent, that arising of non-conceptual knowledge is like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) because it accomplishes the purposes of the world in all its aspects.
He states the establishment of the example, beginning with "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth.

A young girl whose eyes are empowered by mantras perceives even that which was previously unseen, such as thieves and the like, when the *pratisenā* [divination mirror] is present. Then, the practitioners who have brought about the *pratisenā* go to that place described by the girl and see it with their limited eyes—eyes that are obscured and whose range is restricted to only one part. This is the intended meaning.
yoginī

With eyes empowered by mantras and the instructions of the Siddhas, like a young maiden (*kumārī*), one is unerring; because there is no distinction in the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is no cultivation (*bhāvanā*) in the absence [of an object]. Conceptual constructions such as smoke and so forth would be like an imagined jar or cloth; they would be well-established through the power of thought. A *daṇḍa* is placed before *maya*. Like a web (*jālādivat*), it is unseen; it is unseen in the *pratisenā* (magical mirror/divination). It is partial (*pradeśika*); having gone with those partial eyes, the practitioners see that [object].
If it perceives that which has the nature of existence, why does it not perceive its own face? If it perceives that which has the nature of non-existence, why does it not perceive the horn of a hare?
One does not see with another's eyes, nor does one see with one's own eyes; that which is being seen is unborn, just like the birth of a barren woman's son.

Furthermore, by the first [verse], beginning with "The means by which Buddhahood is accomplished is called the state of a yogin" (CST I, cd–ab), it is taught that here the state of a yogin is twofold: mundane and supramundane. Among these, the supramundane state of a yogin is Buddhahood.
Its qualification is "supreme merit," because of the complete fulfillment of the accumulation of merit (*puṇya-sambhāra*).

Likewise, that which is "pure and the destroyer of evil" is the moon of the *bodhicitta*, which, because it is completely filled with the equipment of knowledge (*jñānasambhāra*), perceives that supramundane reality in the sky which is inaccessible to ordinary people who have not been instructed.
And because that [reality] is devoid of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), he says "if" (*yadi*).

Since it is not seen at other times by other eyes, and because one's own eyes are covered by the blindfold, through this analogy of the *pratisenā* (divinatory mirror-image), the direct perception of the yogi is in every respect unborn due to the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Like the perception of a girl’s son in a dream, the knowledge of the Omniscient One is established.
And it has been said: "Just as a maiden in this very dream... and so forth [cf. *Samādhirājasūtra* IX].
Now, he explains the sequence of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) by means of the *Saṃvara-tantra* and others, beginning with the words "the state of a yogin" (*yogitva*).

And it is said in the *Laghutantra*: "The state of a yogin is supreme merit, pure, and the destroyer of evil; it is accomplished through the recitation of mantra, through meditation, and through bliss."

Verses *ab* differ slightly in the manuscripts of the *Laghutantra* (*Herukābhidhānatantra*): *sidhyate japan mantram japena dhyānam eva ca* (Kaiser Library, MS , Mf. C /, fol. b-); *sidhyate japen mantram jāpena dhyānena ca* (Gaekwad Oriental Institute, Baroda, MS ).

"Purifying, destroyer of evil"—thus that state of Buddhahood is accomplished through the recitation of mantras and through meditation with ease; thus it is said here that the state of a yogi is accomplished for yogis by this means.
"Is accomplished" (*sidhyate*) is the reading of the scripture. This means is the yoga of six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), which is stated here in reverse order from the middle, omitting every other limb.
That very [member] which has not been explicitly stated previously is to be understood solely by the power of the subsequent stated member.
Just as when it is said, "This is the sun," the other—the moon—is apprehended by implication even though it is unstated;

likewise, a mutually dependent property, though unstated, is apprehended through the stated property. Therefore, in this tantra, although three subsequent members are indicated with one intervening [from the first], the middle stated member must be performed first; such is the tradition of the Guru, based on the Guru’s oral instruction.

Otherwise, if one were to follow the sequence of recitation as stated in the Tantra, then what indeed would be the "guru-sampradāya" (the tradition of the guru)? Therefore, by the phrase "guru-sampradāyena sam," the meaning is that the stage of meditation (*dhyāna*) must be recited prior to the mantra-recitation (*mantra-jāpa*), etc., according to the middle reverse order.
This [refers to] the three limbs not explicitly mentioned—withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and mindfulness (*anusmṛti*). "This" refers to the Sun.

"Another" means the purifier (*pavitra*): A, A₁, B; *pavitra*: C; *papitram*: B₁. "The destroyer of sin" (*pāpanāśanam*): A, A₁; [the word *pāpanāśanam* has been erased] because of the fulfillment of the equipment of knowledge (*jñānasambhāra*): B; "the destroyer of sin" means that very thing because of the fulfillment of the equipment of knowledge: B₁; "the destroyer of sin" because of the fulfillment of the equipment of merit (*puṇyasambhāra*): C. It is accomplished (*sidhyate*): A, A₁, B, B₁; it is accomplished (*sidhyati*): C.

And by means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). The word *ca* (“and”) appears only in manuscript A. “The state of being a yogin mentioned here” (*ihokta-yogitva*): A, B, C; “the state of being a yogin mentioned here” (*ihokta-yogitva*): B₁; “the reality of the yogin mentioned here” (*ihokta-yogatattva*): A₁; “buddhahood” (*buddhatva*): T (*sangs rgyas nyid*).

It is accomplished by yogins: *sidhyate yoginām*: A, A₁, T (*rnal ’byor pa rnams kyis [... ’grub par ’gyur ro*); *sidhyati yoginām*: C; *sidhyati yoginā*: B, B₁. In manuscript C, there is a daṇḍa after *sampradāyaḥ*, whereas in manuscript A, there is a daṇḍa after *sampradayena*.
Regarding the missing parts (*anuktāṅga*): other [parts] not mentioned here are to be understood as being found in other commentaries (*vyākhyā*) and translations (*bhāṣāntara*), etc.;
by that, one should understand them in every case.
Alternatively, [they are to be understood] through the commentary composed by a Bodhisattva, and not through those composed by those who merely imagine themselves to be learned.

Therefore, in this context, the other three limbs should be understood through the passage beginning with "by means of meditation" (*dhyānena*). The meaning condensed into these three limbs from the six limbs taught in other *aparatantra* [tantras] should be understood here. Regarding this, the Blessed One said in the *Samājottara*: "Withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), likewise meditation (*dhyāna*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), retention (*dhāraṇā*), recollection (*anusmṛti*), and meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—this is held to be the six-limbed yoga."
Therefore, withdrawal (pratyāhāra) should be understood as being preceded by meditative concentration (dhyāna).

Breath control (prāṇāyāma) should be understood as being preceded by mantra recitation (mantrajāpa). Here, by the term "mantra recitation," the recitation of the neuter [syllable] or the vajra-recitation, which is the retention of the vital breath (prāṇadhāraṇā), is meant.
The recollection of bliss preceded by happiness is to be understood here;
by the word "bliss," meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is meant. Thus, through these six limbs, the state of a yogin—that is, Buddhahood—is accomplished.

This refers generally to the accomplishment of worldly external yoga. The venerable Vajrapāṇipāda stated that in this *Laghutantra*, [the details] are to be understood from what is taught in other tantras, such as the *Śrīsamājatantra*.
In the *Śrīsamājottara*, in the eighteenth chapter,

it is stated that "vajra-recitation" (*vajrajāpa*) is the recitation of the neuter [syllable] by way of its presence in the *avadhūtī*; it is the contemplation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the ultimate recitation (*paramārthajāpa*), and the mental construction of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) above at the tip of the nose.
At the culmination of the excellence of that cultivation, breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) is cessation (*nirodha*).

And it should be understood as stated in the *Vimalaprabhā*: "By means of that [method], one should understand everything everywhere. [The reading] *boddhavyam* is found in A₁ and B; *bodhavyā* is in B₁. [The phrase] *nānyayā* is in B and B₁.

By those who have become arrogant through [false] scholarship (*pāṇḍityābhimānabhūtaiḥ*): A, A₁; *paṇḍitābhir mānabhūtaiḥ*: B, B₁; *vaṇḍitābhimānabhūtaiḥ*: C₁. By [the method] performed (*kṛtayeti*): B, B₁; *kṛtayā iti*: A, A₁, C. It is to be understood by means of [the passage beginning with] "etc. (*°ādināvagantavyam*): B₁, C; *°ādinā 'vagantavyam*: A, A₁, B₁. By what is stated in other tantras (*aparatantrāntaroktaiḥ*): A, A₁, B₁; *aparam tantrāntaroktaiḥ*: C; *aparatanträntaktiḥ*: B. The meaning (*'rtho*) is to be understood (*avagantavyaḥ*): A, A₁, B, B₁; *avantavyaḥ*: C. In the *Samājottara* (*samājottare*): B, B₁, C, T (*'dus pa phyir mar*); *śrīsamājottare*: A, A₁. The Blessed One said (*bhagavān āha*): A, B, B₁, C; *bhagavānn āha*: A₁. Withdrawal (*pratyāhāras*): A, A₁, B, B₁; *pratyāhāra*: C. Meditation (*dhyānam*): A, A₁, B, B₁; *dhyāna*: C. Recollection and meditative absorption (*anusmṛtiḥ samādhiś*): A, B, B₁, C; *anusmṛtisamādhiś*: A₁. Therefore (*ato*): A, A₁, B, B₁; T reads *ces so | de'i phyir* (*iti / ato*). Withdrawal preceded by [the practice of] mantra-recitation (*°pūrvaḥ pratyāhāro*): A, B, B₁; *°pūrvapratyāhāro*: A₁; *pūrvam pratyāhāro*: C₁. (The *daṇḍa* before *mantrajāpapūrvaḥ* is missing in Ac and A₁). Breath-control preceded by [withdrawal] (*°pūrvaḥ prāṇāyāmo*): A, B, B₁; *pūrvaprāṇāyāmo*: A₁; *°pūrvam prāṇāyāmo*: C. Recollection preceded by [breath-control] (*°pūrvānusmṛtir*): A, A₁, C; *°pūrvā 'nusmṛtir*: B, B₁. It is said (*ucyate*): A, A₁, B₁; *ity ucyate*: B (in this manuscript the word *ity* has been erased), C₁. Buddhahood (*buddhatvam*) is missing in C. By what is stated in other tantras (*°tantrāntaroktaiḥ*; *tantroktaiḥ*: G, T₁ [*rgyud gzhan du gsungs pas*]). Breath-control (*prāṇāyāmo*; *prāṇāyāmau*: G). [The Blessed One said: For beginners, for childish yogins, the worldly result is attained through the recitation of mantras, through meditation designated as withdrawal, through the mind that cultivates conceptualizations such as the maṇḍala-circle, through bliss, through the bliss of the movement of syllables [in the *karmamudrā* and *jñānamudrā*], and through the worldly truth up to the Akaniṣṭha realm.
Thus, through both stages, mundane and supramundane yogic accomplishment is achieved;

herein, supramundane yogic accomplishment is achieved by means of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), as it is explained: Here, "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*) means the non-engagement of the visual and other sense-faculties with external objects such as forms, and the engagement of the visual consciousness and other consciousnesses with internal objects by means of the divine visual and other sense-faculties.

The limb of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is said to be the vision of all phenomena as unconstructed by means of the objective support of internal emptiness—like a young girl seeing her own reflection in a mirror of emptiness. One should contemplate that [the breath] goes upward from the navel to the vision of the Buddha-image of the three realms as one desires, until the limit of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). One should contemplate the inhalation (*ucchvāsa*) in the nose, and likewise the exhalation (*niḥśvāsa*) below, until non-apprehension, as one desires.
The comprehension of words is the supreme, most secret tradition.

"Thus" means by means of the recitation of mantras (*mantrajāpa*). "Withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*) is the utterance of the syllable *oṃ* and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the divine eye-cognition (*divyacakṣurvijñāna*) and others; by the word "and so forth," the inclusion of the divine ear-cognition (*divyaśrotravijñāna*) and others is intended. [This pertains to] beginners (*ādikarmika*), [also called] child-yogins (*bālayogin*). [The term] "yogins" refers to those who practice yoga. The mundane result is absent in the Tibetan translation (*T*). After "result" (*phala*), a punctuation mark (*daṇḍa*) appears in manuscripts B, B₁, and C. "With a mind that cultivates non-conceptuality" (*avikalpabhāvanācitta*): A, B₁, C (in A and B₁ a *daṇḍa* follows here). A₁ reads *vikalpanābhāvanācittena*; B reads *cittena*; the term "conceptuality" (*vikalpa*) is absent in T. "With bliss" (*sukhena*): A, A₁. B, B₁, C, and T read *sukhena ca* ("and with bliss"). Regarding *jñānamudrā*, it is absent in C₁. Before "worldly truth" (*laukikasatya*), a *daṇḍa* appears in A and A₁. It is absent in T, which reads "with worldly happiness" (*'jig rten pa'i bde bas*). "The realm of Akaniṣṭha" (*akaniṣṭhabhuvana*): A, A₁. B, B₁, C read *akaniṣṭhan bhuvana*. "Supramundane" (*lokottara*): A, A₁, B, C. B₁ reads *lokottara*. Before "just as" (*yathā*), a *daṇḍa* appears in B, B₁, and C. "It is thus said" (*tathocyate*): A, A₁. B, B₁, C read *tathā ucyate*. Following these words, the compound *ṣaḍaṅgayoga* is added as a subtitle in the margins of A and A₁. "Non-arising" (*apravṛtti*): A, A₁, B (followed by a *daṇḍa*), C. B₁ reads *pravṛttiḥ*; it is absent in T. After "cognitions and so forth" (*vijñānādīnām*), a *daṇḍa* appears in all manuscripts. B, B₁, C read *pravṛttir*; A, A₁ read *pravṛtti*; it is absent in T. The term *iti* is absent in T. A *daṇḍa* precedes "all entities" (*sarvabhāva*) in B, B₁, and C. "Vision of existence" (*bhavadarśana*): A, B (corrected from *bhāvadarśane*). A₁ reads *bhāvanadarśanam*; B₁ reads *bhāvadarśana*; C reads *bhāvadarśane*. "In a mirror of clairvoyance" (*pratisenādarse*): B (corrected from *pratisenādarśanam*), B₁, C, T (*pra phab pas me long la*). Ac reads *pratisenādase*; A (corrected from *pratisenādarsene*), A₁ (corrected from *pratisenādarse*) read *pratisenādarśake*. After "like" (*iva*), a *daṇḍa* appears in B, B₁, and C. After "it is said" (*ucyate*), a *daṇḍa* appears in B, B₁, and C. "Buddha-image" (*buddhabimba*): A, A₁, C. B (corrected from *buddhadhabimba*), B₁ read *buddhabimba*. "Exhalation" (*niḥśvāsa*): G reads *nisvāsaḥ*. "By means of mantra-recitation" (*mantrajāpeneti*): T₁ (*sngags bzlas pas zhes pa la*). G reads *vajrajāpa iti* (followed by a *daṇḍa*). "By that name" (*tatsamjñena*): T₁ (*de'i ming can kyis so*). G reads *tatsamjñakena*. "Because of hearing" (*śanād iti*).
Then, "meditation" (dhyāna) refers to the state when all phenomena are seen as empty; "wisdom" (prajñā) refers to the engagement of the mind with them;
and "discursive thought" (vitarka) refers to the mind's grasping at entities.
Investigation (*vicāra*) is the realization that grasps the nature of phenomena;
passion (*rati*) is the mental application toward all phenomena;
and immovable bliss (*acalasukha*) is the attainment of happiness arising from all phenomena. Thus, there is entry into the navel, heart, throat, and forehead, but no exit to the exterior.
"The placement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the drop" is said to be the branch of meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*).

From that arises what is called "recollection" (*anusmṛti*), which is the vision of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) in the form of a reflection. Inhalation is characterized by entry; cessation is the state of stability; and exhalation is the nature of departure.

This meaning is established through one's own experience, is of definitive sense (*nītārtha*), and is accepted by the great Bodhisattvas such as Vajrapāṇi and others; it is not a subject for disagreement. Others, however, [explain it] otherwise, according to the influence of different purposes.
The vision of one’s own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*)— the direct realization of the non-conceptual Caṇḍālī—

is said to be the limb of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) by means of the intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣā*). Thereafter, through the central channel (*avadhūtī*), one should [visualize] the inhalation and exhalation as Rāhu and the Sun by means of the syllable *Oṃ*.

The limb of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is said to be the non-emergence [of the breath] externally at the forehead and the settling of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the drop (*bindu*). Thereafter comes the limb of recollection (*anusmṛti*): others, however, say it is the state free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
From that arises a circle of light (*prabhāmaṇḍala*) whose form flashes with many rays;
thereafter, the manifestation of the triple world (*traidhātuka*) in its manifold forms flashing forth—this is called the limb of recollection.

Then, from devotion to one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), there arises the attainment of imperishable bliss; the unification of the mind within that is called "concentration" (*samādhi*)—the mind devoid of subject and object—by the Tathāgatas.
Here, the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) has been taught in brief.
In detail, it should be understood by the yogi through the instruction of a true guru, either in the *Lakṣābhidhāna* or the *Paramādibuddha*, for the sake of attaining Mahāmudrā-siddhi.
In this regard, the instruction on the cultivation of the path beginning with the six limbs has been taught in other tantras.
Here, in the *Śrīsamājottara*, it is stated as service (*sevā*), near-attainment (*upasādhana*), attainment (*sādhana*), and great attainment (*mahāsādhana*).
The Blessed One himself said that very thing:
During the time of service (*sevā*), one should diligently visualize the form of Mahoṣṇīṣa;
during the time of the subsidiary practice (*upasādhana*), however, the form of Cakrī with the earrings of nectar;
and during the time of the main practice (*sādhana*), the practitioner intent on yoga should meditate upon the form of the deity.
That which reveals the reality of phenomena to beings of superior inclination by means of the employment of contradictory speech— that was spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhyābhāṣita*).
By that which has been thus described as the defining characteristic;
for the defining characteristic of the six corners (*ṣaḍkoṭi*) has been stated in the Tantra.
And so it is said in the *Śrīsamāja*:

The state of being at twilight, not at twilight, the interpretable meaning, and the definitive meaning; the throbbing mandala, the throbbing form, and the act of throbbing—I bow to that which is the instrument. Here, the grasped and the grasper are explained in detail for the sake of the yogi’s accomplishment through the teaching of the Buddha. Thus, in other tantras, the Blessed One stated in the *Śrīsamāja*: "At the time of the great sādhana, the uṣṇīṣa, the kuṇḍalī, the image, the Lord of Buddhas, the All-pervading One."

In this regard, by means of intentional terminology (*sandhyābhāṣā*), one should establish the *uṣṇīṣa*-image—the image of the Buddha—within the *dharmodaya* in space, encompassing the three realms without exception, as the mind-vajra (*cittavajra*). At the time of service, during the first stage, one should meditate by means of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and stabilize [the visualization] through the limb of meditation (*dhyānāṅga*). This is the promise of the Blessed One:
"Having abandoned all thought, one should examine for a single day.
If no sign (*pratyaya*) should appear therein, then those words of mine are false."
Thus, in this context, conviction arises from signs such as smoke and so forth, and not from anything else such as mantras, which could produce conviction for practitioners within a single day.

Therefore, having abandoned the notions of existence and non-existence and rendered them supportless, that which is profound in the void and beyond literal expression is proclaimed as *narutam* (the unspoken), the "Sixfold Apex" (*satkoṭi*).
It is clearly stated that the explicit teaching of reality was uttered without intentional ambiguity for the sake of awakening beings with dull faculties,
as appropriate within the rituals of the mandalas and so forth, and in the conduct [of the yogin].
An explicit explanation of the meaning is that which is spoken according to the literal sound;
words such as *koṭākhyaka* and others are excluded from both worldly usage and the treatises.
That which is proclaimed by the Tathāgatas as a conventional designation is called "unreal"; the Jina speaks that which explains the concealed reality as being of interpretable meaning (neyārtha).
Furthermore, he speaks the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) in order to illuminate the reality that truly exists.

Thus, "the reflection of the Buddha" refers to the vision of the three worlds—the triple realm—consisting of the various *saṃbhogakāyas* appearing as a black line situated within the great bindu. "All thought" is whatever conceptualization is performed by means of discursive thought (*vikalpa*).
The pervasive one, without support and without basis.

In this regard, when smoke and so forth are seen, there arises an internal cognition of the form of the Buddha; that cognition is cultivated as smoke and so forth by the yogin—this is the rule of the Tathāgata. Likewise, one should accomplish the three worlds by means of the instruments through the application of the bonds.

And thus, by means of the instruments such as the razor and so forth, one should accomplish the image of the Buddha within the three worlds. This very instruction is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru.
Therein, by the Guru’s instruction, the yogi first perceives smoke in the sky and not a mirage; this is to be known through one's own experience.
Then follows the mirage, and thereafter that same [vision] beginning with smoke, free from conceptual construction, like a *pratisenā* (magical reflection). Thus is the first sign, smoke.
The second is the sign of a mirage;
the third is the sign of a firefly;
the fourth is the sign of a lamp.
"The fifth sign is like a cloudless sky"—this was stated by the Blessed One both in the *Samājottara* and in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*.
Regarding that, the Blessed One said in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*:
"The mirage-sign is the second. This means that in other tantras it is understood in reverse order, such that the mirage-form is first.

This should be understood from the instructions of a true guru, from the commentaries composed by Bodhisattvas, and from one's own experience. Primarily through the non-duality of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), the five signs beginning with the mirage (*marīci*)—which are the forms of the purification of the five elements—are taught in the *Śrī-samāja* and other tantras. This is because even the space element (*ākāśa-dhātu*) is mentioned in the tantra; as it is said in the eighteenth chapter: "I bow to all those vast ones, equal to the Bodhisattvas: water, fire, wind, earth, and space" [GSU, cd]. The dissolution of earth into water takes the form of a mirage (*marīcikākāra*).
The dissolution of water into fire takes the form of smoke (*dhūmākāra*).
Because fire dissolves into air, it has the form of a firefly;
because the subtle element undergoes the three appearances, it has the nature of a mass of light like a lamp—therefore it is a "lamp" (dīpa). [The term] *marīcikā* refers to a mirage.

The *daṇḍa* after *paścāt* is missing in A, A₁, and B₁. *dvitīyam* in A, A₁, and B; *dvitīyakam* in B₁. *pradīpanimittam* in B, B₁, and C; *dīpanimittam* in A and A₁. *°sannibham nimittam iti* in A; *°sannibhanimittam iti* in B, B₁, and C; *°sannibham nimi* in A₁. *samājottare* in A and A₁ (with a *daṇḍa* after the word);
*samājottare 'pi* in B and B₁. *°oktam* in A and A₁; *oktaḥ* in B and B₁. After *āha*, a *daṇḍa* occurs in all manuscripts.
Primarily (*mukhyataḥ*), in the *Śrīsaṃāja* and other [tantras]...

from the element (*dhātoḥ*). Of the earth (*pṛthivyāḥ*), [the elements] beginning with earth... in the wind (*vāyau*). That [lamp] has the form of a lamp (*dīpākāram*). That indeed has omniscience as its cause; it brings one back to the vicinity of accomplishment (*siddhinikaṭe*).

"Subsequently, [one perceives] the form resembling an illusion, the form resembling a dream, moment by moment," and so forth. Therefore, according to these words of the Blessed One, at the beginning there arises the cognition consisting of the meditation on the signs such as smoke; yet some will say that [this occurs] at the time of accomplishment. All of them are violators of the Blessed One’s promise. Abandoning all thought, one should examine the cognition for a single day—such people are detractors of the Blessed One’s word. That worldly sign such as smoke which exists at the time of accomplishment is not like an illusion or a dream.

Because it possesses the capacity for the actual acts of burning, such as smoke and flames, there is likewise a rain of saffron, flowers, jewels, gold, and so forth; therefore, through the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), smoke and the other signs become the causal conditions. Thus, the Blessed One said in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*: "Therefore, one should meditate upon the six limbs, which are equal to self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*);

thereafter, one should perceive the signs by means of the sequence of the forward-order procedure. In this context, "self-consecration" refers to the vision of the truth of conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisatya*). [Cf.]

PK III, by means of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). The "sign" (*cihna*) refers to an appearance like clouds, smoke, and so forth; because it is the dissolution of appearances into their primordial nature (*prakṛti*), it is like a cloudless sky; and because its form is constant light, it is equal to a cloudless sky—thus there are five signs. And it was said previously: "The earth goes into water, water goes into fire, fire follows after wind, and wind enters consciousness (*vijñāna*). Consciousness, having become the limb of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), then enters the radiant (*prabhāsvara*)."

[Karmāntavibhāga, as quoted in GSPU, p. ... The first half of this stanza is hypermetrical; see above, p. ... °nikațe nivartakam A, A₁, C; °nikațe nirvvartakam B; °nikater nirvvartakam B₁ || °opamākāram A, B, B₁, C; °opakāram A₁.

A, A₁, C: *kṣaṇam*; B, B₁: *akṣaṇam*. A, A₁, B, B₁: *bhagavato*; C: *bhagavatokta°*. A₁, B, B₁, C: *vadiṣyanti* (with a daṇḍa following in B, B₁, and C; *vadiṣyante* in A₁). B, B₁, C: *bhagavataḥ* (with a daṇḍa following); A, A₁: *tathāgataḥ*. In T we read *de bzhin gshegs pa'i*, i.e., *tathāgataḥ*. *nimittam tan māyāsvapnopamam*.

It is like an illusion or a dream. By its power, one should perceive the sign of the jewel as equal; one should perceive the vision of truth, the vision of truth. In emptiness, there is a vision, an appearance like smoke and so forth—an appearance like smoke and so forth. Therein, the appearance of smoke and so forth first goes toward water; it goes toward water. It possesses the nature of being a limb of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and that is seen first, up to the limit of a lamp.

Then, in this tantra, another set of six signs beginning with the flame and ending with the drop has been taught by the Blessed One in the *Māyājāla* on the chapter of meditative absorption (*samādhi*),
as follows: "The self-arisen one born from space, the great fire of the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*), Vairocana of great radiance, the light of gnosis (*jñānajyotis*), the illuminator."

"The lamp of the world, the torch of gnosis, of great splendor, and luminous; the king of sciences, the foremost mantra, the king of mantras, the accomplisher of great purpose"—thus, in the *Māyājāla* through the yoga of day, the six signs whose nature is the purification of the six aggregates are taught by the verse beginning with "arisen from space."

In the *Śrīmad-Ādibuddha-tantrarāja*, however, the ten signs (*daśanimitta*), which are the forms of the purification of the objects, senses, wisdom (*prajñā*), and means (*upāya*), are primarily expounded. By means of these—namely, the divine eye and so forth obtained through the limbs of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*)—and by means of the conjunctions of binding because they are the cause for binding the vital breath (*prāṇa*), they take the form of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). The intended meaning is that this very withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is indeed [that]. This is because it is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*).
And it is said in the *Samājottara*:

The withdrawal of the ten sense-objects from all sides while they remain within their own respective domains is declared to be *pratyāhāra*; this is its specific definition with respect to the withdrawal of desires.

The sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*indriyārtha*), as well as their respective functions—meaning their engagement in the form of subject and object—are established therein. Regarding "established in their own function" (*svavṛttistha*): all things are divided into inferior, middling, and superior categories; these are "desires" (*kāma*) because they are desired and longed for as objects of enjoyment. These are forms (*rūpa*) and so forth, which are [perceived] by the senses. Beyond that, in the *Māyājāla-paṭala*, it is said: "He who arises from space, the Self-born (*svayambhū*), the light of gnosis (*jñānajyotis*), the eye of gnosis, the torch of gnosis, arisen from gnosis, the King of Knowledge (*vidyārāja*), the Supreme Mantra (*agramantra*), the King of Mantras (*mantrarāja*), the King of Kings in the Net (*jāle tantrarāje*). The sense objects and faculties are the branch of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). This is the intended meaning. "Free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous" (*kalpanāpoḍhābhrānta*) means free from the pride of conceptualization and non-delusory. It is declared that the "food" (*āhāra*) of the sense objects is taken from all sides. By these two verses, the Blessed One has taught in the *Māyājāla* another sign regarding the food established in its own function. Through the language of intentional terminology (*sandhyābhāṣā*), he refers to the appearance that arises from the previously mentioned cloudless sky; this is "arisen from space, the Self-born," meaning it arises from a mind devoid of all conceptual constructions. Here, "the fire of the wisdom of insight" (*prajñājñānānala*) refers to the appearance of flames.

"Vairocana, the great radiance" is the reflection of the moon; "he himself is the light of gnosis, Virocana" is the reflection of the sun, [meaning] "the lamp of the world"; "the torch of gnosis" is the reflection of Rāhu; "of great splendor, luminous" is the reflection of lightning;

"the King of Knowledge, the foremost Mantra Lord" is the reflection of the *bindu*, appearing in the form of a blue-colored lunar disc. "The King of Mantras, the accomplisher of great purpose"—this is seen by the yogi through the practice of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) as the reflection of all phenomena of the three realms in all their aspects, equal to an illusion, a dream, or a mirror-image. This occurs by means of the instruments of the senses, such as the eyes.

Then, by means of these instruments— the conjunctions of the bonds through the practice of breath control— one should accomplish the three worlds characterized by the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, which consist of both stable and moving natures. Thus the Blessed One said in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*:

The entire triple world, including all that moves and is stationary, together with as many beings as possess vajra-bodies in all the world-realms, is accomplished without exception or remainder. The repeated taking up and grasping of each [object] again and again is *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal); this is the specific instruction for the first limb.

It is the subsequent sign, the previously mentioned appearance, the moon, the light of gnosis (*jñānajyotis*), the radiance of the agitation of gnosis, Vairocana, the lamp of waking, the torch of gnosis, the great splendor arising from gnosis, the blue king of mantras, the king of mantras of all forms, and the *pratisenā* (magical reflection) for the yogin by means of withdrawal.

By means of these—the primary faculties (*indriya*), the bond of the faculties (*indriya-bandhana*), and the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpya*)—whether stable or moving (*sthiracala*), in that very manner, the *vajra* [nature] is entirely, without remainder, the triple world with its moving and non-moving beings (*traidhātukacarācara*). Thus, through the cultivation of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayogabhāvanā*), this is the rule of the Blessed One. Likewise, in the *Śrī-samāja*, the Blessed One said: "In the absence [of intrinsic nature], there is no cultivation; cultivation is indeed not cultivation."
Thus, being is not being, and no mental cultivation (bhāvanā) is perceived.

Therefore, here, in the absence [of objects], within the cloudless sky, mental cultivation is withdrawal (pratyāhāra). That very thing is the absence of mental cultivation in the absence [of objects];

thus, mental cultivation is indeed not mental cultivation. Here, that mental cultivation which is withdrawal in the absence [of objects], within the cloudless sky—that cultivation is indeed not cultivation.

"Because it is devoid of conceptual cultivation (*vikalpabhāvanā*). That entity which is perceived through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) would not be an entity, because one perceives entities of the past, future, and present as being non-conceptualized; therefore, conceptual cultivation is not found within the cultivation of withdrawal. This is the word of the Blessed One.
This cultivation was also spoken of by the Blessed One in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, as follows:

That reality which has been seen and made manifest through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) characterized as previously described is neither a [conventional] entity nor a non-entity; for how could it have a conceptualized form?

This is because, through one-pointedness of the non-conceptual mind, there is the vision of entities—past, future, and present—which are themselves non-conceptualized. Thus, a limb of meditation (*dhyāna*) is described. And it is said: "In brief, the five objects of desire are the application of the five Buddhas; conceptualization is called meditation (*dhyāna*), and that meditation is fivefold."
And applied thought, and sustained thought, and joy, and likewise pleasure.

"By the cultivation of the six-limbed yoga," "by the cultivation of the six-limbed yoga," "by the cultivation of the six limbs," "by the cultivation of the six-limbed yoga," "the six-limbed cultivation"—in the *Śrīsamāja*, in this assembly, in this existence, in non-existence, in the cloudless sky, in non-existence itself, there is cultivation; the cultivation of entities, the cultivation of the state of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), the cultivation of the nature of withdrawal, the cultivation in the cloudless sky, in the sky—there is cultivation, cultivation indeed, cultivation indeed—thus it is called "cultivation. It is conceptualization; it is an entity; it is an entity. Thus, as an entity, it is unconceptualized; as unconceptualized, it has come into the present. Because of the perception of entities, because of the perception of the non-existence of entities, because of the non-perception of entities and non-existence, and because of the non-perception of entities and non-existence occurring in the present, no cultivation is apprehended. Regarding cultivation, there is speech; such as might be said, or is being said. Then, indeed, Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the venerable Subhūti in this way:

"O noble Subhūti, where will he who attains yoga in this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) attain that yoga? Subhūti replied, "Kauśika, he who attains yoga in the perfection of wisdom will attain yoga in space; he will attain yoga in the open air, Kauśika. One-pointedness of mind—these five are the constituents of meditative absorption (dhyāna). The three secrets, as well as applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra), arise from its enjoyment."

The third is the appearance of joy; the fourth is the gathering of bliss. One's own mind is to be known as the fifth, wherein the arising and passing away of both knowledge and the object of knowledge occur.
It consists of all Buddhas, is peaceful, and is established in all space.

Thus is the explanation of the second limb for the purification of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). The five objects of desire, such as form and so forth, which have become the objects of the sense faculties, are unified with the sense faculties in brief; the five Buddhas, such as the Eye-Buddha and so forth, are joined together through their application as the five Buddhas. Therefore, the conceptualization that even form and the other [objects] are the five Buddhas—such a purified conceptualization is meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), and that is fivefold according to the divisions of applied thought (*vitarka*) and so forth.

Regarding the passage beginning with "vitarka" (initial inquiry) and so forth, this is an explanation of the classifications. The "three secrets" (*guhyatraya*) refers to the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses;

the five sense faculties and the cognitions of those faculties, along with their objects, have the nature of the five Tathāgatas. The thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*) of this is "initial inquiry" (*vitarka*).
The state of sustained investigation (*vicāraṇa*) within that very [knowledge] is "sustained inquiry" (*vicāra*).

For one who investigates in this way, that which has the characteristic of mental well-being (*saumanasya*) due to being oriented toward entering reality is what resembles joy (*prīti*). That bliss (*sukha*) which is attained through the penetration of reality and has the characteristics of physical pliancy (*kāyapraśrabdhi*) and so forth, is the inclusion of bliss. For one who practices in this manner, by reaching the ultimate limit of excellence, there occurs the arising of knowledge—the six functioning consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness—and the objects of knowledge, from form up to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); this is "the arising of knowledge and the object of knowledge. The cessation of that [arising] is the one-pointedness of mind characterized by the thorough knowledge of the emptiness of subject and object; this is called "one's own mind" (*svacitta*).

Thus, such a mind—consisting of all Buddhas, peaceful, mere appearance, and having the single ultimate of universal emptiness as its final resort—is born; this is the second limb, characterized by five divisions:
"space" through the yoga of night, and "open space" through the yoga of day.

Of the gods, of the deities, O Indra, the long-lived one—Indra, the long-lived one—here, here he will drink, he will eat, he will attain, he will obtain, he will consume, he will reach, he will succeed; Subhūti will obtain, he will eat, he will attain, he will obtain, he will eat, he will reach, he will succeed. In the open air—and thus "in the open" (avakāśe) and "and also" (ca)—there are three and three: applied thought (vitarka) upon applied thought, reasoning (tarka) upon reasoning, investigation (vicāra) upon investigation, inclusion (saṃgraha) upon inclusion, passing away (vyaya) upon passing away; all space, all desire, the faculties (indriya), the faculties—the application; the instigation.
Investigation (*vicāra*) is the state of investigating; investigation is the investigation of stability (*sthiti*), which is pliancy (*praśrabdhi*);
one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*) is single-mindedness.

"Whoever, desiring to attain the body of the directions during the day, thinks they should train in the *prajñāpāramitā*"—this refers to the meditation on *mahāmudrā*, which the Blessed One has described as being like a reflection or an illusion in a cloudless sky. Thus, the limb of service (*sevāṅga*) is said to consist of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Then, by the term *amṛtakundalī-bimba* (the reflection of the Amṛtakundalī), the wind is spoken of through the language of intentional terminology (*sandhyābhāṣā*). That [wind] is of five kinds; likewise, the Blessed One said in the *Samājottara*: "One should emanate the breath consisting of the five jewels, empowered by the five Buddhas, and visualize it in the form of a sphere at the tip of the nose."

Thus, here, by the term "five jewels" (*pañcaratna*), the five elements beginning with earth—which possess the nature of the five maṇḍalas of the *rasanā*—are meant; the breath consisting of these is the "five-jewel breath" in the right nostril. Likewise, the five aggregates beginning with consciousness—which possess the nature of the five maṇḍalas of the *lalanā* and consist of the five Buddhas—are meant; the breath presided over by them is in the left nostril. By the passage beginning with "by means of the designation of the form of Amṛtakundalī," the third limb, *prāṇāyāma*, is described. And it has been said: "The great jewel of five colors is known as *prāṇāyāma*."

"Having meditated on one's own mantra in the heart, one should place the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the *bindu*. This is the specific instruction that is stated. That which consists of five syllables and has the nature of the five Tathāgatas is therefore the "Great Jewel. That by which the vital breath—the life-force—is restrained (*āyāmyate*), meaning extended for a long duration, is known as *prāṇāyāma*.

Having meditated upon one’s own mantra in the heart—that is, in the lotus of one’s own heart—because it is practiced day and night by means of the *bindu* whose nature consists of entry and so forth, one should place the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as having entered the *bindu*; this is the third limb.
[Before *savyanāsāpute*, there is a *daṇḍa* in B; in B and C, the *daṇḍa* is missing before *tathā*. Regarding the term *°dharmiṇo*: A, B, B, C; *°dharmine*: A.]
Before *tair*, the *daṇḍa* is absent in A, AB, and B.
This is also quoted in PK I (ed., p. ...), AK (ed., p. ...), and GSPU (ed., p. ...).
"Smṛtaḥ" means conjectured; "smṛtaḥ" means considered.
Before *svāhṛtaḥ*, there is a *daṇḍa* in the line.
Having meditated; having known; in T we read "having reflected."

Having thus emitted [it] "in the form of a *piṇḍa*," here the *piṇḍa* refers to the unification of the left, right, and central mandalas within the central channel (*avadhūtī*) of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*).
Having emitted that vital breath in the form of a *piṇḍa*, one should visualize it at the tip of the nose.
Here, by the word "nose" (*nāsikā*), the pericarp of the lotuses located at the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown of the head is meant.
One should meditate upon that at the tip of the nose; one should meditate within the pericarp, in the center of the pericarp, and not on the petals of the lotus to the left or right.

Thus, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is restrained in the form of a drop (*bindu*) at the location of the *bindu*; by that very means, its retention (*dhāraṇā*) is described. In this way, the secondary practice (*upasādhana*) is performed by means of the orb of Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
That very secondary practice is called "vajra-recitation" (*vajrajāpa*).

It should be recited with the tongue not separated from the middle [palate]; thus, it is not by means of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the left or right channels. When the image of the *uṣṇīṣa* is seen, the vital breath is subsequently restrained in the form of a sphere (*piṇḍa*) at the location of the drop (*bindu*). By that means, its retention is described; this is the limb of retention (*dhāraṇā*). And it has been said:
"When one's own jewel-like sense organ is restrained, one should maintain [the mind]—this is known as retention."
This is its detailed explanation:

one's own forms and so forth are the objects (*viṣaya*), and the eyes and so forth are the sense faculties (*indriya*). When those respective sense faculties have ceased—that is, dissolved—into the jewel that serves as the substratum for both object and faculty, and when the jewel of the mind (*cittaratna*) has also ceased and set along with the regulation of breath (*prāṇāyāma*), whatever one maintains therein is "retention" (*dhāraṇā*). What is that? It is the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). This is the fourth limb, known as retention.

The explanation of the phrase "it should be recited with the central [channel] undivided from the limbs" is: "by means of the non-circulation in the left and right channels of one who is without breath.

And it has been said: "One who eats alms-food should not recite, nor should he be intent on begging for alms. [The unity of the mandalas: *piṇḍamaṇḍalānām ekatvam* (the oneness of the clusters and mandalas): A, A T; *piṇḍamaṇḍalānām ātmakatvam* (the nature of the clusters and mandalas): B, B C.

This is also quoted in the GSPU and in the SUȚ: "When one's own jewel-like faculty has ceased" (niruddhe svendriye ratne) [G, GSPU]; "the jewel-like faculty has ceased" (niruddham indriyam ratnam) [SUȚ, GSPU, SUT]; [in the GSPU and SUT, *smṛtam* was later corrected to] *smṛtim* [G].
"By non-practice" means: by non-application.
"By one who subsists on alms-food... [as found in] G II st., NGMPP, Mf. A/3, fol. ba.

"The practitioner should perform [this]," such is the Guru’s instruction; it is to be understood through the language of intentional terminology (*sandhyābhāṣā*). Next, the "subsidiary means" (*upasādhana*) consisting of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is described.

Then, regarding the "deity-image in the means" (*sādhana*): here, by the power of concentration, the yogi perceives the Caṇḍālī blazing at the navel—free from all obscurations, resembling a *pratisenā* (magical reflection), the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), emitting clouds of infinite Buddha-rays, and resplendent with a circle of light. That is called "recollection" (*anusmṛti*); that is called the "means" (*sādhana*).
The rule is that at the conclusion of the *dhāraṇā*, one should meditate upon the yoga of *caṇḍālī*.

Then, by the flame of her gnosis (*jñānārcis*), the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), and so forth—consisting of consciousness and the rest, as well as earth and the other elements, which are of the nature of the mandalas and situated within the left and right channels—are burned and become unified as one. Having entered the lunar mandala in the forehead, they [merge].

Then, when the moon has been melted by the flame of gnosis (*jñānārcis*) of the Caṇḍālī, that bodhicitta descends in the form of a drop (*bindu*) through the throat, heart, navel, and the secret lotus, having the nature of joy (*ānanda*), supreme joy (*paramānanda*), and cessation (*viramānanda*); thereafter, up to the vajra-jewel, it has the nature of innate joy (*sahajānanda*).

Alternatively, it has the nature of the distinct characteristics of the diverse (*vicitra*), the ripening (*vipāka*), the crushing (*vimarda*), and the signless (*vilakṣaṇa*). Thus, with the sixteen digits complete, one should recite the mantra whose limbs are indivisible, which effects the enjoyment of all things at all times.
Thus, "alms-food" (*bhaikṣa*) refers to eating alms; "articulation" (*uccāraṇa*) is called "perception" (*upalambha*);
"mantra" refers to the convention known as the reality of mantra, which consists of entry, abiding, emergence, and analytical observation;
and "the indivisible limb" is suchness, the ultimate, which is the state of the indivisible middle way.
"Recollection (*anusmṛti*) is said to be the means.

*bhinnākārākṣaram*; *bhinnā akārākṣaram*: G | *bhikṣāśanam*; *bhikṣā bhikṣā aśanam* (followed by a daṇḍa): G | *pravyāhāro°*: G, *Yogimanohara* by Muniśrībhadra (ed. p.); in T₁ we read *so sor sdud pa* (*pratyāhāro°*).
*saṃketa*; *sāṃketam*: In G II, after *pāramārthikam*, there is a daṇḍa.
In G II it says: "When [it] gives bliss included within [the body] by the power of meditative cultivation, similar to the bliss of emission (*cyavana-sukha*)"—this is merely an illustration.
In its essential nature, the pleasure born of the two organs does not equal even a thousand-millionth part of the supreme unchanging pleasure (*paramākṣarasukha*).
Here, that state of unchanging pleasure which consists of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) is an indescribable state, unknowable to novice yogins;
by the Bodhisattvas, it is called the "samādhi of emptiness" (*śūnyatāsamādhi*).
Furthermore, it does not follow the meaning of nihilism merely by conforming to worldly convention.
Thus, through the six-limbed yoga, the recitation of mantras, meditation, and bliss, the supreme Buddhahood of yogins is accomplished—[a state] most meritorious, pure, and destructive of evil.
In this very life, the rule regarding the goal and the practitioner has been declared by the Blessed One.
One should indeed stabilize that [wind] and expand it through the path of the vajra into the elements of space (khadhātu).
Having visualized it by means of recollection, one should cause it to pervade in that very form.

Thus, by means of the vajra-path through the sequence of the five signs that are difficult to traverse, one should emanate the stable and pure mind in the form of the *dharmakāya* throughout the *lokadhātus* within the *khadhātus*.

Having thus meditated upon and directly realized oneself as having entered the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), one should cause that very same [mind] to pervade [all things] in that same sequence, in the form of the *bhūtakoṭi* which was previously reached through recollection (*anusmṛti*) in the manner of a mirage and so forth.

This fifth limb just mentioned, "recollection" (*anusmṛti*), is that state whose nature is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*); by the words ending with "is called the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatābodhi*) by the Bodhisattvas," meditative absorption (*samādhi*) has been described.
And it has been said:
Having briefly withdrawn all phenomena through the meditative union of wisdom and means, one should visualize the image in the center by means of the yoga of the mass;
this instantaneous perfection of gnosis is designated as "samādhi."

II 135. Furthermore, in reality (*tattvataḥ*), the cause here is both with all aspects (*sarvākāra*) and without aspects (*nirākāra*).

The entity perceived through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*)—such as a pot or a cloth—which appears like a reflected image (*pratisenā*), possessing all aspects, free from conceptual construction, and non-erroneous because it is seen directly (*pratyakṣa*); which is formless because it transcends the nature of atoms and is devoid of conceptualization; and which is accessible only to those whose eyes are closed or half-closed: therefore, it is neither form, nor other than form, nor accessible by the eye, nor without the eye. Thus, the cause that is both with-aspect and without-aspect is the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) endowed with the excellence of all aspects, and so forth.
This very same point was stated by the venerable Mahābodhisattva Śrīvajragarbha in the *Śrīhevajraṭīkā*, beginning with the words:
"The entity is that which is to be meditated upon," and so forth.
Here, in this space, the entity to be meditated upon is like a dream, transcending the nature of even the most subtle atom.

Through the thorough knowledge of that [reality], one should realize the non-existence of existence; that is, having unified all existence—both the stationary and the moving—which exists by way of the union of conventional and ultimate truth through the meditative absorption of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya-samāpatti*) in the form of a single mass, namely the form of Mahāmudrā, one should contemplate and know the state of the Great Vajradhara, whose nature is the union of the two, in the midst of that which is stationary and moving. By this sequence, the instantaneous perfection of gnosis in a single moment is "samādhi"; this is the sixth limb.
Thus, according to the sequence of the *Samāja*, is the sequence of the six-limbed yoga, beginning with the words "existence" (*bhava*) and "that which is to be realized" (*bhāvya*).
Furthermore, in terms of reality:

Possessing all aspects yet devoid of aspects; seen as appearing [like] a prognostic image (*pratisenā*). "Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is said to be that which is a clear appearance, free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*)," and so forth.
Thus it was stated in the *Tantrottara* by the venerable Mañjuśrī, the Lord of the Ten Bhūmis:

"The one endowed with the power of the Ten Powers has taught the cultivation of emptiness through the six [branches] beginning with withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). Furthermore, at night there is the yoga of smoke and so forth, and during the day as well, the lamp and so forth in the sky. Through withdrawal, the yogi perceives that which resides in the expanse of the sky—the form of the three times. Therein, by means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he makes the mind firm, having abandoned external entities."

During the night of darkness, one should cause the vital wind (*prāṇavāta*)—devoid of both moon and sun and free from inhalation and exhalation—to flow by means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Furthermore, by means of the limb of meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*), through the recollection (*anusmṛti*) of the drop (*bindu*) in space, great rays of light issue forth from one's own reflection like those of the moon; through meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the semen (*śukra*) proceeds to the head, completely filled with the bliss of stainlessness.

Through the sky-like vision of delusion (*moha*), its destruction occurs by the perception of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); through the internal vision of passion (*rāga*), its destruction occurs when the vital wind is restrained.
"Through the thorough knowledge of existence and that which is to be meditated upon, wisdom arises;
and likewise, through the thorough knowledge of non-existence, Heruka is to be meditated upon"— thus it is stated in the Śrī Hevajra Tantra.
By the Holder of the Great Vajra, who possesses the power of the Ten Strengths,
the cultivation of emptiness is the realization of the emptiness of all aspects at night in the darkness.
During the day, when there is light,

it has the form of the three sacrificial fires; at night, within the *avadhūtī*, it is devoid of inhalation and exhalation due to the absence of outward emission, possessing the forms of the desire, form, and formless realms.

From one's own reflection (*svabimba*) and the universal reflection (*viśvabimba*), by means of the gaze directed toward space—the gaze suspended in the intermediate state—there is the destruction of delusion (*moha*), which is its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*); and that is Locanā. By means of the internal gaze—the gaze at the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), and so forth—there is the destruction of passion (*rāga*), which is its lack of intrinsic nature; and that is Pāṇḍarā.

By means of the gaze of love—the gaze of innate passion (*sahajanurāga*) toward the empty image endowed with the excellence of all aspects—there is the destruction of hatred (*dveṣa*), that is, worldly hatred, which is its lack of intrinsic nature, its unobstructedness, and the illumination of the manifestation (*pratibhāsālokana*); [this is] the illumination of the terminology (*paribhāṣālokana*).
