[The sequence of] the aggregates, sense-bases, and so forth; [the sequence of] the aggregates and so forth, the sense-bases and so forth (later corrected); emptiness; [the state of] emptiness. Through the gaze upon the nose, there occurs the destruction of hatred by means of the bliss of the stainless semen; through the gaze upon the tongue, there occurs the destruction of pride by means of the unstruck Brahma-sound. When breath-control is restrained, the stainless mandala indeed arises from the Buddha-image. The pair of stages occurs respectively in the head and throat, and in the heart, navel, secret place, and crown of the head.

Because the Teacher, the Buddha, is free from the three impurities and possesses the vajras of body, speech, and mind, even though the semen (*śukra*) has ascended upwards and the *rajas* has descended downwards, he remains untouched by the unstruck Brahma-sound (*anāhatabrahmaghoṣa*).
That state of great hatred is Vajradhātvīśvarī; that bliss which arises from the purity of the semen is [the state of] Māmakī.

Through the "nose-vision"—that is, through the vision directed toward the intermediate space characterized by the nose—there is the destruction of ordinary pride, which is its state of being without obscuration (*nirāvaraṇatā*). And that [destruction] is Māmakī, arising from the unstruck Brahma-sound, which is the manifestation of the sound of unstruck great bliss.

When the breath is restrained through the absence of outward emission during *prāṇāyāma*, and the limb of *dhāraṇā* becomes manifest, the innate *caṇḍālī* of non-conceptualization becomes vivid; from the Buddha-image, which is the universal image, the stainless lunar disc—the circle of pure radiance—comes into being and arises. Because worldly envy is exhausted, she is the Savior (*tāraṇī*).

When the six wheels are present, through the semen (*śukra*) moving upward and the passion (*rajas*) moving downward, from the unassailable sound of Brahma arises the radiance of the supreme syllable of great bliss (*paramākṣara-mahāsukha*), which is the destruction of envy; and she is the Mother of the Universe (*viśvamātā*). Thus, by means of the sequence of perceiving two stages (*bhūmi*) at each wheel, one becomes a master of the twelve stages.
For instance, at the secret wheel (*guhyacakra*), by the cessation of three thousand six hundred inhalations and exhalations, the two stages of Pramuditā and Vimalā are attained;
likewise, at the navel wheel (*nābhicakra*), by such cessation, the two stages of Prabhākārī and Arciṣmatī are attained.
In the same way, the two stages beginning with Sudurjayā are in the heart-lotus; the two stages beginning with Dūraṅgamā and Acalā are in the throat-lotus;
and the two stages beginning with Sādhumati and Dharmameghā are in the ūrṇā-lotus.

These Bodhisattva stages are indeed five dyads; likewise, the Buddha stage is the Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhā*), and the Vajradhara stage is the Knowledge-Possessing (*jñānavatī*). Thus, through the cessation of twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths, one becomes the Blessed Buddha—the Lord of the twelve stages, the teacher of non-conceptual Dharma, whose body, speech, and mind are vajras, and who is free from the three stains.
By this sequence, the purification of the six wheels beginning with the [Bodhisattva] stages is shown through the direct realization of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*).

The arising of each of the five eyes is described as follows: [the eyes] are located in the head, throat, heart, navel, and secret place. Furthermore, for the earth element, there are two in the head; likewise, in the head, throat, heart, navel, and secret place, they occur in sequence.
Also, that which is "yat" is "yatat";
[the eyes] are the nose and the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
By means of the view, there is no punishment; and she is Māmakī; Locanā is Māmakī.

After *°ghoṣād*, there is a daṇḍa in II; before *buddhabimbād*, there is a daṇḍa; before *vimala*, there is a daṇḍa in II; before *mātsarya°*, there is a daṇḍa in *prabhākary*; *prabhākarī*: *pañcadvayāny eva*: in this [text] we read *Inga kho na* (= *pañcaiva*); *pavau*: *tathaivo°*; *tatathaivo°*: II. For dogs and the like, it is the flesh-eye (*māṃsacakṣuḥ*); for gods, by virtue of their natural qualities, it is the divine eye (*divyacakṣuḥ*); for Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, it is the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) located in the human heart; this is the third.

The fourth is the stainless and pure eye of wisdom (*prajñācakṣus*) among the Bodhisattvas; the fifth is the all-seeing eye of knowledge (*jñānacakṣus*) of the Buddhas, which is free from the three stains. The seminal essence (*śukra*) is the bliss of immobility and the thunderbolt (*kuliśa*); by holding that, one is indeed Vajradhṛk. *Jinajik* is the seed-syllable of the body. That bliss which exists at the navel-wheel is the object of perception; perceiving that, the Lord experiences supreme bliss at the heart, and he is Ārolika. He by whom the immovable bliss is held in the throat is the experiencer, and he is Ratnadhṛk.

[39] By whomsoever this stainless bliss of semen (*śukravaimalyasaukhya*) has been held upon the head in the tantra— that wisdom (*prajñā*) which is the supreme unchanging bliss (*akṣaraparamasukha*) full of sixteen joys in the *uṣṇīṣa* at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*),

that wisdom which is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvā*), the sixteenth digit of the supreme moon, full at the end of the full moon, that infinite knowledge (*vidyā*) whose head is with the thunderbolt (*sakuliśa*)— he is the sixth Vajrasattva. [40] When the disks of the moon and sun have vanished, when the vital wind (*prāṇavāta*) is always restrained in both paths, when the lotus and the thunderbolt are awakened, and when the molten moon has entered the great solar disk.

By means of the words beginning with *nāma*, [the author] now states that for one who has been rendered free from obscurations through the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) and who resides in the pericarp of the lotuses of the six wheels, there is the nature of the six Tathāgatas—due to the influence of the qualities of primordial nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*) and the influence of the qualities of caste (*jāti-guṇa*). He says this starting with the word *niḥspanda*: *Vajradhṛk* is Akṣobhya; *Jinajik* is Vairocana; *Ārolik* is Amitābha; *Ratnadhṛk* is Ratnasambhava; and *Prajñādhṛk* is Amoghasiddhi. By this, the purification of the six aggregates (*ṣaṭskandha-viśuddhi*) is stated.

When the orbs of the moon and sun have vanished and been destroyed within one’s own body— the tongue, the throat, and the channels— and when the vital wind (*prāṇavāta*) is restrained in both paths, namely the two nostrils, due to the absence of the outward emission of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* winds; when the lotus situated in the space of the five wheels has become manifest as the image of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), or when the external lotus of the woman, or the *vajra*, or the *cittavajra*, or the *bola* has awakened— meaning it has been raised up according to the previously mentioned sequence, thus "the awakened *vajra*"— and at that time, the moon which is the semen (*śukra*) has melted, [it enters] into that great solar orb, the innate joy (*sahaja*).

Consciousness and gnosis become one when the moon and sun are obstructed by the wind; in this way, in that way, and likewise in another way, there are these three types, and nothing else exists.

The wheel is pure on all sides; the triple existence is bliss, its passion is the jewel, the destruction of afflictions is the lotus, the sword is the vajra, for the body of great gnosis is indeed indivisible.

The "cutting" here refers to the agency of ignorance; those six families produced by these [elements] should also be understood in this way: when the moon has entered, gone, and melted into the support—the reflection of the channels, elements, and sense-faculties—which is like space, of a single flavor, and wherein existence and non-existence have become one, it is the body that has attained the threefold existence, inseparable from emptiness and compassion.

When the *anāhata*—which is free from the impurities of speech and mind—is fully awakened through the radiance of supreme unchanging great bliss (*paramākṣaramahāsukha*), at that time, in the moment of the arising of great bliss, that yogin who has realized the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) proceeds to the supreme state, the ultimate state, established in the innate bliss of the primordial joy (*sahajānandasukha*).
For that yogin, there exists no duality whatsoever characterized by the attachment to self and other.

And when the *prāṇa* and *apāna* winds are restrained, the moon (*śaśadhara*), agitated and melted by the flame of the fierce woman (*caṇḍālī*), goes toward and embraces the solar disc (*sūryabimba*).

The meaning is that when the *vajra*, which is the *bodhicitta*, and the *padmas* and *cakras* have been awakened—that is, when the Tathāgata has been raised up according to the previously mentioned sequence—and [the *bodhicitta*] flows, having become liquefied (*druta*), then this "Moon-bearer" (the *bindu*) becomes one with the radiance of the solar orb; consciousness (*vijñāna*) and gnosis (*jñāna*) become one, and when the Moon and Sun are obstructed and thus free from obscuration, that which has arisen as supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*) cannot be expressed in words, and is therefore to be understood through experience alone. It consists of the essence of the syllables *E* and *VAṂ*. By means of its threefold vocalization, he declares its truth in every respect.

The purification of the signs is described by the words "the wheel" and so forth. "In the three realms" means [abiding] in existence (*srid par gnas pa’i*). Of whom? Of him. Whose? Of him. When obstructed (*niruddhe*), when opposed (*viruddhe*). There would be nothing further (*bhaven nāparam*). The sword (*asiḥ*). The great gnosis-body (*mahājñānakāyaḥ*). Then the gnosis-body (*jñānakāyaḥ*). But here, the excellent knife (*kartrī varā*). Even the six (*sad api*). Even the six (*ṣaḍ api ca*).

That in which the form of birth (*jātirūpa*) goes to its destruction is called the Great Form (*mahārūpa*); that in which the suffering of saṃsāra goes to its destruction is called Great Sensation (*mahāvedanā*).

That in which the notion of saṃsāra reaches its end is the notion of the Great Vajra; that in which the perception of saṃsāra reaches its end is indeed the vajra-formation (*vajrasaṃskāra*). For the sake of maturing those who are deluded, there is the clear wheel of Vairocana;

By means of the phenomenon of unobstructed perception, for those possessed of passion, there is the lotus of Amitābha as the cause of great passion; for Amoghasiddhi, there is the sword signifying the destruction of the afflictions; for Akṣobhya, there is the vajra signifying the indestructible body; and for the sixth family, there is the curved knife signifying the cutting away of ignorance. He who was Ratneśa became the bearer of the lotus for the sake of those suffering from passion, while Amoghasiddhi, with his lotus-hand holding a sword, appeared for the purpose of destroying the obstacles of passion. In whom all delusion goes to its destruction, she is Locanā; in whom all pride goes to its destruction, she is Māmakī; in whom all passion goes to its destruction, she is Pāṇḍarā; in whom all envy goes to its destruction, she is Tāriṇī, and she is the wind element. He who perceives forms, whether visible or invisible, in the mind or indeed in space, is the eye; he hears sound clearly from afar, for this is the great faculty of hearing belonging to the Jina. That nose of the Lord which grasps every scent that brings supreme bliss is the tongue, which always tastes the nectar of its own moon and bestows happiness.

That faculty of the diamond-body which always removes the touch of the vajra on all sides is the mind; that mind which enters into equal bliss through the union of wisdom and means is his Dharma-faculty.

These Bodhisattvas, divided into six types according to the distinction between subject and object, together with their consorts, [perceive] the seen and the unseen, the concealed and the unconcealed, in the mind, in space, in the non-mind, and in the non-non-mind;
in equal bliss, in immutable bliss;
[they perceive] the Dharma and the Dharmadhātu.
By this it is said: "Having hands and feet everywhere, having eyes, heads, and mouths everywhere, and possessing hearing everywhere in the world, He stands pervading everything."

Arising from the pure, unceasing, producing supreme bliss, untainted, and accessible through gnosis—there is no other object of apprehension in the three realms; yet they are accessible through the gates of the senses for the entire world.
Though inaccessible even to the Buddhas, the illusory emanations of the Buddhas, possessing immeasurable qualities, manifest themselves within the abode of the three worlds, just like Indra’s net.

Distinguished by various states, they enter the respective minds of the Victors, gods, and humans; these phenomena are unarisen, like the sky reflected in water, and their appearance here is merely the arising of delusion.

The wrathful Buddhas together with their goddesses, as well as Rasakuliśa, Bhūmigarbha, and the others, indeed become manifest in the sky; at the time of accomplishment, the yogins become joyful of heart at dawn and at midnight on a moonlit night, and for him there is the attainment of his desired goal. Through the conjunction of time, there occurs on the surface of the earth a shower of jewels or flowers;
in the image of immutable bliss, form and the other sense objects are neither born nor ceased.
They are untroubled by the impurities of body, speech, and mind, and are undisturbed; they are accessible through gnosis (*jñāna*), to be known through the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*),
and accessible through the gates of the senses— they are to be grasped as such and nothing else, this is the implication—
because they are inaccessible even to the Buddhas, being impossible to enumerate.
And it has been said:
"Victorious is the one King of Bliss, uncaused and eternally arisen,
at the very moment of whose proclamation the Omniscient One became impoverished of words."

The emanation-māyā of the Buddha Vajradhara is Viśvamātā, the Buddha’s emanation-māyā. Like Indra’s net (*śakrajāla*) or a magical illusion (*indrajāla*), and like the appearance of the sky in water, so too is arising here a source of delusion. The "vajras of taste" are the six Tathāgatas, such as Bhūmigarbha and Kṣitigarbha. At the time of accomplishment, during the time of the attainment of Mahāmudrā, at dawn when the disk of the rising sun appears—[in this state] is the assembly (*viśva*).

At dawn (pratyūṣe), in this primordial Buddha (ādibuddhe), the Lord has revealed the Vajra-word clearly through summary, detailed exposition, and further elaboration.
To accomplish this very [goal], the path of signs beginning with smoke—the meditation on Mahāmudrā—has been revealed:

"Having made the mind one-pointed in emptiness, one should examine for one day. From this word of the Blessed One, the Vajra-word in the *Paramādibuddha* concerning the path of meditating on Mahāmudrā, starting with smoke and so forth, is manifest;
it has not come down through the lineage of the gurus.

There is no need for empowerment by the guru's command, for there is a means of verification for this path; according to the Blessed One’s words, "One should examine it day and night for one day," here, setting aside other means of accomplishment such as mantras or signs like smoke, the sign must be examined by the yogin in a single day, and that sign is also threefold.

The initial sign, the middle sign, and the final sign: the initial sign consists of the path of smoke and so forth, the production of the image (*bimba*) through the six-limbed yoga, and the attainment of the moment of the immutable (*akṣarakṣaṇa*).

The middle sign consists of the attainment of the first stage (*ādibhūmi*) by means of one thousand eight hundred moments of the supreme immutable, the manifestation of previously unseen objects through the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), and the attainment of worldly accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*).

The sign of the end is Buddhahood, the state of holding the Vajra; through twenty-one thousand six hundred supreme unchanging moments, one attains the twelve stages and achieves the Mahāmudrā Siddhi. This, beginning with the "Vajra-word," preceded by signs, was taught by the Blessed One in the *Paramādibuddha*, the King of Tantras, at the time of the new moon and at midnight, because that too is a time for accomplishment. On the day of the moon, on the full moon and the new moon, the desired Siddhi—the Mahāmudrā Siddhi—occurs through the union of time, specifically through the yoga of three fortnights and three years.
The vajra-word, the word of reality, the empowerment, and the characteristic of possession—
these belong to the various tantras such as the *Śrīmadādibuddha*; by the word "etcetera," there is an inclusion of the *Śrīsamāja*, *Samvara*, *Hevajra*, and *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*.

By the repeated request of that illustrious Varapalanāyaka, who is renowned for his steadfastness in the Dharma and possesses devotion toward his guru, compassion for the wretched, service toward Mañjuśrī, great proficiency in the vernacular songs, and an exceeding power for hearing the Dharma—I have composed this commentary (*ṭippaṇī*) which provides a complete six-limbed exposition; and having thus composed this commentary on the *Sadaṅgayoga*, whatever merit I have attained— [The remainder of the verse follows: May it serve as a lamp for the eyes of those whose vision is obscured by the darkness of ignorance, and may it quickly bring about the attainment of the state of Vajradhara for all sentient beings. May the lineage of the masters of the *Sadaṅgayoga* remain unbroken, and may the teaching of the Great Sage endure for a long time. Through this, may all beings attain the supreme bliss of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). May there be auspiciousness! *Śubham astu sarvajagatām!* (Note: The final portion of the text provided consists of the concluding verses of the work.)
By this merit, may the entire world attain the supreme, imperishable state.
The Sadanga-yoga of the various tantras, beginning with the illustrious *Ādibuddha*, is completed. This is the work of the venerable scholar Anupamarakṣita.
The *Ṣaḍaṅgayogatippaṇī* is completed;
this work is by the Great Paṇḍita Raviśrījñānapāda,
the venerable feet of the Illustrious One, [protected] by the Peerless One (*Anupama*).
In the language of India:
Ṣaḍaṅgayoga; in the language of Tibet: Sbyor ba yan lag drug pa (The Six-Limbed Yoga).
Homage to the glorious Kālacakra!
To you who have cleared away the net of clouds that are obscurations,
and in whom all the winds of conceptual thought have completely subsided;
May the one possessing excellent light, who has arisen within the expanse of his own space, be more radiant than the full moon, the Lord of the World;
he who, though free from the focal points of cyclic existence and peace, is non-different from them and is the pervasive self;
and though empty, he transcends abiding in a nature of mere compassion—he is the Lord of the Earth.

May those who possess realization, though they cause bliss to expand without exception, abandon conceptualization; may some dawns that are motionless, protectorless, and free from mind become an ornament for the minds of wandering beings.
For those who grasp at even slight conceptualizations as if they were demons, they are bound by holding them for the sake of their own ruin.
Alas! Having abandoned the path of renunciation, they have fallen for a very long time into a state from which there is no liberation.

Thus, having been led astray from the sublime path, I constantly prostrate with devotion to the supreme Guru—who reveals the nature of space and compassion, and whose form is like space, transcending the ordinary mind.
Therefore, it is precisely the proclamation of one's own realization that constitutes the proclamation of such a great-souled master;
for when the fire, which has the nature of blazing form, is absent, [there is no heat].
The surging forth of the peak of heat is not a stream of faults consisting of the pride of realization in one who lacks realization;
rather, by means of its very engagement, it accomplishes the welfare of others.
When the speaker’s expression is not fixed,
how can people engage for the sake of fulfilling their desires?
[This concerns] those wicked mantrins who, conceited through their understanding of the provisional meaning, have abandoned the paths of the noble ones.
Due to their inferior wisdom, even those who have attained realization do not understand [this] through the gateway of practice; however,
by the command of the glorious Vajradhara, the Lord Mañjuśrī has spoken the *Laghutantra* of the Blessed One Kālacakra with words of great clarity for the sake of the three worlds.

Having obtained from the Buddha Ratnagarbha— whose nature is merit— the *Vimalaprabhā* (Stainless Light), a detailed commentary composed with words that are extremely clear and meaningful for all, by the emanation of the glorious Great Compassionate One, the Blessed Lord of the World;
By relying on the nectar of definitive meaning, one overcomes the poisons of cyclic existence and finds joy;
it is the foundational support for the entire collection of objects of knowledge— a name that accords with the title of the Blessed One, the Omniscient One.
That very Sublime One is the ocean of jewels, where Īśvara and the others are explained as the roots;
she is the mother who gives birth to the Buddhas, the pure nature arisen from space, who utterly destroys the conceptual trees in which all the Perfection of Wisdom is gathered.
In the stainless sky where emanations open the eyes, moistened by the expansion of great compassion, one is free from the conceptual support of intentionality that distinguishes between existence,
non-existence, both, or the substantial and the insubstantial.

One should correctly collect the precious scriptures, such as the *Śrī-mūla-tathāgata-kāya-guhyaka*, which accord with the meditation on the path of Mahāmudrā that clarifies the completion stage— wherein all [phenomena], beginning with earth and so forth, arise adventitiously as the followers of emptiness— and which bestow the fruit of perfect buddhahood itself.
That which was taught as the *Ādibuddha* in the *Buddharatnakaraṇḍa-tantrarāja*:
because the vowels and consonants, the moon and the sun, are not the single vajra-throne;
nor is there any other color or form desired, [other than] the sign of the syllable *HŪṂ* itself and its complete transformation.

To this Lord of Victors who holds the manifold illusion— the bindu possessing all aspects, endowed with the supreme faculties, and characterized by the cessation of transformation through non-transformation—
belongs [this state]. Because it is thus, the yogi who delights in accomplishing the supreme unchanging bliss and has received the oral instructions of the sublime guru [attains it].
Having completely abandoned evil companions, having thoroughly meditated on signs such as smoke and so forth, being a beginner who has purified the middle way,
whose mind is bound by supreme compassion for all sentient beings as if they were an only child,
and who relies upon the mundane and supramundane truths.
Without regard for this [world], his wife, and so forth, or even his own body;
remaining aloof from the utilization of the property of the assembly hall, the temple, or the guru;
relying upon the path of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; and abiding in the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra) of loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity.
Having abandoned the desire for mundane accomplishments such as pacification and so forth,
and desiring to abide in the state of omniscience,
one completely relinquishes the cultivation of conceptualizations such as the maṇḍala circle and so on.
In the expanse of space, one perceives the certainty of unarisen phenomena—emptiness in all its aspects—as if reflected in a mirror;

one contemplates these as being like mental projections, optical illusions, dreams, and so forth. By analyzing phenomena that consist of an aggregation of subtle particles, one sets aside a nihilistic emptiness and becomes attached to the inner bliss of self-knowing phenomena.

Having completely abandoned the phenomena of pleasure to be cognized by the external sense faculties, he is uniquely skilled in stabilizing the bodhicitta that consists of the nature of wisdom and skillful means.

Having obtained the pith instructions on the path of the wisdom of supreme immutable great bliss, one does not desire the phenomena of the imagined support and supported— the signs, colors, hands, shapes, and deities of the mandala— and likewise,
[one does not desire] the reality taught by the Tathāgata through the paths of various conceptualizations and so forth.
Regarding the fourth, that which consists of sixteen divisions is not attained by being devoid of the path.
And as for the *hūṃ* spoken of in the generation stage—
The yoga of the completion stage, which is free from conceptualizations such as the syllable *phaṭ* and so forth, is itself the only other means for accomplishing reality; it is not otherwise.
Just as fire resides within wood as its latent mark, yet is not seen by means of cutting or splitting, but rather through the friction of the fire-drill, the fire-board, and the hands.
Just as that which abides there is seen,
so too the appearances of the mind are not seen by means of the methods of conceptual meditation.
In that very state, some will see [the signs] by uniting the *iḍā* and *rasanā* into one;
likewise, the signs such as smoke and so forth will appear.
By means of prāṇāyāma, [the vital energy] flows into the central channel; by means of the observance of the vidyā, the vajra does not fall, and likewise the semen flows upward.
By these paths, [one attains] the state of the Buddhas.
"Supreme bliss is unchanging"— through this,
the yogin will attain the innate nature of all female messengers or manifest accomplishments.
Through the mastery of meditating on the maṇḍala circle by conceptualizing form and so forth,
one will achieve worldly accomplishments (laukika-siddhi).
How could there be any great accomplishment of desire for those who, out of compassion for sentient beings, constantly strive for the virtuous activities of others?
For pure disciples, the paths arise through the grace of the sublime guru;
this precious, excellent path [is lost] to those who are heedless.
When given to other sentient beings,
one's own home becomes a wilderness where one is plundered by the bandits of base regions.
Even by the thieves of doubt, regret, sleep, laziness, and restlessness,
one who has entered the dense thicket of worldly kinship [is not easily plundered].
The precious noble path is plundered by killing,
taking what is not given, the wives of others,
lying, harsh speech, and slander.
The thieves of boastful speech, covetousness, malice, and wrong views,
as well as actual sins and proximate sins.
Killing, malice, and sensual desire—
these five thieves are constantly plundering one's jewels.
By those thieves of various and manifold enjoyments— excellent food and drink—
even one who possesses diligence will become heedless.
Since one who is already in a state of fainting cannot perceive for themselves, how could they become highly valuable? Thinking thus, they do not show it to others who might recognize its worth;
by such words, they cast away the jewel.
Whenever those who possess great and noble knowledge enter into the thorough examination of the great jewels,
they do so by means of their various modes of expression.
One should recognize one's own jewel:
the Perfect Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas,
fathers, mothers, daughters, and sisters.
Māras create obstacles through the forms of sons, siblings, and beloved wives;
therefore, [one should practice] that which has been authorized by the sublime Guru.
The disciples of the Excellent Path Jewel, having completely abandoned their kinsmen who are like robbers,
should conceal [the teaching] very well with great joy.
Neither the stage of the hero nor the stage of self-consecration is the path for the sake of liberation; rather,
there is only the single stage of utterly pure gnosis.
The Buddhas have taught this for the sake of liberation;

even those who have committed the five deeds of immediate retribution will be correctly embraced by the Lord of Victors within the tantra whose nature is method and wisdom, through whatever bliss constitutes the purpose of empowerment.
The stage of the hero is not external; this was taught regarding the very exhaustion of life within the body.
Through the stage of self-consecration, when the three realms are seen as empty, the cycle of existence is revealed to be essence-less and exhausted;
from that, the Buddhahood of the person arises.
Just as the ripened fruit of a plantain tree arises from the very decay of that plantain tree,
so too do the sinful spirits, woodworms, and sentient beings arise from that which destroys them. In the same way, the mind of yogins brings about the total destruction of illusion.
Non-dual, immovable, and without dualistic realization; desirous, supreme, and of great passion;
both entity and non-entity; primordial wisdom and the intentionality of Samantabhadra;
free from conflict, of great sound, the co-emergent, glorious, and the holder of the bodhicitta-tilaka.
The glorious Kālacakra is the vajra, the yoga that is the very nature of wisdom and method. Thus,
this vajra-yoga is that which has been relied upon and stabilized by immeasurable Sugatas,
and it is perfectly gathered by all the Bodhisattvas, the supreme Vajra-holders, and the masters of secret mantra and vidyā.
First, one must properly rely upon a guru who possesses the samaya, abides preeminently in the Vajrayāna,
meditates on reality (*tattva*), is free from attachment and stains, is of a patient disposition, enters the path,
bestows the path upon disciples, removes the fear of hell, and is endowed with pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
That very Vajra-breath for the Māras is also renowned as Vajrasattva upon the foundation of the earth.
Whatever the object of the deity may be, it becomes twofold here: direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
Through the application to reality (*tattva*), that direct perception appears as manifold like stars in the sky, [constituting] the Saṃbhogakāya.
If it were not perceived through direct perception, it would be like the body of one who has died; since it would then not be reality, what could be inferred?

Therefore, regarding this object of meditation for yogins whose intellect is not yet fully matured—such as those viewing painted images—and whatever divine visualization yogins have by the power of the intentions of sentient beings, it becomes twofold: [that which is] through direct perception and that which is through inference.
Of those two, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), that which is direct perception becomes like a star in the sky through the yoga of reality (*tattva*).

Like a multitude of stars, it is the manifold *saṃbhogakāya*, which is to be grasped by the eyes of the flesh and so forth, and is like a dream and an illusion within the three realms and the three times.
Here, first of all, the beginner yogin, lacking supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), perceives the reflected image with the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*).
Thereafter, by the power of the stage of supernormal knowledge, he perceives it with the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*).
Then, by the power of the stage of freedom from passion (*vītarāga*), he beholds it with the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*).
Then, by virtue of the stage of a bodhisattva, he beheld with the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*).

Then, by virtue of the stage of a perfectly awakened buddha (*samyaksaṃbuddha*), he beheld with the eye of primordial gnosis (*jñāna-cakṣus*). Thus it is said: "Completely liberated from all [remaining] obscurations."
Thus, the five eyes of the Tathāgata, such as the flesh eye and so forth, are taught for the purpose of perceiving emptiness;
other sentient beings are like those born blind regarding the object of viewing emptiness—this is the certainty of meditating on reality (*tattva*).

Regarding any conceptualization that is not reality, if it is not perceived directly through a means of proof that is not reality, it is like inferring a dead body. What is imputed by that which is not reality...

Regarding the phrase "that is to be viewed in paintings and so forth": having drawn or fashioned paintings and images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or having depicted the mandala circle, one should view them with a focused mind;
this is for the purpose of meditation for inferior, childish yogins. This is the certainty regarding the meditation on conceptualization.
Service (*sevā*) is performed through the five nectars and so forth, the ocean-like vajras, and the recitation of mantras;
near-attainment (*upāsana*) is brought about by the nectar born from the vajra and lotus, such as through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the rest.
Accomplishment (*sādhana*) is the meditation on the three vajras becoming of one taste with the water-born [lotus] through the stages of joy (*ānanda*) and so forth.
Regarding the great accomplishment definitively established through the subtle yoga of the non-transmigrating union with wisdom: here,
a beginner first performs the service (*sevā*) according to the ritual of the *sādhana*,
wherein the five outer nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) consist of excrement and so forth.
By the word "and so forth," meat and the like are included; by eating these for the sake of pleasing the deities, one performs the service (*sevā*).
Internally, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) are the five aggregates (*skandha*), and by the word "and so forth," the five sense faculties are the five lamps.
To be indifferent toward those [worldly things] is "service" (*sevā*),
which means completely abandoning craving for the body and material possessions. Through such service, the gods will grant supreme boons, but not by eating excrement and the like.
"By those who are like oceans of jewels and vajras" means being without regard for the enjoyments of the body,
being without regard for the enjoyments of speech,
and being without regard for the enjoyments of the mind.

This means being indifferent to the pleasure of abundant enjoyments, [maintaining] the vows of body, speech, mind, and celibacy (*brahmacarya*). By this, one will grant the supreme deity, and not out of attachment to the enjoyments of existence (*bhava*).
Regarding the phrase "by means of mantra recitation and so forth," here "mantra recitation" refers to the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇasaṃyama*).
By the word "and so forth," it is meant that the yoga of exhaling, inhaling, and the vase-breath (*kumbhaka*) is the constant service (*sevā*).
Through this, the supreme deity will grant boons, but not by failing to restrain the vital breath (*prāṇa*); such is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
According to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), one should perform recitation and so forth with the counting rosary and other means.
This is for the sake of common accomplishments (*sādhāraṇasiddhi*). Now, the near-attainment (*upāsādhana*) will be explained, beginning with the words "individually" (*pratyeka*) and so forth.

Regarding the term "individual withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*): here, for those in cyclic existence (*saṃsārin*), withdrawal is the grasping of objects such as forms by means of the sense faculties, such as the eyes.
The complete abandonment of that is to be described as withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*);
for the apprehension of objects by the eyes and the other [senses] with respect to the form of emptiness is the proximate accomplishment (*upāyasādhana*).
Likewise, there are meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and retention (*dhāraṇā*).
It is accomplished by means of the nectar born from the vajra and lotus according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
According to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), it is accomplished through the external elaboration of deities; such is the near-attainment (*upāsādhana*).
Now, the attainment (*sādhana*) is taught, beginning with the words "joy" (*prīti*) and so forth.

Here, through joy and the other [feelings], the three vajras—the bindus of body, speech, and mind—become of equal taste within the lotus; this is what is to be accomplished through meditation. The meaning is that the bindus abide in the heart, the navel, and the secret place. Thus is the practitioner.
Then, as for the "great accomplishment" (*mahāsādhana*): when one applies wisdom (*prajñā*) and non-transmigrating bliss arises, that is the great accomplishment.

Regarding the phrase "from the subtle yoga," according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), it refers to the great accomplishment in the definitive sense arising from the perfect union of the seminal essence (*śukra*) upon the *suṣumṇā* channel.

156 END_OF_PDF_PAGE_148 | According to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), it is certain that one should place white mustard seeds and so forth upon the tip of the nose of the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) of wisdom;
in this way, the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*) is effected.
First, emptiness and awakening are determined, and thereafter, the moon and the drop (*bindu*) are correctly held.
Then, generating the forms and manifesting the supreme and most excellent families of flavors—this very state of resplendence is the general service (*sevā*).

Through the vajras of the water-treasure, the middling accomplishment (*sādhana*) also occurs here by way of four methods; likewise, it pertains to the branches of accomplishment for those who are inferior and those who are steadfast.

12.8 Here, regarding the statement "first, emptiness is awakening" in the context of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*): that which consists of the total relinquishing of the aggregates at the end of the death of sentient beings and the grasping of the aggregates characterized by birth—that single moment of emptiness which perceives the three realms—is what is called "emptiness.
Certainly, and without doubt, immediately after that moment, one perfectly holds the lunar drop (*candrabindu*).
Thus, here, the fact that the ālayavijñāna grasps the drops of semen in the mother’s womb is "perfect grasping.
Thereafter, the phrase "the generation of forms from the grasped semen and so forth" means that the womb is completed during the seventh month; it means the completion of the body.

Then, with the words "by the families of the supreme flavors" (rab mchog ro’i rigs rnams), there is the arrangement of syllables for the six aggregates, such as the eye and so forth; it means the thorough engagement with objects such as form and so on.
Likewise, even in the yoga of the deity, one should meditate on the nature of the examined self; this is for the beginner.
This is the general propitiation (sevā).

"By the vajras of the water-treasury" refers to the completion of the vajras of body, speech, mind, and gnosis; this is the middling accomplishment, which is the completion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Here, it becomes fourfold by way of method: regarding the branch of service (*sevā*) and the branch of near-accomplishment (*upāsādhana*), there are the inferior and the stable;
regarding the branch of accomplishment (*sādhana*), it is likewise at the limit of sixteen years—this is the certainty.
19. Here, "inferior" refers to a child who has just been born; "middling" refers to a child whose teeth have not yet fallen out; and "youth" refers to one whose teeth have fallen out.
Furthermore, from birth, after sixteen years, one reaches youth because of the very act of producing offspring;
likewise, the yogi should meditate upon all the deities as having four limbs—this is the certainty of worldly truth.

"First, regarding 'emptiness as enlightenment,' one should not contemplate anything at all in the darkness. Then, 'perfectly holding the lunar drop,' one becomes Vajrasattva oneself."
Alternatively: one should not associate with the consort of wisdom (prajñā) until the ten [suns] have risen.

When the yogin completely cuts off external distractions, the signs become individually withdrawn; thus, through the ten aspects, he becomes a Lord of Victors (Jinendra), and meditative concentration (dhyāna) is immovability itself.
Prāṇāyāma is also Khaḍgin; again, it is of ten types. Dhāraṇā is Ratnapāṇi himself.
Anusmṛti is Padmadhara for the female [deity]. The glorious Samādhi is Cakrin.
Each is divided by five, and furthermore, they are differentiated by the vowels and consonants.
Withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is the non-engagement of the ten objects and their corresponding subjects within the body.
Meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) consists of discernment, analysis, joy, unwavering bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.
Vital effort (*prāṇāyāma*) is the cessation of the two paths and the entry of the vital breath into the central channel.
When the vital breath has fully entered the bindu and the movement of both [channels] is obstructed, one maintains single-pointedness of mind.
Whatever appearance of *caṇḍālī* definitely occurs within the body and space becomes *anusmṛti*.
Through the power of immutable bliss by means of the nature of wisdom and method, there is *samādhi* upon the form of gnosis (*jñāna*).
Through the various divisions such as the inferior and so forth, there are three types of *sādhana* for the manifold *pradhāna*.
By virtue of traversing the three mudrās and the three stages, there are the three: karma, conceptualization, and the supreme.
Through *pratyāhāra*, the yogi is freed from sense objects; may all the pedestals (*maṇḍalas*) empower him.

The five superknowledges will be attained; O Lord of Men, purified by the yoga of meditation, purified by the exertion of vital breath, free from the moon and the sun, and honored by the Bodhisattvas.
Having destroyed Māra, the afflictions, and the like, one enters the ten powers through the power of retention.

Then, from the form of primordial wisdom—the stainless light-mandala of correct recollection—one accomplishes the body of primordial wisdom through the purity of meditative concentration over the course of several days. If, through practices such as withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), the desired goal of the mantra practitioner and others is not accomplished, one should practice *nāda*;
by the power of the vajra-jewel abiding within the lotus, one blocks the *bindu* and thus achieves accomplishment.

Regarding *sevā* (service), there are the ten initial yogas; through the wrathful gaze of the Wheel-Bearer in the sky and the gaze of Yamāntaka, one enters the path of nectar. Furthermore, regarding *upasevā* (close service), the six branches of knowledge involve the three immutables: the conceptual moon-drop abiding at the vajra-jewel. These constitute *sādhana* (accomplishment).
In this yoga of the innate wisdom, which is solitary, peaceful, and undiminished bliss, there is the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*). Now, the six-limbed yoga shall be explained;
regarding "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*), for the beginner it is the "sovereign sense-organ," which is the aggregate of gnosis (*jñānaskandha*).

Furthermore, there are ten types of distinctions of signs: smoke, mirage, the appearance of space, a lamp, a blazing fire, the moon, the sun, Rāhu, lightning, and the vision of the bindu; through these distinctions, there is the aggregate of non-conceptual primordial wisdom.
Dhyāna is indeed Akṣobhya; it is the aggregate of consciousness.
The ten aspects consist of the ten objects and subjects being meditated upon as a single unity within the manifold form.
Prāṇāyāma, or else, the wielder of the sword.
This refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); it has ten aspects because the ten maṇḍalas of the left and right [channels] have become merged into one.
Furthermore, there are ten aspects: the Holder of the Jewel in Hand.

This refers to the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), which is tenfold according to the distinction between the inhalation and exhalation [of breath] at the lotuses of the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown of the head.
"Recollection for G.yung mo becomes Padmadhara" refers to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

Furthermore, that recollection on the central channel of G.yung mo is tenfold, according to the division of the ten stages of desire; it is the one possessing the wheel of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), namely Vairocana.
The ten types of meditative concentration are for the purpose of arresting the ten winds.
Thus, the Blessed One is one who has attained non-abiding nirvāṇa, in the sense that the winds do not blow within him.
Now, the characteristics of pratyāhāra and the others shall be explained, beginning with the words "individually" (prati) and so forth.
In this context, "withdrawal" (pratyāhāra) refers to the non-engagement of consciousness through the connection between the ten objects and their corresponding sense faculties within the body.
The other five [faculties], such as the eye and so forth, engage with the objects of emptiness.

Regarding that very form: "insight" (*prajñā*) refers to seeing; "discernment" (*vitarka*) refers to grasping at the entity; "investigation" (*vicāra*) refers to ascertaining its meaning; "joy" (*prīti*) refers to attachment to the form; and "unwavering bliss" (*niścalasukha*) refers to making the mind one-pointed together with the form.
Thus, through the distinction between the apprehended and the apprehender, there are ten types of meditative concentration.
Regarding what is called "the exertion of life" here, it refers to the cessation of the two paths—the left and right paths—and their entry into the central path.
Furthermore, there are ten aspects regarding the cessation of the maṇḍala.

Likewise, the Blessed One said in the *Śrī-guhyasamāja*: "There is no entity and no meditation; meditation itself is not meditation. Thus, the entity becomes non-existent, and meditation is without objective reference.
Here, "non-entity" refers to the sky free of clouds, and "meditation" is *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal); it is precisely that non-entity which is "without meditation."

Regarding the statement "cultivation is not cultivation itself": here, the absence of any objective entity in the cultivation of individual withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), which consists in meditating upon the cloudless sky—that is what constitutes "cultivation is not cultivation itself," because it is precisely the state of being free from the cultivation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Thus, whatever entity is seen through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) becomes a non-entity, because one sees entities that are unconstructed (*avikalpita*), whether past, future, or presently arisen.
Therefore, the Blessed One has said that in the cultivation of withdrawal, the cultivation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not become an object of focus.
This meditation was also taught by the Blessed One in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, as follows: Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the venerable Subhūti:
"Noble Subhūti, how does one who practices yoga with the *prajñāpāramitā* practice that yoga?"
Subhūti said: "Kauśika, whoever practices the yoga of the perfection of wisdom practices the yoga of space.
Kauśika, whoever thinks that they should practice the yoga in the open air is one who thinks that they should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Thus, the branches of application through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) have been explained.
Thereafter, the winds are taught through another intentional terminology by means of the names of the reflections of Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
Furthermore, there are five types;
as it was said by the Blessed One in the *Aparimitāyur-jñāna-sūtra*:
"It is filled with the nature of the five jewels."
Blessed by the five Buddhas,
having been extracted in the form of a sphere,
one should meditate upon it at the tip of the nose.
Thus it is said.

the breath blessed by them flows through the left nostril. Thus it is said.

There, by means of the fire of primordial wisdom (*jñānāgni*), the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, and so forth, become incinerated and merge into one. Then, as the moon is melted by the fire of the wisdom of *caṇḍālī*, it descends in the form of the drop (*bindu*) of bodhicitta; it abides in the throat, heart, navel, and secret lotus with the nature of joy (*ānanda*), supreme joy (*paramānanda*), and special joy (*viramānanda*), and then, up to the vajra-jewel, it abides with the nature of innate joy (*sahajānanda*).
It is because its nature is free from various aspects, ripening, manifestation, and characteristics. Thus it is said.

Thus, when the sixteen parts are full and have reached as far as the interior of the jewel, bliss is connected through the power of meditation; the statement that this is "like the bliss of emission" is merely a metaphor. In its own nature, it cannot rival even a thousand-millionth part of the innate joy (*sahajānanda*) of the state of the unchanging (*akṣara*), which arises from the two organs. That state is not to be cognized as anything at all by the yogi who has attained mastery.
The emptiness of bodhisattvas is called "awakening"; it does not follow the non-existence that is renowned in the world.

Thus, through the recitation of mantras, meditative concentration, and bliss of the yoga of the six limbs, yogins will attain buddhahood. "The supreme merit that purifies and destroys sin, in this very life"—this certainty regarding the practitioner was spoken by the Blessed One. Furthermore, in that same place it says: "Here, the cause is the formless [reality] in all its aspects. This is because whatever objects are seen through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*)—such as vases, cloths, and so forth—are seen by means of a non-conceptual, non-erroneous direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that is similar to a reflection in a mirror, appearing distinctly in all their aspects.

That which is formless does not transcend the nature of subtle atoms, because it is itself devoid of conceptual construction. Since it is to be realized by eyes that are neither closed nor open, it is therefore neither form, nor is it other than form; yet it is not to be realized by the eye with its vision, nor by the eye without its vision.

Thus, being devoid of all aspects is the cause; as it is said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*: "The emptiness endowed with the supreme of all aspects," and so forth. This very point was stated by the great bodhisattva Śrīvajragarbha in his commentary on the *Śrīhevajra*, as follows: "The ultimate meditation of the aforementioned wisdom and method shall now be described: 'That which is to be meditated upon is a real entity,' and so forth."
The entity to be meditated upon here in space is like a dream; it transcends the nature of even subtle particles.

"The thorough knowledge of that [object] as being without intrinsic reality is to be cultivated; with a mind free from conceptual construction, seeing the reflected image while being free from discursive thought and unerring is called 'direct perception' (pratyakṣa)," and so forth.

Likewise, in the later tantra, Mañjuśrīpa, the lord of the ten stages, stated: "One endowed with the power of the ten powers should practice the meditation on emptiness by means of the six [limbs], beginning with withdrawal."
Furthermore, there are yogas such as the smoke at night, and also those such as the blazing in the sky during the day.

Therein, one should also demonstrate the mind through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and completely abandon external objects.

Through emergence and entry, one makes it inferior once again; by means of the limb of grasping, it becomes a drop (*bindu*).
Through recollection, great rays of light certainly stream forth from one's own form, like the moon in the sky.

From the vajra, the essence of meditative concentration, there arises the stainless bliss that completely fills the head; through the gaze of space, ignorance is brought to its ultimate end by the vision of emptiness.

Through the vision of the formless, one brings hatred to its very end; from the stainless bliss of the seminal essence, [it arises].

The view of a life-force (jīva) results in the extreme of pride; this is from the *Unassailable Brahma-Melody* [36]. Once the vital breath and effort have ceased, the supreme mandala, free from stains, arises from the form of the Buddha.
The secret [place], the navel, the heart-lotus, the throat, the head, and the crown—these are the stages of the earth-elements in sequence.
From the realm that cannot be overcome by semen ascending above or by dust descending below, the Vajra Body, Speech, and Mind, free from all stains, is the Teacher who reveals the Buddhas.
[37] The canine and other such eyes are the "fleshly eye," while the divine eye of the gods and others arises through the power of natural qualities.

That which is the supreme sixteenteenth part of the moon, whose nature is wisdom, at the end of the full moon;

When one thoroughly and correctly realizes that existence and non-existence have become one—thereby abandoning the three fears and becoming free from anxiety—* ||

At that time, for that yogin, when duality has somewhat ceased, he proceeds to the supreme state. When the life-force (*prāṇa*) and downward-clearing wind (*apāna*) have been obstructed, he proceeds to the form of the sun, which moves like the moon.
When [the winds] awaken within the vajra-lotus, this [wind] is once again melted by the fire-flame of the solar form.

Thus, E-Vaṃ and likewise those three arise; there is nothing else whatsoever.

This is called "the wheel that completely purifies the three realms of existence. This is the attachment to the jewel of bliss, the exhaustion of the afflictions of the lotus, the sword, the vajra, the body of primordial wisdom, the great indivisible one.
The six supreme families, such as the curved knife that cuts through ignorance—

Wherever the forms of the families have become equal, that is said to be the great form.

Where the increase of saṃsāra has come to an end, that is indeed the vajra-formations (*vajrasaṃskāra*).
That state in which the conditions of sleep and so forth have ceased is taught as consciousness (*vijñāna*).
That state in which the objects of sensory cognition have ceased is the primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) of the Sage.
These are the six supreme and sublime Victors, such as Vairocana and the others, who constitute the six families.
The others are the divisions of the six elements: earth, fire, water, wind, space, and peace.
Where all delusion has been brought to its end, that is Locanā; she is the earth element. Where all pride has been destroyed, she is Māmakī; she is the water element.
Wherever all passion is completely destroyed, she is Pāṇḍaravāsinī; she becomes Fire. Wherever all envy is completely destroyed, she is Tārā; she is also Wind.
Wherever all hatred is completely destroyed, she is Vajradhātvīśvarī; she is Space.
That in which all stinginess has utterly perished is the Mother of Diversity; she is the Unchanging.
That which beholds forms—whether seen or unseen—in the space of the mind, that is the Eye.
Hearing sounds clearly from afar, as if they were right before one, this is the Great Ear of the Victor.

That which perceives all fragrances that produce supreme bliss is the excellent nose of the Pervasive Lord; that which constantly experiences its own moon, bestowing the bliss of nectar, is the tongue.
That which completely grasps all vajra-tangible objects is the sensory faculty of the body, which is always vajra-like.
That mind which enters into equanimity through the thorough union of wisdom and method—this is its Dharma.
These objects and subjects, distinguished by the sixfold division, together with the Bodhisattvas and their consorts,
are all these forms and so forth— the objects of the Supreme Victor.
They are to be realized through stainless primordial wisdom, which is supreme bliss, unborn, unceasing, and utterly pure.
Not to be grasped by others, it cannot be realized through the gates of the faculties of all beings within the three realms;

nor is it even to be realized by the Buddhas. Possessing immeasurable qualities, the illusory emanation of the Buddha manifests itself within the abodes of the three worlds, just like the net of Indra.
Pervading the individual minds of gods and humans, together with the Victors, through the manifestation of diverse entities—

There, a particular realization will arise within you."
