Now, one might ask: "Are there not other paths for the sake of liberation? Why then such devotion to this one? To this, it is said:
"O Hero," and so forth.

The stage of the hero (*vīrakrama*) is characterized by the visualization and so on of offerings to external wrathful deities. The stage of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhānakrama*) is characterized by the mind’s focus on the gateway of the yoga of peaceful deities.
It is said that these were not correctly taught by the Buddhas for the sake of liberation.
If one asks what this teaching is,
it is said: "The single stage of utter purity," which is the non-dual yoga of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*).
If one asks how this is to be understood, it is said:
"by which.
This refers to that cause by which even those who have committed the five deeds of immediate retribution are correctly embraced—that is, comforted—by the Lords of the Victors.
The five actions of immediate retribution are: killing one's mother, killing one's father,
killing an arhat,
causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and [shedding the blood of a Tathāgata].
Regarding "drawing the blood of a Tathāgata with an evil mind":
among these five [offenses], each constitutes an *ānantarya* (immediate) transgression; one will remain in hell for an eon without interval.
Therefore, they are called "immediate" (*ānantarya*).
"By bliss itself" means by means of the bliss of skillful methods (*upāya*). "By the meaning of empowerment" means by the meaning of the fourth [empowerment].
Otherwise, for those who commit the five acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), it is the sequence of the Hero (*vīra*).

Those who are not free from attachment to fierce activities and whose continuum of habitual tendencies consists of the stages of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna-krama*)—which greatly increase the pleasures of cyclic existence—do not attain liberation;
such is the meaning of the phrase "for that reason.
Now, if you think that these two stages are not a [proper] sequence, then for what purpose did the Blessed One teach them?

It is said, "of the hero," and so forth. Because this was taught regarding the exhaustion of life within the body, it is therefore not the external stage of the hero (*vīrakrama*). Well then, is it not clear that self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) pertains to the body? It is not so, because it is the manifestation of one's own mind being consecrated.

Furthermore, that is the vision of emptiness itself as the three realms. "Name" means that which is well-known. It is also stated that this establishes the sequence of the utter purification of those who perform the welfare of beings. Now, if it is taught that self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) is precisely the vision of the three realms, and because one does not turn back from that vision, how could Buddhahood—which has the characteristic of abiding in saṃsāra—possibly exist?
It is said:

"Regarding 'saṃsāra' and so forth: in saṃsāra—that which consists of the three realms, which is essence-less, false, and deceptive by nature—there is buddhahood itself, namely omniscience and the knowledge of all aspects."
The knowledge of the path itself, the knowledge of the aspects of the path itself, and the ten powers.

The fruit, characterized by the perfect endowment of qualities such as the fearlessnesses, becomes the essence. Immediately after that exhaustion—that is, the exhaustion of saṃsāra—how does it arise? It is said: "like the fruit of a tree."

"Just as a core fruit ripens within a pithless plantain tree, and through the decay of the plantain tree it truly emerges, so too is buddhahood. If one asks, "In that case, if buddhahood is asserted to be the bodhicitta of the bodhisattva who accomplishes it, then since it is said that the means of accomplishing reality is reality itself, and because that [bodhicitta] is also born from illusion, illusion is self-awareness," [it is replied:]...
If one asks how that which is not the reality currently being entered can be suitable as the means for accomplishing Buddhahood itself, it is said:

"Sin," and so forth. "Sin" refers to the *śuka* insect; "kuli-ra" refers to the *karkata* crab. Just as one's own mother, who arises from the context of the occasion, is harmed by those [creatures], so too does the yogi contemplate.

Yoga is the meditative union of wisdom and method. In that regard, whatever mind exists there is the conventional birth arising from the occasion of the transference of awareness—the illusory [wisdom] of the fourth empowerment.

It will bring about total destruction. Because it is free from illusion, saṃsāra is said to be without return; this is for the purpose of providing encouragement to those yogins who realize suchness. Now, one might ask: "The bodhicitta is described here as an insentient element, yet how can it be said that it accomplishes buddhahood—the supreme non-insentient gnosis?
This is indeed true.

This is from the statement: "One should meditate on the supreme unchanging through the nature of the unchanging seminal essence (*bindu*). For that very reason, the sixteenfold division of this yogic mind in its aspect of the supreme unchanging is taught in the passage beginning with "non-dual" (*advaya*). Here, "dual" refers to the minds of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

That which does not exist in either of those two is "non-dual. Because there is no movement from the jewel and the lotus, it is "immovable. Having realized the two, this aspect of wisdom and method does not exist [therein]; thus, it is "free from dualistic conception. Because it bestows unsurpassed bliss, it is "desire"—this is the fourth yoga. Because it stops twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths, it is "supreme unchanging. Because it is free from attachment, the white and black sides, and because there is neither staying nor going for oneself, it is "great passion. Because it is definitively liberated from both with-form and formless aspects, it is "entity and non-entity. Because it perceives all objects of knowledge without exception, it is "gnosis"—this is the third yoga. It is preceded by that which delights the world, and is the primordial state of sentient beings.
He is called Samantabhadra because he is sublime in both the middle and the end. He is called "the Speaker" (vādin) because he is free from Māras, afflictions, and conceptual constructions;
that is, he is one who proclaims the inner and outer expressions.

Alternatively, because this battle does not exist [for one who possesses] the lion’s roar that resounds and descends in all directions, it is "without clamor. Because its nature is an invincible sound, it is "the sound," which is great renown. This is the second yoga. Because of having completely abandoned worldly conduct and because the obscurations of the four bodies of the innate have been exhausted, he is the "Glorious Holder of the Bindu of Bodhicitta. Because emptiness and compassion are inseparable, he is the "Glorious Vajra of Kālacakra. Because the accumulation of ethical discipline is perfectly complete, he is the "Yoga whose nature is Wisdom and Means. This is the first yoga. Now, for the purpose of serving the Guru, the examination of the Vajra Master is taught, beginning with the words "First," and so forth. Here, in the system of Mantra, disciples who desire mundane and supramundane accomplishments must rely upon a Guru, and that [Guru] must be thoroughly examined. Thus it is said.

He possesses the commitments (*samaya*) for the sake of guarding the bodhicitta. He is to be attended upon; that is, he should be pleased by his sons, wife, and so forth. He abides preeminently in the Vajrayāna, which means he abides preeminently in the Mantramahāyāna. He cultivates reality (*tattva*) because he is a practitioner who meditates on supreme unchanging gnosis (*paramākṣarajñāna*). He is free from attachment because he has no regard even for his own body, let alone for all his sons, wife, and so forth. He is stainless because he is devoid of the defects of passion and the like. He is of a patient disposition (*kṣānti-śīla*); that whose nature is to engage without regard for results is one whose character is patience. The path is the path of the perfectly enlightened Buddha (*samyaksaṃbuddha*).

One whose nature is to enter that is one who enters the path. When this Guru has been pleased, he bestows the path upon his disciples and robs them of the fear of hell. Furthermore, through that very reality, he possesses celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and has attained supreme unchanging bliss (*akṣarasukha*). He is like a vajra-staff for the Māras—that is, for the four Māras—and is thus a "Vajradanda."

Because he is the one who performs the conquest; and because the glorious Guru, whose characteristic is that which is expressed, possesses a body blessed by the four and five [deities] of Vajradhātvīśvarī and Vajrasattva, he is renowned as Vajrasattva through his nirmāṇakāya. Now, for the sake of mundane and supramundane accomplishments, the visualization of the deity is taught.

It is called "direct perception. It arises from the application to reality by the yogi who meditates on the various reflected images. "Like a cluster of stars" refers to the vision of the infinite *saṃbhogakāya* Buddhas within the center of the *bindu*, which has the form of a blue jewel and a lunar mandala; preceded by this, there is the vision of the three realms, such as vases, cloths, and so forth.

The fleshly eye sees objects even when separated by a distance of a hundred *yojanas*, through such things as the supernormal power of miraculous abilities (*ṛddhi*). The divine eye sees subtle and other forms, even those separated by infinite world-systems.
The Buddha-eye knows the minds of others.
By means of the eye of wisdom— that which has the characteristic of non-conceptuality regarding all phenomena—
and by means of the eye of primordial gnosis (*jñāna*), which perceives all aspects of all entities;
whereas other sentient beings are those who see only what lies on this side.
"Like a dead body" means it is devoid of movement and motion;
"made" refers to being formed from earth and so forth; "spherical" refers to being shaped like a cauldron and so forth.
The five such as excrement are the *viraśumāmu*;
the five such as cow dung are the *gokudahana*. Internally, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) are the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Regarding the statement that "the five sense faculties are the five lamps," it is taught that from the *bindu* day and night, a white stream flows; this is not *māmaki*, nor is it wine and the like.
From day to day, [the elements] emanate into the eyes and so forth, but never at other times.
The deities who abide in their own families anoint the pure body with the five nectars;
through the mind’s entry into emptiness, there is the innate bliss of the mind of union. This is not born from a womb—so it is known.
The yoga of exhaling, inhaling, and the vase [retention] consists of the individual discernment of the syllable OṂ as it goes out, the syllable LAḤ as it enters, and the syllable HŪṂ as it abides.
"Unrestrained" means not having made [the breath] stable;
it is for the sake of common accomplishments, that is, for the sake of worldly accomplishments such as pacification and so forth.

"Collection" (saṃhāra) means bringing [the mind] into presence; it is the meaning of "individual collection" (pratyāhāra) because it consists in the very abandonment of being directed toward worldly forms and so forth.
As for the forms and so forth of others, they consist of supramundane forms and so forth that transcend the nature of subtle particles (paramāṇu-dharma).
Dhyāna has the characteristics of wisdom, conceptualization, discernment, joy, and unwavering bliss.
Prāṇāyāma has the characteristic of destroying the movement of the moon and the sun.
Dhāraṇā has the characteristic of arresting the bindu by means of the gates of going and coming at the secret place, the navel, the heart, the throat, and the forehead.

The "vajra-lotus" refers to the lotus of the *uṣṇīṣa*; the meaning is that because the nectar produced therein from the very nature of the vajra-lotus does not allow the bodhicitta to flow away, it becomes of equal taste within the lotuses of the heart, the navel, and the secret place. As for the "suṣumnā channel," this is the *śaṅkhinī*; it is from the perfect union of the seminal essence (*bindu*) upon that [channel], that is, from the movement of the bodhicitta.
This explains the subtle yoga.
Now, the stages of approach and so forth will be described according to the distinction between the inferior and the supreme, beginning with the words "first," and so on.

"From the complete casting off of the aggregates" means: from the grasping at the aggregates belonging to the portion of birth, which arises from having completely abandoned the present body; that is, from grasping at all existence (*bhava*) that emerges [therefrom]. *D₁: "Five. D₁: "Also. D₁: "Is. D₁: "Ste. D₁ adds "ste. D₁: "ni. D₁: "'ga'. D₁ adds "la. D₁: "bsnyen. D₁: the two shads are not present. D₁: "kyis. D₁: "byang. D₁: "rje. D₁: "'pho. D₁: "to. D₁: "ga. D₁: "da ltar ba'i lus yongs su btang ba las so skye ba'i char gtogs pa'i phung po'i 'dzin pa las so 'byung ba'i srid pa kun 'dzin pa las so"*
In the center of this, up until it is filled, is that which has the characteristic of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
"Seeing the three existences" means seeing the three existences directly.

The *ālayavijñāna* enters the mind into the center of the atomic particles and the drops of semen—the support for all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)—which is called "grasping the drops of semen in the mother's womb," meaning it truly takes hold [of them].
"By seven months" refers to the general nature [though some say "by nine months"];

this is by way of the analogy of the womb for the accomplishment of the deity. Therefore, the phrase "from that point" and so forth clarifies the three branches, such as the accomplishment of the *jñāna* (wisdom) and others.
These consist of the six aggregates, characterized by form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and gnosis (*jñāna*).
This is the general service (*sevā*), which is the service for mundane accomplishments (*laukika-siddhi*).

Likewise, there are the near-attainment (*upāsādhana*), the attainment (*sādhana*), and the great attainment (*mahāsādhana*). For this very reason, it is said that [the practice] beginning with the ocean of waters brings about the perfection of body, speech, mind, and gnosis (*kāya-vāk-citta-jñāna*).
The "middling accomplishment" (*bsgrub pa 'bring po*) refers to the near-accomplishment (*upāsādhana*), because this term "middling" specifically qualifies the accomplishment itself;
for that very reason, it is explained as the "completion of life-force" (*prāṇapūrṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "in this," it refers to the previously mentioned *sevā* (service) and *upasevā* (near-service).
The phrase "the methods are fourfold" means that they consist of the categories beginning with the "lesser" (*mṛdu*) and so forth.
Within those four, there are two intermediate types; therefore, they are [divided into] *sevā* and *upasevā*.
Regarding the "four aspects," the two beginning with the "minor" (mṛdu) are to be purified later, namely in the *sādhana* and *mahāsādhana*.
Therefore it is said: "in the limb of *sevā* and in the limb of *upasādhana*.
Furthermore, "the inferior and the stable" refers to *sevā* and *upasādhana*.
This is connected with the practice (*sādhana*) and the great practice (*mahāsādhana*) that will be explained.

Furthermore, for the sake of the meter, the first and the last [words] are combined through elision (*samāsa*); therefore, it should be understood that even children and youths of middling capacity can grasp this here.
"Firm" (*sthira*) means "in the prime of youth."
The phrase "suchness in the root" means that it pertains to the branch of great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*).
"Youth" refers to the essence of the third branch, which is not inferior.
By this, the four [stages] beginning with approach (*sevā*) are correlated with the four [qualities] beginning with inferiority.

Regarding the phrase "only the born and sixteen," and so forth, birth is demonstrated by means of a fixed body; having given an illustration, it is shown here [and so on]. "The inferior" refers to the infant.
Thus, the gathering of the lunar drops (*candrabindu*) is called the "inferior" boundary of the birth-place.

By means of the distinctions such as "inferior" and so forth, it is said that "the stages are attained"; this means that the four [categories] beginning with the inferior are each applied to three stages.

Through the attainment of the twelve stages culminating in those endowed with primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), such as the Joyous (*pramuditā*) and so forth, one becomes the sovereign of the twelve stages.

Therefore, since the meaning of the verse beginning with "the twelve aspects of the true meaning" and so forth has already been explained by me in the *Amṛtakaṇikā*, my commentary on the *Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti*, it shall not be elaborated upon here.
Now, the path that accomplishes supramundane siddhi will be described, beginning with the words "emptiness."
The path of emptiness, smoke, and so forth, should be meditated upon through the stages that will be explained, by means of the guru’s definitive empowerment.
Regarding "at the limit of the reflected image": the reflected image is manifold and possesses all aspects;
it is said that one should reach the culmination of that with the mind.
From that junction, the yogi also stabilizes the life-sustaining wind (*prāṇavāyu*) within all the channel-wheels (*cakras*), as well as the downward-clearing wind (*apānavāyu*).
Thereafter, it is called the "obstruction of the moon," just like Rāhu;
"the moon" refers to the bodhicitta.

"Yogin" refers to one who possesses yoga (*yoga*), which is the perfect union of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the downward-clearing breath (*apāna*). [The yogin] is so called because he possesses that [yoga]. He arrests and pacifies the moments of the destruction of the bodhicitta; through the [four results of] natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) and so forth, he renders it immutable, and for that reason, there is the natural outflow, the ripened result (*vipāka*), the result of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), and the stainless state (*vaimalyatva*).
Whatever is slightly inexpressible, that he performs.
By means of a few days—that is, by the days of the three years and three fortnights of the *Kālacakra*—one attains the siddhi of Mahāmudrā; this is the meaning.
Now, the six-limbed yoga is taught in verse, beginning with "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth.
When a beginner meditates on the signs such as smoke and so forth, "the Lord of Victors" refers to Vajrasattva;
"the one with the sword" refers to Amoghasiddhi.
Regarding the phrase "from the division of the ten stages of desire": [these are] loss of appetite, longing, fever of the body, parching of the mouth and lotus, and lack of interest in food.
Pride, madness, extreme delusion, mental confusion, and violent fever—
these ten clearly manifest forms of the one possessing the vajra (Vajradhara), such as smoke and the rest, appear within the bodies of living beings in this world.
Those who desire victory over the mind should understand these clearly manifest states as the stages of mental accomplishment.
Thus it is said.

It is the cessation and pacification of the ten winds—the vital wind (*prāṇa*), the downward-clearing wind (*apāna*), the equal-abiding wind (*samāna*), the upward-moving wind (*udāna*), the pervasive wind (*vyāna*), the serpent wind (*nāga*), the tortoise wind (*kūrma*), the lizard wind (*kṛkala*), the Devadatta wind, and the Dhananjaya wind—becoming immutable.
Because there is no partiality regarding attachment or freedom from attachment, it is non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*).
Each is divided by its respective [vowel], and furthermore, they are distinguished by the vowels beginning with *a* and the consonants beginning with *ka*.

Thus, the thirty consonants—ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, and sa—which possess the nature of the elements of space, wind, fire, water, earth, and gnosis, are differentiated by the five short vowels; likewise, they are differentiated by the five long vowels, such as ā and so forth, which possess the nature of earth and the other elements, through the sequence of emanation and reabsorption.
There are three hundred and sixty breaths, distinguished by the twelve transits of the sheep, ox, and so forth.
During the southern course, there is a single consonant and a short vowel;
during the northern course, there is a stacked consonant and a long vowel—this is the sun.

Regarding the transference (*'pho ba*): it is the triple-stacked illuminator and the extremely long one, namely Rāhu. The meaning is that it moves and is to be differentiated according to the distinctions of the primordial mothers—sattva, rajas, and tamas.
"By others such as the eyes" refers to death and so forth.
"Seeing" is the seeing of various forms.
Grasping at entities is the definitive realization of entities.
"Of that" means that the definitive determination of the meaning of entities is the definitive grasping [of them] as having the nature of emptiness.

Attachment to form is reversed by turning [the mind] inward toward the mind alone; by focusing on the divine self (*devātman*), one enters into reality and is oriented toward it through the analytical investigation of the single flavor of supreme wisdom and method. That very state of mental well-being is "joy" (*prīti*), which means delight.
The bliss of extreme physical pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and so forth is "bliss of immobility" (*niṣkampasukha*).

Regarding "thoroughly entering the Middle Way": this refers to the entry of the subtle life-wind (*prāṇavāyu*), characterized by the process of entering, abiding, and arising, which occurs solely within the central channel (*madhyamā-mārga*) once the ten mandalas—space and so forth—have dissolved and the *lalanā* and *rasanā* have ceased; this is the section ending with the term "vital exertion" (*prāṇāyāma*). "The path of both has been destroyed" refers to the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and...

Because the *uṣṇīṣas* are devoid of coming and going, they are said to be devoid of movement; thus, it will be taught that "retention" (*dhāraṇā*) consists in the mind’s vehicle—the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*)—becoming of one taste with emptiness within the drops (*bindu*), once the winds have sequentially ceased.
The ten aspects have already been explained previously.

This means that for a mind engaged in apprehension, there first appears the individual manifestation of the ten signs, such as smoke and so forth, which naturally precede the vision of the deities of the complete mandala; this is non-conceptual and has the nature of a reflected image, from which many rays of light are emitted.
Then, it is said that the ten stages of desire, beginning with the visualization of the emanation of the divine wheel within the three realms, constitute "recollection" (anusmṛti).

Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth": because it has been perfectly clarified by the blazing of *caṇḍālī*, the bodhicitta remains undiminished at the tip of the head of the vajra-jewel. Thereafter, through the gradual cessation of twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths within the six wheels, the nature of the body—which is the essence of the Great Vajradhara, the nature of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), the identity of the union (*yuganaddha*), and the nature of immutable great bliss—is called "meditative absorption" (*samādhi*).
The fruit of *pratyāhāra* and the other [five limbs] is characterized by the subsequent praise of the six limbs.

Regarding the phrase "the bodhisattva becomes [a Buddha]," this is because he does not yet engage in birth, awakening, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and so forth; for it is intended that through such engagement, he will indeed come to be designated as a "Buddha" who has perfected the buddha-field.
"Such as the ten masteries" refers to the mastery over lifespan,
karma, aspiration, mind, requisites, and prayer.
[These include] mastery over miraculous powers,
rebirth, primordial wisdom,
the Dharma, and so forth.
The mind of the grasped and the grasper is the agent.
Furthermore, the subsequent praise is spoken: "Through withdrawal, one enters meditative equipoise; all mantras are empowered by the equipoise of dhyāna and primordial wisdom."
The five superknowledges will be attained;
through the exertion of their vital breath,
the Bodhisattvas certainly behold them.
Through the power of constant grasping,
Vajrasattva enters into equipoise;
this arises from the application of recollection.
The mandala of light will arise;
by the mere mastery of meditative concentration,
one will become endowed with it without obstruction.
Thus it is said.
Because of being inferior, there is an obstruction to the flow through the left and right [channels], which is due to the life-force not being restrained.
Through the practice of *nāda*, one practices the coemergent joy (*sahajānanda*) of primordial wisdom.
By means of power—that is, through the *nāda* of the syllable *hūṃ*—the drops of bodhicitta are arrested within the lotus of wisdom and the vajra jewel.

Having inserted the penis according to the ritual into the *kakko* (vagina) of the supreme beloved who is filled with passion, as previously described, one sustains it in an immovable state. Pressing the vajra-jewel against the opening of her clitoris, one should render it immovable for a moment through the flavor of intense bliss.

Then, when the occasion for transformation arises, one is oriented toward that which is preceded by the utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*—brought about by the grace of the Guru’s feet—and experiences the fourth joy, the innate (*sahaja*), which is the cessation of the drops (*bindu*) of bodhicitta; thereafter, the moment of the unchanging is seen. This is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "in this very Śrī Kālacakra," and so forth: *śakti* refers to the power of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
One goes to another dwelling, namely, the dwelling that is without objective referents.

Regarding "the limit of twelve," this refers to the left nostril, which extends from the mandala of space and so forth down to the mandala of earth; that is, from sixteen finger-widths (aṅgula) down to a limit of twelve finger-widths.

Regarding "the end of the six," this refers to the twelve finger-widths (aṅgula) up to sixteen finger-widths, starting from the earth mandala and so forth up to the end of the space mandala in the right nostril.

By the utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*, through the union of the life-sustaining (*prāṇa*) and downward-clearing (*apāna*) winds, they are blocked at the navel; that very power of the life-force is like lightning-fire and resembles lightning-fire.
"Moving" means shaking.
"Like a needle" means being similar to a needle.
"Thur du sel ba" means "to go," that is, to proceed or enter.
In another village, it is like another body.

If one asks, "What would happen if one were to enter another's village even with only this much? it is said: "In that case, one should act as follows. That is to say, by means of this sequence, through the awakening of the vajra—that is, through the awakening of the gnosis of supreme bliss.
"In the mind" refers to the mind in which the grasped and the grasper have become blended into one.
That which possesses its object is the capacity for the sense faculty and the object to become blended into one.
As for "wandering in space," one proceeds as a sovereign master with mastery over the limits of the realm of Akaniṣṭha.

It is said, "Not only that," referring to the phrase "clairvoyance" and so forth; the nature of the five superknowledges (*abhijñā*) consists of the nature of miraculous powers (*ṛddhi*), the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and recollection of former abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*).

It also becomes Vajradhātvīśvarī; through the passion of wisdom in Mahāmudrā, the non-conceptual *caṇḍālī* blazes, which is called "the yoga of the three immutables. This refers to the cessation of the mental *bindu* when it reaches the secret place, and the cessation of the vocal *bindu* when it reaches the navel.
Because bliss is not lost, the collection of *bindus* does not shift from the vajra-gate; thus, the *bindu* of primordial wisdom is arrested—this is the yoga of primordial wisdom.

From the conclusion of the phrase "this refutation of the dual winds" (16), the siddhi of moving on the earth is clarified; from the conclusion of the phrase "becoming one who moves through space," the siddhi of moving at the limit [of the sky] is realized; and by the phrase ending with "Vivid Mother" (*Viśvamātṛ*), the siddhi of Mahāmudrā is clarified.
When it reaches the heart, the bindus of the body cease. "Mudrā" refers to Mahāmudrā.
That which conforms to illusion is like a reflection in a perfectly clear mirror;
it is the mental activity of the mind and space, yet devoid of a [substantial] mind.
For this very reason it was said: "Like a form in a mirror. "Like a form" means spreading forth in a manner similar to a form.
The external and the body are inseparable; the objects and the sense faculties have become blended into one.
Because its essential nature is the manifestation of phenomena as distinct from the subject, it is free from objects and mental forms.
The manifold nature embraces the minds of beings; that alone is to be abandoned.
For that very reason, it is the nature of mind—the nature of a mind that is without mind.
The supreme mudrā is the very essence of that which appears as one's own body, a mere appearance in which the mind and its objects—the grasped and the grasper—have become entirely intermingled.
It has arisen—that is, it has come forth—in one's own mind, in the nature that is both endowed with all aspects and devoid of aspects.
That is the blazing flame of gnosis; it is the increasing blaze of the inner heat (caṇḍālī) of gnosis.
Together with its objects, it is the host of Māras—the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields—along with their circles, which is the net of the conceptual mind.
It is also said: "Māra is one's own mind; there is no other Māra."

The bliss of peace through dying and striving is the bliss of innate joy (*sahajānanda*); it arises from the union of the years, meaning the "teeth" of the *Kālacakra* at the time of three years and three fortnights.
Wisdom is what is called "gnosis" (jñāna) according to their respective enumerations; wisdom is the realization that all phenomena are emptiness, and that is the mind.

Its "mind of the object of apprehension," which is the appearance seen from all sides such as smoke and so forth, is the gnosis of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Into this apprehended mind, characterized by smoke and so forth, the apprehending mind has entered emptiness and become entirely merged with it.
The recollection that was taught is called "Stainless."
Regarding the phrase "of the childish, the youthful, and the fickle," there are two types of bliss resulting from the transformation of method: that of the childish and that of the youthful.

"Vajradhara" means the nirmāṇakāya of Vajradhara.
That should be explained as entering into the appearance of this very mind— the appearance of the mind that is like a reflection in a mirror—

Regarding the phrase "the aspect of earth" and so forth, this refers to the characteristics of form: here, the individual appearance of emptiness—which is not a substantial entity—is seen as earth and so on, yet it is not solid.
That which has the aspect of being liquid, like the water in a mirage, is not water, because it lacks moisture. Likewise, the aspect of fire is not fire, because there is no burning of grass.
Because the body, which moves by means of wind, is itself insubstantial, that which is without movement is not wind.
Because it is devoid of substantiality, it has the aspect of emptiness; even so, it is to be viewed as such.
Like a city of illusions, although it possesses colors such as white and so forth, it is not color because it lacks substantial reality.
Although it possesses all aspects, it is not an object of vision for the spiritually immature at all times.
Why is that? It is because it arises from the power of the māra of the afflictions, due to the vital breath flowing through the left and right channels; this is the certainty.
Now, the exhaustion of the five maṇḍalas is taught by the words beginning with "earth," and so forth.

In this regard, when the yogī has unwinking eyes and fixes his mind on emptiness with a wrathful gaze, at that time—indicated by the word "earth" (sa)—if the yogī practices meditation when [the breath] flows through the right [nostril], then it is in that manner; it is not, however, when it flows through the left channel, but rather according to the sequence beginning with the mandala of space and so forth.

Therefore, because it possesses the very nature of whichever life-mandala flows through either the left or the right, that specific mandala is taught. Thus, from the earth mandala, the life-force moves into the water mandala on the right channel, and likewise up to the gnosis mandala;
on the left channel, it moves by way of space and the other elements.

Likewise, emptiness definitely becomes the ten types of signs, such as smoke and so forth; and these signs become the form that is the transformation of all aspects, yet do not deviate from form. That itself is primordial wisdom, the very nature of the perfection of insight (prajñāpāramitā).
From primordial wisdom arises miraculous power, such as traveling through the sky and so forth, and one will become a sovereign over the three realms, possessing the ten siddhis.
"For human beings, O Lord of Men, it is in this very life"—this is the certainty regarding the entry upon the path.

Thus, these four signs are established as the four fruits (*phala*). Moreover, the *Caturmudrā-niścaya* states: "The smoke-like sign is the sign of the wind-āśraya; the mirage-like sign is the sign of the water-āśraya; the firefly-like sign is the sign of the fire-āśraya; and the lamp-like sign is the sign of the earth-āśraya. Thus, these four signs are established as the four bases (*āśraya*). Furthermore, the *Caturmudrā-niścaya* states: "The smoke-like sign is the sign of the wind-lakṣaṇa; the mirage-like sign is the sign of the water-lakṣaṇa; the firefly-like sign is the sign of the fire-lakṣaṇa; and the lamp-like sign is the sign of the earth-lakṣaṇa. Thus, these four signs are established as the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Additionally, the *Caturmudrā-niścaya* states: "The smoke-like sign is the sign of the wind-svabhāva; the mirage-like sign is the sign of the water-svabhāva; the firefly-like sign is the sign of the fire-svabhāva; and the lamp-like sign is the sign of the earth-svabhāva. Thus, these four signs are established as

In this Mantra system, three types of valid cognition (*pratyaya*) have been taught: first, the valid cognition of the tantra; second, the valid cognition of the guru; and third, the valid cognition of oneself. Through these three valid cognitions, the path of the perfectly awakened one (*samyaksambuddha*) becomes completely pure. Otherwise, the path described by a guru, if devoid of these three valid cognitions, does not bestow the fruit of perfect awakening upon the disciple, because the disciple is dull-witted regarding faith. Through the instruction of a true guru, the commentaries composed by Bodhisattvas, and one's own experience—[removing] restlessness, regret, lethargy, sleep, and agitation—the lords of Jinas have summarized that which is called the "dissipation of the winds in the body" as self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*).
Buddhahood arises within that very saṃsāra, which is devoid of essence, among all sentient beings upon the earth; for when that saṃsāra has withered,
it is like the ripened fruit of a banana tree once the banana tree itself has dried up.
Since those scorpions, bees, and *aliṅgiras* that are born perish [in turn], just as a yogi [perceives] the illusory nature of the mind;
thus, the single stage of perfect purity has been taught by the Buddhas for the sake of liberation in the tantra whose essence is wisdom and means.
If it is asked, "How is this known? he says:
"In the sense of initiation" means for that reason, by which reason the Lords of Jinas have gathered even those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution;
by that very [reason] it is known...
But if this is so, does not the stage of perfect purification belong only to those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution?
It is not so;
for even those who act for the benefit of the world are established in a perfectly pure sequence.
Thus, the unchanging, singular essence is the supreme [state], being devoid of succession.
The supreme syllable, the great passion, existence and non-existence, and gnosis;
the being Samantabhadra, the soundless great resonance;
the innate, the glorious bodhicitta, the glorious Kālacakra, the bearer of the vajra, gnosis, means, and yoga.

Regarding the phrase "by the non-sequential" (*niranvayena*): *anvaya* is the phenomenon (*dharma*) characterized by subject and object, consisting of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). That which has discarded this *anvaya* is "non-sequential" (*niranvaya*); thus, it is said "by the non-sequential. He by whom the sequential phenomenon characterized by subject and object, consisting of wisdom and means, has been discarded is [described] as such.
This very Vajrayoga has been thus praised and lauded in many ways by the Tathāgatas, by the assemblies of Bodhisattvas, and by the glorious Vajradharas who are knowers of mantra.

The practitioner of the pledge (*samayin*), mounted upon the Vajrayāna, is one who contemplates true reality (*satattva*), is free from greed, and has removed all impurities. Endowed with fortitude and diligence, he moves along the path and bestows the path upon his circle of attendants.
Dwelling without fear of hell, virtuous, and having truth as his essence, he wields a firm staff; here, through direct perception and inference, he is the very element of the deity.
Through the application of reality, direct perception has the form of a star;
inference, however, has the form of a corpse and is devoid of direct perception.
That which is indeed shown in a painting consists of conceptual construction and is bereft of reality.
For the sake of meditation for yogis whose intellects are not yet fully matured,
the domain of the deity is [attained] through perception and inference;
through the yoga of reality, it becomes a direct perception in the form of a star.
Because it is perceivable by the four types of eyes beginning with the fleshly eye,
it resembles illusion, dreams, and the like; appearing as the three worlds throughout the three times,
the fleshly eye first beholds the universal image.
Without the superknowledges (*abhijñā*):
then, by the power of the superknowledges, he sees with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*);
by the power of dispassion (*virāga*), he sees with the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*).
Subsequently, by attaining the ten stages of a bodhisattva, one sees with the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*).
By attaining the state in which all residual conditions (*upādhi*) are exhausted, one sees with the eye of knowledge (*jñāna-cakṣus*).
In the vision of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the five eyes beginning with the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) are impelled by the Buddhas.
In the vision of emptiness, others are indeed like those blind from birth;
here, the definitive conclusion lies in the meditation on reality.
Because of the absence of knowledge of reality, inference takes the form of a corpse.
That which is indeed shown in a painting— consisting of mental construction, devoid of reality,
having the form of an artisan's work, and clothed in the appearance of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth,
or the form of a maṇḍala or a wheel— is a constructed form.
This is presented for the purpose of meditation by those yogins who are slow-witted;
herein lies the definitive conclusion regarding conceptual meditation (*saṃkalpa-dhyāna*).
Service (*sevā*) is performed with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth, and with the mantras of the four vajras and so forth.
Success arises through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other [limbs of yoga],
by means of the nectars born from the lotus of the *kuliśa*.
With the three vajras together with the lotuses as the wealth, one possesses the intellect of equal flavor (*samarasa*).
It is performed through joy and the other [aesthetic flavors];
it is the great accomplishment, indestructible in the embrace of wisdom,
ascertained by means of subtle yoga.
The yoga of reality is meditation on the form of all forms;
it has the luster of a circle of stars,
and by means of jars, cloths, and so forth situated before one, it possesses the appearance of the three worlds.
In the center of the *bindu*, one sees infinite Buddhas in the form of bodies, appearing like a dark-blue lunar mandala;
with the power [of this vision], the fleshly eye perceives up to a hundred *yojanas*.
Through this, the five superknowledges (*abhijñā*), such as miraculous powers (*ṛddhi*), arise.
"Power" (*śakti*) means capacity.
The "eye of wisdom" (*buddhacakṣus*) knows the minds of others.
The "eye of insight" (*prajñācakṣus*) consists of non-conceptual knowledge regarding all phenomena.

The eye of wisdom perceives everything in all its aspects. *The Mānasollāsa*, *Mānasāra*, *Viṣṇusaṃhitā*, and *Silparatna* (verse 255) state: In the internal [practice], the means (*sādhana*) is the cow; in the external, the satisfaction of the cow. In the internal, the bliss of emission (*cyavanasukha*) is the yoga; in the external, the yoga. In the internal, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) are the sense organs; in the external, the five nectars. In the internal, the aggregates (*skandha*) are the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*); in the external, the five lamps. Feces (*viṭ*) is form (*rūpa*), the cow’s body; blood is perception (*saṃjñā*), the dog’s tongue. Semen (*śukra*) is feeling (*vedanā*), the one to be tamed (*damya*); the eye is formation (*saṃskāra*), the elephant’s trunk. Flesh is consciousness (*vijñāna*), the human ear; urine is Māmakī, the wine, the cow.

Pervasion (256), *upasādhana*, food, the empty-form (*śūnyatābimba*), the non-falling (*acyuta*), emission, *āḥ om hūṃ*, bringing face-to-face (*āḥ mukhīkaraṇa*), counteracting, food, awakening to emptiness, grasping the moon-drop (*candrabindu*), the arising of the image, and the placement of syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*)—here the form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are exactly as before. General service (*sāmānyasevā*) is likewise; similarly, soft service (*mṛdu sevā*): Body-Vajra, the infant (*bāla*, i.e., *jātabāla*), awakening to emptiness, grasping the moon-drop, the arising of the image, and the placement of syllables. Firm *upasādhana*: Speech-Vajra, middle-infant, the accomplishment of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Soft *sādhana*: Mind-Vajra, the youth (*kumāra*). Firm Great Accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*): Wisdom-Vajra, the mature (*praudha*). The twelve aspects, the twelve aspects: having placed [the mind] upon the Vajra and the Lotus in the central channel, one should practice the union of inhalation and exhalation (*prāṇāpāna*).
One should gradually dissolve the drops into the drop within the wheel, and the drops into the vajra;
by the power of wisdom, one attains the vajra-jewel, which has emerged from the void through the guru’s instruction and is free from sense objects.

The yoga of realization is innate; therein, Śiva is subtle and connected to the aggregate of gnosis through imperishable bliss. He is considered to have ten characteristics according to his definitions;
furthermore, being connected to the aggregate of gnosis, he is formless and again tenfold.
That Akṣobhya is indeed the samādhi, the kinsman of the aggregate of consciousness;
the unity of the sense objects within the Universal Image is the aggregate of consciousness.
The Khaḍgin is also the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), the kinsman of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra).
Due to the entry into the ten mandalas of those situated in the two channels,
Ratnapāṇi likewise meditates; he is remembered as the kinsman of the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) and is tenfold in the wheels of the navel, heart, and throat regions.

In the Dombya [channel], mindfulness is the earth-holder; it is the kinsman of the aggregate of perception, tenfold, and the support for the ten states of passion. This wheel is divided, and that glorious Samādhi is tenfold through the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The Blessed One has attained non-abiding nirvana;
for him, there is the cessation of the objects of the senses and of the senses themselves in embodied beings,
as well as the cessation of the activity of sensations, which is the very image of emptiness.
The vision of the image is wisdom (*prajñā*); its characteristic state is reasoning (*tarka*).
Investigation (*vicāra*) is the stability of the intellect (*dhīratī*), and unwavering bliss is steadfastness (*sādhiratva*).
Through the non-differentiation from the object of vision, meditation (*dhyāna*) is considered to have ten characteristics according to its aspects.
That movement is radiant in the center; indeed, breath control (prāṇāyāma) is distinguished by its division.
This entry of the breath into the drop (bindu) at the forehead is the coming and going of the breath;
it is called mindfulness (smṛti), and because of its one-pointedness, it is called meditation (dhyāna).
As before, mindfulness is tenfold in the space of the three worlds;
through the yoga of the unity of knowledge and the object of knowledge, the movement becomes steady in the reflection of gnosis.
Meditation, beginning with the absence of breath and so forth, is considered tenfold according to its characteristics.
This is the accomplishment of Kālacakra through the yoga of the six limbs.
According to the divisions of "mild" and so forth, this accomplishment is considered to be threefold:
the mild is the movement of the emission of the *bodhicitta*; the middling is the movement of vibration; and the great is the immovable, which is the supreme stability.

Physical pliancy is *rasanā*; the maṇḍalas are the *avadhūtī* at the navel; at the heart, in the drop (*bindu*) located in the wheels (*cakras*) beginning with the navel, there is the bliss of emission through the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), the bliss of vibration through the wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*), and the bliss of non-vibration through the great seal (*mahāmudrā*). The drop is the vision of *caṇḍālī*. Vision (*āloka*) is that which exists in the body and in space; this is recollection (*anusmṛti*). Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the action-partner (*karmāṅganā*), while the universal image (*viśvabimba*) is the wisdom-image (*jñānabimba*). Longevity, karma, liberation, requisites, aspiration, miraculous power, phenomena, mind, rebirth, and gnosis—these are the empty images. Therefore, it is pure; therefore, it is pure: the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is as described, endowed with the qualities mentioned in the tantras. The state of flowing and dripping, on the upward path, is the unique and peaceful empty image within the body of another, by virtue of imperishable bliss.
Here, that single moment of bodhicitta which occurs by virtue of inexhaustible bliss is called "pacified.
Here, during the great realization, the innate yoga of gnosis arises.
The unification of the mind with immutable bliss occurs.
The fourth limb is the Great Realization (*mahābodhi*).
The *mudrā* is similar to an illusion; she appears in the mind and in space like a reflection in a mirror.
Spreading manifold rays like lightning or fire, she illumines the three worlds.
External to bodies, devoid of sensory objects, consisting solely of light, she dwells in space.
Made of mind, though she is one, she encompasses the mind of the manifold world.
She is merely a manifestation of one’s own mind; she is born within one’s own mind, like a reflection in a mirror.
She, who was honored by the Buddhas—the sons of all the Victors—must be honored by the great yogins, the lords of yoga.
Inflamed by the flame of primordial wisdom, she consumes all the hosts of Māra, together with their objects as well as attachment and the rest.
Within one year, she bestows the equal pleasure (*samasukha*) upon the bodies of the yogins.
GBh: "By virtue of passion for wisdom" means by virtue of the non-conceptual flame of Caṇḍālī.
The *bindu* of mind, having reached the secret place, is restrained; the *bindu* of speech, having reached the navel, is restrained; the *bindu* of body, having reached the heart, is restrained.
The *jñānabindu* is restrained "by means of imperishable bliss," that is, by means of the collection of *bindus* that have reached the tip of the *vajra* and do not fall.
This is the "yoga of gnosis.
Regarding this topic, see the commentary on LKC V (ed., vol. III, p. ...).
GBh: The *mudrā*, namely the *mahāmudrā*, is "similar to *māyā*," that is, similar to an image reflected in a clean mirror.
She "appears in the mind and in space," meaning in a mind that is non-mind (*acittacitta*); and for this very reason it has been said that she is "like a figure in a mirror" [...].
She is not separate from external reality in terms of the bodies of *māyā*, or in other words, she is fused with objects and the sensory faculties.
Yet she is separate from those objects and sensory faculties: "she is devoid of sensory objects," which are reflections of *dharmas*. She is "one" and yet "embraces the mind of the manifold world."
Therefore, "she is made of mind" means she possesses the nature of a mind that is non-mind.
In the *Vimalaprabhā* (ed., vol. III, p. [blank], line [blank]), Puṇḍarīka provides no commentary on this verse and simply writes: "The verse is easily understood. GBh:
The divine *mudrā* is "merely an apparition," a reflection of "one's own mind" in which its two aspects—the perceived and the perceiver—are perfectly fused.
"She" is merely wisdom; knowledge is the mind. To it belongs a tenfold image.
Initiation is immersion into this mind—the luster (*nibhā*) of the stainless (*vimala*) moon—which is like an image reflected in a mirror.
From this arises the imperishable bliss of nirvāṇa, which is innate, unchanging, and the fourth.
The glorious Master is he who possesses this face of the Buddha within his heart and mouth.
Here, *prajñā* and *jñāna* correspond respectively to the subject-consciousness (*grāhakacitta*) and the object-consciousness (*grāhyacitta*).

Knowledge—that is, the perceivable mind—is the tenfold image beginning with smoke, which can be seen as a magical image or a reflection in the mirror of the perceivable; this belongs to its cognizer, namely, wisdom, the perceiving mind.
This image is precisely knowledge, the perceivable mind.

In a similar manner, our eye perceives itself in a mirror as an appearance born—that is, arisen—within one’s own mind, which is endowed with all aspects (*sarvākāra*) and yet simultaneously devoid of all aspects (*nirākāra*).
She is “intensified by the flame of gnosis,” namely, by the flame of *caṇḍālī*. [...]

The "armies of Māra" (*mārasenā*), which are joined with their "objects"—namely the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*)—constitute the "net" (*jāla*; Tib. *dra ba*) of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). As it has been said: "Māra is one’s own mind; no other Māra exists. (The full verse is quoted in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, ed., p. [blank]; cf. also the *Vyākhyāyukti*, ed., vol. I, p. [blank]: "That which is called Māra for sentient beings is the mind of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) stained by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); that which is called Buddhahood is the mind free from the habitual tendencies of cyclic existence.")
"She bestows equal pleasure," that is, the pleasure of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), "within a year," namely, within the year of Kālacakra, which consists of three years and three fortnights.

Alternatively, if we accept the reading *°upame* instead of *°upamā*, which appears more consistent with the context, the sentence may be translated as follows: “Initiation is immersion into this mind, which resembles an image reflected in a mirror, as radiant as the stainless moon. From this immersion arises . . .”
This reading appears to be followed also by the Tibetan translation (see also Gnoli-Orofino, note).
The editors of the VP suggest the reading *upamam* (“immersion, which is similar…”) as an alternative possibility;
however, their conjecture does not fit the context of the ṢY based on the GBh.
Raviśrījñāna appears to accept Pundarīka’s gloss, according to which *majjana* (“immersion”) entails the first four limbs of yoga.
Furthermore, he regards the word *vimala* (“immaculate”), the first member of the compound ending in *upamā*, as an implicit reference to *anusmṛti*—
like a reflected image.
Initiation is immersion into this mind.

Here, in the context of the sixfold yoga, the entry of the perceiving mind into this perceived mind—which corresponds to withdrawal (pratyāhāra), defined as non-engagement with external objects—as well as meditative concentration (dhyāna), breath control (prāṇāyāma), and retention (dhāraṇā), is called "immersion."
From this immersion arises the imperishable bliss of nirvāṇa, which is innate, unchanging, and the fourth bliss.
The meaning is that this bliss is superior to the vibratory states known as the "infant" and the "youth."

It is beyond all worldly comparison and free from the conduct of both the *karmamudrā* and the *jñānamudrā*. Its characteristic is emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects; it is Vajradhara. (109) Ejaculatory bliss (*kṣarasukha*) is twofold: that of the child and that of the mature. Vibratory bliss (*spandasukha*) is [the bliss] of the means (*upāya*). Therefore, the bliss of the means is twofold—child and mature; the bliss of vibration belongs to wisdom (*prajñā*), which is the aged. When there arises the motionless state of those two by way of the *mahāmudrā*, that is non-dual, devoid of the two sense organs. (275) (10) The digit (*kalā*) and the drop (*bindu*) are space (*ākāśa*) and the open expanse (*abhyavakāśa*). (61) (62) (63) The digit.

(The Support-Cause): Those whose minds have attained a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) with space, as expressed by the words "space" and so forth—by them, with eyes half-open and breaths directed into the *avadhūtī*, one perceives four signs through the yoga of night: smoke from emptiness, a mirage, fireflies, and a lamp.
Then, in a cloudless sky during the daytime yoga, there are six [signs]: the flame, the moon, the sun, the black jewel, the lightning, and the light of the clear moon; these are the ten signs.

In their midst, within the great bindu, is the Buddha-image—the vision of all forms such as jars and cloths, empty of external objects, the vision of an image consisting of many non-conceptual enjoyment bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*), the manifestation of all appearances in a single instant like an illusion.
The earth element, being empty, dissolves into water; water dissolves into fire.
Fire dissolves into the subtle element, and wind dissolves into the mind.
The mind dissolves into the mental factors, the mental factors into ignorance, and that [ignorance] too passes into the clear light; this is the cessation within the three realms.
Of this Vajrasattva, whose nature is supreme great bliss—having become one with the four bodies that are free from all conceptual proliferation—the cognition is the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
The cognition of emptiness appears in all its aspects within the intermediate state as a reflected image (*pratisenā*); it is a phenomenon unattached to space, free from superimposition (*samāropa*).

[Stanza 27] It is an entity (*bhāva*), the thought of the practitioner (*sādhakacintā*), an insentient phenomenon (*jaḍadharma*), the practitioner himself, an illusion (*māyā*), and conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
One does not see with the eyes of another— those produced on the forehead and so forth— nor even with one's own eyes, because [the object] is not seen at other times.
Just as a young girl might see her son born within this bedchamber—
exceedingly joyful when he is born, and dejected in mind when he has died— in that same way, one who understands all phenomena through such analogies [knows them].
(Expedient means) (expedient means).
(The limb separated by one [stage]).
(Efficacy).

(The state of being a practitioner of) mutually dependent dharmas, even in this very life, through the essence of recitation and meditation. 133. Through the six perspectives (*koṭi*)—namely, *sandhyābhāṣā*, *nosandhya*, *neyārtha*, *nītārtha*, *yathārūtha*, and *anartha*—[the sequence is: 1) withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), 2) meditation (*dhyāna*), 3) breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), 4) mantra-recitation (*mantrajāpa*), 5) recollection (*anusmṛti*), and 6) bliss (*sukha*, i.e., *samādhi*). The Victor (*Jina*) utters the literal meaning, which is an explanation of the remaining truth. 69ab.
Prāṇa and smṛti (recollection) should be understood as preceding sukha (bliss).
Here, śūnyatā (emptiness) is the vision of all phenomena (sarvabhāva) that is devoid of all conceptual constructs (sarvabhāva-vikalpa).
[The channels] are rasanā and avadhūtī.
Oṃ, Āḥ. 142 Vāruṇa, Agni 143. Bindu.

Having made the mind free from [distractions] for one day, one should examine the sign. If, according to the procedure taught in the Tantra and through the instruction of the Guru, no conviction arises in the disciple, then the word of the Blessed One would be false.

However, if the Guru does not become the bestower of the path to the disciple according to the procedure taught in the Tantra, then it is not the Blessed One’s promise that becomes false; rather, it is due to the Guru’s lack of knowledge of the path and his teaching of a perverted and impure path.

In this case, one should not examine another sign for a single day as the means for accomplishing the maṇḍala-cakra, setting aside signs such as smoke, according to the word of the Blessed One. 72, 73, 89, 147,
There, Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One Subhūti:
"Noble Subhūti, regarding this perfection of wisdom, one who attains yoga—where does he attain yoga?
Subhūti replied:
Kauśika, whoever attains yoga in this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) attains yoga in space. Kauśika, whoever desires instruction in the perfection of wisdom should desire yoga in the open air.
This was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Samājottara*.

One should meditate on the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which consists of the five jewels and is empowered by the five Buddhas, as having a dense form at the tip of the *nāḍī* toward the downward-voiding wind (*apānavāyu*).
Likewise, the five Buddhas consist of the five aggregates (*skandha*) beginning with consciousness, which have the nature of the mandala of the *lalanā*.
The vital breaths presided over by them flow through the left nostril.
One should meditate on the *prāṇa* and *apāna* winds at the tip of the nose in the form of a cloud;

therein, the state of being a "cloud-form" is the gathering of the mandalas of the right and left [channels]. It is the gathering of the two, *prāṇa* and *apāna*, within the central mandala of the *avadhūtī*.
In this manner, one should meditate on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) up to the limit of the exhalation; one should contemplate it in the form of a dense mass at the tip of the *nāḍikā*.
Here, by the term *nāḍikā*, the pericarps of the lotuses of the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown of the head are meant.
One should contemplate its root at the tip [of that pericarp]; as at the center of the pericarp, so one should contemplate it within the pericarp.
But one should not [place them] on the right and left sides like lotus petals; rather, one should establish the prāṇa and apāna breaths in the place of the dense-form bindu,
for in this way concentration (dhāraṇā) is accomplished.
Therefore, one should contemplate the form of the deity during the practice;
there, by the power of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), the yogi beholds the *caṇḍālī* blazing at the navel—unobscured, like an illusion.
She is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), radiating a mass of rays from infinite Buddhas and shining forth with a circle of light.
That mindfulness is said to be the means; and at the conclusion of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), one should contemplate the yoga of Caṇḍālī. As it has been stated:

"Then, burnt by the fire of one's own gnosis, the aggregates (*skandhas*), elements (*dhātus*), sense-bases (*āyatanas*), and so forth—both consciousness and the like, as well as earth and the rest—along with the mandalas situated on the right and left paths, attain a single flavor and enter the lunar mandala in the forehead."

Then, the Moon, having been melted by the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*) through the Caṇḍālī, drips as the *bindu* of bodhicitta. Passing sequentially through the lotuses of the throat, heart, navel, and secret place— attaining the states of joy (*ānanda*), supreme joy (*paramānanda*), cessation-joy (*viramānanda*),
and innate joy (*sahajānanda*)— it reaches the vajra-jewel and becomes of the nature of innate joy.
Alternatively, its form is characterized by various ripenings and transformations;

therefore, it is said that here, having obtained a jewel full of sixteen digits (*kalā*), one bestows a bliss equal to the bliss of liberation through contemplation. Nevertheless, this is merely an illustration;
in reality, even a fraction of the supreme immutable bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*) is not obtained through the bliss born of semen and blood produced from two parts.

In this context, the stability of the mind of a bodhisattva who perceives an entity whose intrinsic nature is ineffable and devoid of an essence consisting of all verbal expressions is called his "concentration on emptiness" (śūnyatā-samādhi).
This emptiness is said to be unknowable by those like me;
it does not, however, follow the worldly convention of nihilism.
Possessing all forms yet devoid of form, holding the sixteen, the half, and the quarter-bindu; partless, beyond calculation, and holding the pinnacle of the fourth dhyāna;
possessing all forms yet devoid of form—direct perception is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous.
“That consciousness which has gone toward and relies upon the sense-faculties (*akṣa*) is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
[... By means of the passage beginning with “the state to be cultivated,” one should here in space cultivate the state that is like a dream, transcending the nature of atoms.
Through the thorough knowledge of that, one should cultivate non-existence with a mind free from conceptual construction;
thus, wisdom (prajñā) is the letter *e*,
and likewise is Heruka.

Existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*) are that which is to be cultivated—the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), Heruka, Great Bliss. As is wisdom, so is means (*upāya*). Through the thorough knowledge of that, both existence and non-existence become the means. From the word "likewise" (*tadvat*), it follows that as is the cause, so is the fruit.
One who understands existence and non-existence in this way never becomes attached to any existents.

He who is never attached to any entities touches the signless (*animitta*) concentration—[that is,] the direct perception of the mind, the direct perception of the yogin, and the direct perception of self-awareness. That very knowledge is the instructor, the motivator, the achiever, and is characterized by experience; that very manifestation has been established by means of nine examples.
It is, for example, like a reflection, a magically created city, an echo, a dream, an illusion, a machine, a mirage, a mirror-image, the moon in water, and space [15.34].

Where semen is the vajra, by way of reversal, Vairocana and the others [are located] in the navel and so forth; this has already been explained in the Tantra regarding the body by means of the "motionless" (niḥspanda) and other [states].

Furthermore, that sixteenth [digit] which is at the end of the full moon is wisdom (*prajñā*); because it is infinite through the infinity of space, it is located in the head together with the *vajra*, meaning it is endowed with the upward-pointing *vajra*. Thus, it is the sixth.
And it has been stated by Vajragarbha: "In this context, Vairocana is the leader in the earth-circle, and Akṣobhya is in space."
Amitābha is in water,
Ratnasambhava in fire, and Amoghasiddhi in wind.
Vajrasattva is the leader in the wheel of gnosis. [1] Once the *prāṇa* and *apāna* have been restrained, the agitated moon enters into the solar image.
[2] Once the vajra has been awakened in the lotus, this [moon] melts together with the flame of the solar image.
[3] Once the moon and the sun have been suppressed, consciousness (*vijñāna*) and gnosis (*jñāna*) become one with the wind.
It is threefold: Evam, Evam, and Evam.
The wheel is the purity and clarity of the entire threefold existence (tribhava) on all sides.
The jewel is the nature of bliss; the lotus is attachment to bliss; the sword is the severing of the afflictions;
and the vajra is the indestructible gnosis.
The scissors that cut through ignorance belong to the six families beginning with Cakra;

by these, beginning with Cakra, the aggregates (skandhas) are produced, and they too should be known as having such natures as clarity and so forth, and for that very reason, as being of one flavor like space.

Indeed, in this entire *Yoginīyogatantrarāja*, the Vajrin Śākyamuni has concealed the adamantine state (*vajrapada*), which is the bliss of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣarasukha*). Here, in the system of Mantra, the adamantine state is twofold: one according to worldly convention (*laukikasamvṛti*) and the second from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

For those two, according to worldly convention (*loka-saṃvṛti*), the vajra-word bestows the accomplishment of the commitments (*samaya-siddhi*) in rites such as slaying; according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the fourth vajra-word likewise bestows the fruit of the accomplishment of the great seal (*mahāmudrā*). Thus, the vajra-word is secret. In all the kings of tantras, the vajra-word is not manifest; it is to be understood through the lineage of the gurus. "A tantra is to be understood by means of another tantra," according to the word of the Tathāgata. And: "The Buddha, the Dharma, the Gaṇa, the Element (*dhātu*), Awakening (*bodhi*), the qualities (*guṇa*), and finally the activity of a Buddha (*bauddha-karma*)."
This is the body of the entire treatise in brief: the seven vajra-points.
